title: Unveiling carbonate dissolution in coastal sediments and its influence on seawater buffering capacity with δ13CDIC and 224Ra–228Th disequilibria
content:
Unveiling carbonate dissolution in coastal sediments and its influence on seawater buffering capacity with δ13CDIC and 224Ra–228Th disequilibria
Xinjie Ma, Xiangming Shi, Yingxu Wu, Xiangqi Yi, Biqi Zheng, and Di Qi
Biogeosciences, 23, 8559–8575, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8559-2026, 2026
We studied a coastal maricultural bay to reveal the role of sediment CaCO3 dissolution in benthic DIC effluxes and acidification mitigation. In combination of the applications of radioisotopes and stable carbon isotope, we addressed the mechanism that benthic disturbance lowered CaCO3 dissolution. Our study challenges the idea that organic degradation dominates sediment DIC production and presents the processes regulating the sediment CaCO3 dissolution.

title: Cyclone–Anticyclone Asymmetry of Submesoscale Coherent Vortices Near the Mid‐Atlantic Ridge
content:
Abstract
Submesoscale coherent vortices (SCVs) are long‐lived structures that influence the global distribution of heat and other tracers, but are not resolved in climate models. SCVs are commonly generated by the separation of currents from the topography, whereby the subsequent instability of vorticity filaments leads to the formation of coherent structures. While this process is symmetrical, most observed SCVs are anticyclonic. Here, we use a submesoscale‐permitting numerical simulation (GIGATL1) and a vortex identification and tracking algorithm based on the potential vorticity anomaly to study the SCV population near the Mid‐Atlantic Ridge (MAR) in the southern Atlantic Ocean on the 27.8 isopycnal surface (∼2,100 m depth). Our study area is located in the lower tropics, where the Coriolis parameter is small but finite, with a noticeable influence on vortex dynamics. We analyze the statistics of SCVs, including their intensity, size, lifetime, polarity, propagation speed, and direction. Our results indicate that cyclonic SCVs outnumber their anticyclonic counterparts and can be equally long‐lived, lasting up to several hundred days. However, the largest SCVs are predominantly anticyclonic. We also find that these large anticyclones are more likely to propagate away from the MAR than cyclonic vortices. We hypothesize that this polarity bias arises from the enhanced ability of anticyclones to merge and to remain coherent under adverse strain in the turbulent eddy field. Therefore, the emergence of these large and long‐lived anticyclones leads to a higher probability of being detected observationally than cyclones.

title: Molecular Plasticity Contributes to Thermal Resilience in Two Coastal Fish Species
content:
ABSTRACT
Understanding species' capacities to adjust to shifting thermal environments is crucial amidst current climate‐mediated ocean warming. Fish populations displaying high thermal plasticity can undergo molecular, metabolic and mitochondrial modifications in response to heat stress. In the context of heat stress, such acclimation provides a means to maintain functional biological processes through adjusting thermal performance breadth and provides a model to determine which physiological and genetic pathways will confer resilience to prolonged stress in different fish species. Here we combine measures of mitochondrial physiology and gene expression levels based on transcriptomic analysis to investigate thermal resilience and acclimation capacity of two closely related endemic triplefin species, the intertidal common triplefin (Forsterygion lapillum) and the estuarine triplefin (F. nigripenne). Both species evolved in thermally variable environments and were thus predicted to display resistance to heat stress. We observed enhanced mitochondrial function at higher temperatures, although only ATP production was significantly enhanced for both species. Different gene expression profiles were detected between warm and cool acclimated fish, with high interspecific variation in acclimatory responses across brain transcriptomes. Differential gene expression and Gene Ontology analyses highlighted an induction of stress response pathways and oxidoreductase activity in warm acclimated tissues, alongside a rearrangement of metabolic phases and modulation of neural activity in the brain. Our findings indicate thermal acclimation potential in both species, with plasticity in mitochondrial performance enhancing upper thermal tolerance and transcriptional evidence of thermal compensation and homeostatic adjustments under warming conditions. Overall, these results demonstrate robust mechanisms of resilience in coastal fish species that have evolved under climatically variable conditions and provide a low‐cost approach for mitochondrial assays, allowing more researchers to combine genomic and physiological data for future thermal studies.

title: Conserved Transcriptomic Heat Stress Response Signatures in Coral Recruits From Crosses of Thermally Distinct Broodstock
content:
ABSTRACT
Thermal history provenancing can guide the choice of parental broodstock for selective breeding of corals from distinct reefs and has been proposed as an intervention for enhancing climate resilience. However, the genetic and molecular mechanisms underlying resultant offspring responses to heat stress, particularly during early life stages, remain poorly understood. Here, we generated Acropora tersa larvae and recruits by crossing parental colonies from the historically warmer Martin Reef and cooler Davies Reef and assessed the effects of within‐ and between‐reef crosses on genetic diversity using single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) genotyping and transcriptional responses to heat stress using ribonucleic acid sequencing (RNA‐seq). Genome‐wide SNP analyses showed that broodstock from Martin and Davies Reefs were weakly differentiated (FST = 0.008) and exhibited comparable heterozygosity, as did all larval offspring groups. Host RNA‐seq analyses of surviving recruits exposed to heat stress (32°C for 36 days) revealed that the within‐ and between‐reef offspring groups (n = 2 and 1 respectively) activated conserved stress‐response pathways, with seven genotype‐independent heat‐responsive genes detected across all offspring groups. Differential expression and enrichment analyses showed induction of defence, protein homeostasis, intracellular transport, and metabolic processes alongside repression of growth‐ and signaling‐related functions, consistent with the Type A General Coral Stress Response. Taken together, these findings indicate that within‐ and between‐reef offspring generated to test thermal history provenancing exhibited broadly similar genetic diversity and weak differentiation alongside largely conserved host transcriptional responses to heat stress, including seven genotype‐independent heat‐responsive candidate genes.

title: Natural History Insights Decode the Genomic and Sensory Architecture of Niche Expansion in the Papilio xuthus
content:
ABSTRACT
Papilio xuthus provides an ideal system to investigate how subtropical insects track agricultural expansion into temperate regions, yet the genetic basis enabling this species to overcome combined cold and dry stresses while maintaining population connectivity remains poorly resolved. Here, we assemble a chromosome‐level reference genome and, using 117 individuals, reconstruct demographic history and build a population‐scale pan‐genome to trace the molecular correlates of niche expansion. Demographic analyses revealed historical changes in effective population size and gene flow among regional populations. Adaptive differentiation at the northern range margin exhibits a modular architecture: beyond canonical stress‐response genes, high‐latitude populations display pronounced signatures of selection near lipid/cuticle‐associated loci (e.g., FASN3) and genes implicated in thermosensation (e.g., Cirl), suggesting that shifts in cuticle‐associated metabolism and sensory signalling may have contributed to temperate establishment, potentially via desiccation resistance and environmental cue processing. In parallel, a glutathione S‐transferase locus exhibited a sex‐associated genetic signal, although its functional relationship with chemical communication remains to be validated. At the pan‐genome level, gene presence/absence variation (PAV) reveals pervasive co‐occurrence and mutual‐exclusivity patterns among metabolic genes, consistent with distributed functional redundancy as a potential buffer against environmental uncertainty. Together, these results outline a candidate genomic framework in which modular adaptation, sensory‐mediated selection and distributed metabolic redundancy jointly shape range expansion, offering insights into insect range shifts across contemporary environmental gradients.

title: Australian 2019–2020 megafire synthesis dataset
content:
Abstract
Wildfires are becoming more extensive and extreme in many parts of the world, and these changes to fire regimes are a threat to many plant and animal species. After the 2019–2020 Australian megafires, the most extensive forest wildfires globally at that time, multiple studies were funded to evaluate the impacts of the fires on biodiversity. We gathered 62 datasets, predominantly presence/absence or abundance data, collected (1) from the same sites before and after the fires, (2) from burnt and unburnt sites after the fires, or (3) using an unplanned before‐after‐control‐impact design. We curated these into a single dataset and used available data layers to generate consistent site‐level covariates across projects, including those related to location, fire history, ecosystems, climate and land use. The dataset has 809,831 rows, where each row records the response of a taxon on a site within a project, along with site covariates. The dataset includes plants, amphibians, birds, fish, insects, mammals, mollusks, and reptiles, with 48% of records from insect projects and 34% from bird projects. Approximately half of the records are from dry sclerophyll forests, with 15% from wet sclerophyll forest, 15% from alpine and subalpine ecosystems and the remainder from wetlands, rainforest, grasslands, and heathlands. The data are best used to seek emergent patterns of biodiversity responses to wildfire, considering how responses are affected by fire severity, site history, and landscape context. They may also contribute to understanding species‐level fire responses if future analysts can combine them with additional data from other fires. The Australian megafire synthesis dataset provides novel opportunities to explore new ways of analyzing data. This includes new approaches to meta‐analysis that can accommodate data where both positive and negative effects are expected and response direction cannot be accommodated a priori using covariates, as is typical of animal and plant responses to fire. The data are available for reuse under CC BY 4.0 licensing. Please cite this data paper and the data release on Figshare when reusing the dataset. Additionally, please seek collaboration from the lead author or second author if the lead author is unavailable; see Metadata S1: Class III.B.3 within Data S1 for additional details.

title: Migration and colder temperatures constrain microsporidian parasite outbreaks in zooplankton populations
content:
Abstract
Prey frequently encounter multiple natural enemies. An avoidance behavior in response to one natural enemy, such as diel vertical migration in response to a predator, may alter the conditions, including temperature, in which they encounter another natural enemy, such as a parasite. Many aspects of host–parasite interactions are influenced by temperature (host susceptibility, transmission, parasite burden, etc.), so daily temperature fluctuations associated with predator‐driven diel vertical migration could affect disease dynamics. Furthermore, disease outbreaks often occur seasonally. To test how temperature fluctuations associated with daily vertical migrations and seasonal declines in temperature affected disease outbreaks of the microsporidium Ordospora pajunii in Daphnia dentifera populations, we conducted a multi‐phase microcosm experiment lasting 84 days with temperatures chosen to reflect ecologically relevant conditions. We subsampled microcosms weekly for host density and infection prevalence. The first phase of the experiment focused on the effect of daily temperature fluctuations versus a constant temperature on infection prevalence. We found that infection prevalence and outbreak size decreased in the temperature fluctuation treatment, suggesting that diel vertical migration in response to high predation risk reduces parasitism. Epidemics also emerged later in the temperature fluctuation treatment. The second experimental phase was motivated by seasonal changes in temperature and tested the effects of declines in temperature on infection prevalence. Our experimental results showed that drops in temperature ended disease outbreaks. For microcosms starting at a constant temperature during the first phase and then experiencing the decline in temperature in the second phase, total host density rebounded as infection prevalence declined; this, plus lower densities in exposed treatments versus their unexposed controls, support a population‐level effect of this parasite on host density. Overall, our study experimentally tested the impacts of ecologically relevant temperature treatments related to migration and seasonality on infection prevalence, and our results suggest that temperature is a strong driver of disease for this host–parasite system.

title: Stridulation as a sound‐producing mechanism in skates
Identifying most likely migration paths by iso‐logging models
content:
Abstract
Iso‐logging has emerged as a powerful method for reconstructing animal migrations, complementing traditional bio‐logging approaches. Iso‐logging enables us to estimate the migration paths of individuals by comparing spatiotemporal isotope distribution maps (isoscapes) with chronological records of isotope ratios in organisms. However, methods for identifying the most likely migration path in iso‐logging models often overestimate path probabilities in steep isoscape areas or fail to account for multimodality of the posterior distribution. To address these challenges, we propose a novel method that applies a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) to migration paths generated from fitted iso‐logging models. Our simulation experiments revealed that ground‐truth migration paths are more effectively reproduced using the proposed method than using previous methods (smoother maximization and Viterbi methods). We applied the GMM method to skipjack tuna (Katsuwonus pelamis) data, demonstrating that it can explicitly incorporate uncertainty. Our findings suggest that the GMM method provides a robust and biologically plausible migration path, even for complex isoscapes.

title: Forecasts for 80% of wild populations and communities predict no change, and why
content:
Abstract
Broad‐scale shifts in biodiversity demand a deeper understanding of both historical and future time trends across the Tree of Life. Retrospective analyses indicate that some groups, such as birds, fishes, and insects, have experienced significant declines in recent decades. Broader investigations, on the other hand, reveal a more complex picture, with declines and increases roughly balanced. Here, we address the prospective task of statistically forecasting biodiversity trends and assessing the quality of forecasts based on available data. We analyzed 43,403 population‐level and 10,409 community‐level time series from localities across the globe and covering taxa across the Tree of Life. Using unobserved components models and model selection, we found that only 23.5% of wild populations exhibit forecasted time trends (with increasing and decreasing trends roughly equal), while 76.5% show a forecasted constant mean. For communities (temporal α‐ and β‐diversity), this figure rises to 84.0%. The high proportion of no‐change forecasts cannot simply be explained by the inadequacy of information in the time series because data quality (time series length, amount of missing and repeated values) explained only a small part of the variability in forecasts in comparison to biological characteristics of the species. In particular, we identified high variation in the rate of change as the most important predictor of a forecasted constant mean, and it scaled more strongly with real year‐to‐year change (process variance) than observation noise. Biological structure (taxonomy, life history traits, and locality) also contributed to the identification of trends, indicating that forecasts partly reflect biological differences among species and communities. In summary, despite the expectation of time trends in ecological time series data, parsimonious statistical models will very often forecast no change. A forecast of no change does not imply that trends are absent, but reflects the most parsimonious near‐term expectation given the data. Our results offer a tempered perspective that can help realistically inform stakeholders and the general public and guide the assessment of conservation action outcomes.

title: Climate‐associated reductions in water volume alter bottom‐up and top‐down processes in a fishless Amazonian pond
content:
Abstract
Forecasted reductions in dry‐season rainfall due to climate change are an ongoing concern in the eastern Amazon, where freshwater ecosystems are highly dependent on seasonal precipitation to sustain hydroperiod, habitat structure, and aquatic community assembly. Small, fishless freshwater ecosystems in the Amazon are particularly vulnerable to these changes, as precipitation is their primary source of water input. We tested how projected rainfall reductions (20% and 40%) for the eastern Amazon could affect ecosystem functioning and aquatic macroinvertebrate assemblages in a temporary pond, using a single‐factor in situ mesocosm experiment that encompassed the local historical rainfall regime (n = 7 per rainfall scenario). Twenty‐one experimental units were placed on the pond's surface, allowing for natural colonization by aquatic macroinvertebrates and maintaining a water temperature comparable to that of the pond. We manipulated the rainfall by adjusting the water volume inflow to the experimental units. Path analysis results indicated that reductions in water level, driven by projected changes in rainfall, increased primary production (β = −0.59, p < 0.01) and elevated dissolved CO2 concentrations at dawn (β = −0.98, p < 0.01). Reductions in water level had opposing effects on aquatic macroinvertebrate prey abundance, directly reducing it (β = 0.60, p < 0.001) but indirectly increasing it through enhanced primary production (β = −0.30, p < 0.001). On the other hand, these rainfall changes reduced the insects' pupal biomass (β = 0.35, p < 0.01), likely due to greater competition among prey larvae or increased predation pressure in a reduced habitat. Projected rainfall changes in the eastern Amazon are likely to rewire ecosystem functioning in small fishless ponds—amplifying primary production and prey abundance while ultimately suppressing insect pupal biomass and emergence—foretelling cascading impacts on food webs and aquatic‐terrestrial energy fluxes.

title: Statistical analysis of residue contact energies reveals folding determinants of ion channels
content:
by Svetlana I. Tarnovskaya, Boris S. Zhorov, Denis B. Tikhonov

Tetrameric and pseudo-tetrameric cationic channels, which are targeted by many drugs and toxins, play key roles in the cell physiology and pathophysiology. This diverse superfamily of P-loop channels includes but is not limited to voltage-gated potassium, sodium and calcium channels, TRP channels, and ionotropic glutamate receptors. In hundreds of crystal and cryoEM structures of P-loop channels, the general folding is rather similar but subfamily-specific structural details vary greatly. The latter underlie atomic mechanisms of ion selectivity, gating, sensitivity to drugs and toxins, and dysfunction of thousands disease-associated variants. Understanding these mechanisms may benefit from comparative analyses of multiple structures. Here, we propose a statistical method to reveal structural determinants of folding in related proteins, which involves clustering of residue-residue contact energies. We applied the method to a pH-gated potassium channel KcsA and a voltage-gated sodium channel NavAb. Twenty 3D-aligned experimental structures of each channel with universal residue labels were downloaded from database www.plic3da.com and Monte Carlo energy minimized. Residue contact energies clustered in the multidimensional space of contacts automatically discriminated open vs. closed states of KcsA, and wild-type vs. chimeric structures of NavAb. We found and analyzed specific contacts that underlie structural peculiarities. The proposed approach may help detecting folding peculiarities and their structural determinants between subfamilies of P-loop channels, within individual subfamilies, and could be adapted to other proteins.

title: Multi-model forecasting of respiratory disease activity in Germany during the 2024–2025 season
content:
by Johannes Bracher, Daniel Wolffram, Rodrigo Amaral Lind, Nils Bardeck, Micha Böhm, Seba Contreras, Philipp Dönges, Felix Günther, Rolf Kaiser, Jan van de Kassteele, Alexander Kuhlmann, Berit Lange, Barbora Němcová, Viola Priesemann, Ulrich Reinacher, Isti Rodiah, Frank Sandmann, the RESPINOW Study Group , Melanie Schienle

Respiratory diseases cause considerable morbidity in autumn and winter and are a priority in public health monitoring. In Germany, they are subject to a number of surveillance systems, including both pathogen-specific and syndromic indicators. In this paper we present a collaborative multi-target and multi-model real-time forecasting system rolled out during the 2024/25 season, and discuss differences to earlier efforts carried out during the COVID-19 pandemic. We focus on general practitioner consultations for acute respiratory infections (ARI) and hospitalizations for severe acute respiratory infections (SARI), where a total of eight models were run to generate nowcasts and forecasts. In addition, we consider confirmed cases of seasonal influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) where one forecasting model each was available. As all indicators were subject to retrospective revisions, forecasting models were combined with a nowcasting step. For the SARI and ARI indicators, we combined the available models into an ensemble and conducted detailed quantitative evaluations. Nowcasts overall showed convincing performance, even though for some models Christmas break effects led to an upward bias in early January. Forecasts were overall well-calibrated and most models outperformed simple benchmark models. When taking into account age-stratified targets, most observed performance differences to a persistence baseline were statistically significant. Anticipating the peak timing and magnitude, however, proved to be challenging, with many models predicting too flat curves with a too early turnaround (e.g., in late January rather than mid-February for SARI). The combined ensemble forecast was among the best-performing approaches, but unlike in previous related projects did not consistently outperform individual models. We conclude by discussing learnings on the organization of collaborative forecasting projects in post-COVID-19 times.

title: AlphaFold models of host-pathogen interactions elucidate the prevalence and structural modes of molecular mimicry
content:
by Delora Baptista, Lidia Gomez-Lucas, Jürgen Jänes, Nevan J. Krogan, Maria João Amorim, Ylva Ivarsson, Pedro Beltrao

Pathogens exploit host cellular machinery through protein-protein interactions (PPIs), often using molecular mimicry to hijack host cellular processes. While there have been thousands of host-pathogen PPIs determined to date, the lack of structural information for these impedes the study of the prevalence of molecular mimicry and convergent evolution of protein interaction interfaces. To address this, we benchmarked AlphaFold2 and 3 for prediction of structures of host-pathogen interactions observing that accurate models can be retrieved when ranking by modelling confidence, despite an overall low performance. We predicted structures for 6,782 pathogen-human PPIs yielding 803 models of higher confidence. Most pathogen proteins interacting with a common human protein are predicted to do so via the same interface, suggesting a high degree of convergent evolution of protein interaction interfaces. When comparing structural models from host-pathogen and host-host interactions, we observe that a majority of pathogen proteins are predicted to target existing human PPI interfaces. We categorized instances of mimicry into different modes, occurring at different frequencies: 1) via the same domain family (least common); 2) via a similar structural motif; and 3) via a similar linear peptide (most common). We selected examples of linear peptide interactions for binding assay testing, confirming 8 out of 12 predicted interfaces, including 3 viral linear peptide interactions. This validates AlphaFold’s ability to model some host-pathogen interactions and the mechanisms underlying molecular mimicry. This work showcases the value of large-scale structural modelling to study convergent evolution of host-pathogen interactions and how molecular mimicry may contribute to infection or host defense.

title: Large-scale analysis of AlphaFold structures reveals organism-specific physicochemical signatures
content:
by Michael J. Stam, Diego A. Oyarzún, Nadanai Laohakunakorn, Christopher W. Wood

Recent advancements in protein structure prediction methods have ushered in a new era of abundant and accurate structural data, providing opportunities to analyse proteins at a scale that has not been possible before. Here we performed a large-scale analysis of physicochemical properties across 373,779 confident AlphaFold structures. Our analysis revealed systematic variation between proteins from different organisms to such an extent that major features of the tree of life could be recovered from these data. Surprisingly, this relationship persisted even when we restricted our analysis to eukaryotic, cytosolic proteins and proteins from single AlphaFold Database Foldseek clusters. Given the strong functional constraints on protein chemistry, this finding is unexpected and suggests that protein structures have organism-specific physicochemical signatures, which might reveal evolutionary constraints imposed by the cellular environment and could have significant implications for the design and engineering of novel proteins.

title: When should adaptation arise from a polygenic response versus few large-effect changes?
content:
by William R. Milligan, Laura K. Hayward, Guy Sella

When will adaptation involve a few genetic changes of large effect versus a polygenic response? There are compelling reasons to expect polygenic adaptation to be common, yet direct evidence is lacking. Conversely, there are hundreds of examples of large-effect adaptations across species, but it is unclear whether they occur frequently within any given species. These different lines of evidence are hard to synthesize, in part due to the lack of theory that relates them. To address this gap, we frame the question in terms of the properties of an adaptive trait. We ask how the genetic basis of adaptation depends on key aspects of genetic variation in the trait and on the degree to which its selection pressures have changed. To this end, we consider a quantitative trait subject to stabilizing selection and model its response when a population at mutation–selection–drift balance experiences a sudden shift in the trait optimum. Using this model, we delimit how the contributions of large-effect and polygenic changes to adaptation depend on the genetics and ecology of adaptive traits, as well as on other salient factors. Thus, we formulate testable predictions for when different modes of adaptation are expected.

title: ATP8B1–TMEM30B flippase activity maintains stereocilia lipid asymmetry required for hearing
content: Sensory hair cells convert sound-induced vibrations into electrical signals through a process called mechano-electrical transduction (MET). While the protein components of the MET complex are well studied, increasing evidence indicates that MET channel properties are significantly modulated by the surrounding lipid bilayer. The asymmetric distribution of membrane lipids between the inner and outer membrane leaflets is well established to shape membrane mechanics. The recent discovery that the core MET components TMC1 and TMC2 also act as lipid scramblases suggests a direct role for membrane lipid asymmetry in the dynamic shaping of auditory transduction. Because scramblase activity of TMC1/2 disrupts lipid asymmetry, we hypothesized that an opposing flippase may be required to restore and maintain lipid asymmetry. Here, we identify the P4-ATPase ATP8B1 and its chaperone TMEM30B as selectively expressed in mouse outer hair cells (OHCs), enriched in stereocilia, and upregulated following the onset of MET and hearing. Loss of either protein results in elevated auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds, phosphatidylserine (PS) externalization, and rapid hair-cell degeneration, demonstrating that lipid homeostasis is crucial for OHC survival. Together, these findings establish ATP8B1 and TMEM30B as key regulators of membrane lipid asymmetry in sensory hair cells and establish TMEM30B as a novel deafness gene.

Modeling Host-Virus Interactions of Avian Corona Virus Reveals Cytokine Feedback as a driver of Strain-Specific Immune Response
content: The interplay between RNA viral dynamics and innate immunity remains poorly understood, mainly because RNA viruses trigger highly nonlinear cytokine responses. We address this using infectious bronchitis virus (IBV), a major poultry pathogen, as a model system. We developed a set of mathematical models and compared those with experimental data from two IBV strains infecting chicken macrophages.By model fitting and supervised Machine Learning we reveal that positive feedback in interferon- production is essential to reproduce the dynamics of one IBV strain but likely absent in the other. We further provide strain-specific estimations of key parameters such as infection rates, production and decay rates of virus and cytokine levels. Notably, different strains produced distinctive cytokine profiles, highlighting feedback as a key determinant of strain-specific immune signatures. Our results establish a quantitative framework for dissecting host-virus interactions and uncover cytokine feedback as a generic yet underappreciated feature in models of RNA virus kinetics.

title: Model evaluation metrics of Virtual Cell Challenge 2026
content: Virtual cell models aim to predict the effects of genetic, environmental, chemical and other perturbations in silico, reducing the dependency on complex and costly experiments. The Virtual Cell Challenge 2026 motivates the field toward this goal, tasking models with zero-shot prediction of the transcriptional responses to CRISPRi knockdowns in six human cell lines. The faithfulness of a model to the experiment is assessed by metrics that compare its predictions with the real data, and designing such metrics is not trivial. We developed the metrics of the 2026 Challenge around three principles: a metric should (i) reflect the biological information extracted from experiments, (ii) be calibrated on a repeat of the experiment, and (iii) resist shortcut solutions that raise the score without predicting the response. Here we present the six resulting metrics, the reasoning behind each of them, and their evaluations on the Challenge data. Two of the metrics compare the pseudobulk expression profiles of predicted and measured cells, while four assess the genes that respond to each perturbation, the central readout of a Perturb-seq experiment. The metrics are implemented in cell-eval2, an open-source Python package. On the Challenge data, all six metrics score a repeat of the experiment above the mean baseline, and the shortcut solutions that the metrics of the 2025 Challenge left open can no longer raise the score. The new metrics are therefore more robust than the previous ones.

title: NADH regulation shapes competing acetate flux responses in Escherichia coli: kinetic modelling of the tricarboxylic acid cycle and acetate production
content: Overflow metabolism occurs when cells divert carbon towards fermentative products despite oxygen availability. In rapidly growing Escherichia coli, it is primarily characterised by acetate secretion. An elevated NADH/NAD+ ratio has been proposed to contribute to this behaviour, but the mechanisms linking redox imbalance to acetate production remain unclear. We developed a kinetic model linking pyruvate metabolism, the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, and acetate formation to examine how cofactor availability and NADH-mediated enzyme regulation influence carbon partitioning. The model combines thermodynamically consistent reversible rate laws with NADH inhibition of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) and citrate synthase, and was calibrated using Bayesian inference to account for parameter uncertainty. We examined steady-state responses to changes in the target NADH/NAD+ ratio and the total NAD(H) pool size. With both inhibitory interactions included, lowering the target redox ratio increased acetate-producing flux, contrary to the experimentally observed reduction in acetate secretion. Substantially attenuating the effective NADH response of PDH recovered the experimental direction of this response. Additionally, to reproduce the observed reduction in acetate secretion following NAD(H)-pool expansion, a weak but non-zero PDH response was required. These findings suggest that cofactor-dependent kinetics and NADH-mediated regulation can jointly contribute to carbon redistribution between the TCA cycle and acetate production. Within this restricted model, whether a more reduced redox state promotes acetate-producing flux depends critically on the effective NADH sensitivity of PDH.

title: A new thermophysiological model unifying heat balance theory and physiological feedback control: Framework, heat defence functions, and individualisation
content: Coded in Julia using ModelingToolkit, we developed a new computational model (TeMP) that calculates the emergent physiological responses to heat with and without physical activity (PA). Rooted in established physical and physiological principles, we detail the model framework, major novelties, and sources of individual variation. TeMP uses physical heat-transfer and heat-balance concepts to determine the rate of whole-body heat storage (S) over a given exposure period, based on the dynamic relationship between S, tissue temperature, and thermoeffector function. Each thermoeffector (skin blood flow, sweating, and ventilation) operates on independent feedback loops and is modelled based on afferent inputs from central and peripheral/skin tissue temperatures. All thermoeffectors use simple piecewise equations to determine the onset threshold, slope, and maximum functions, removing the need for a central error signal pervasive in alternative models. Skin blood flow is bounded by individual fitness level and is attenuated by PA, whereas sweating is more sensitive during PA due to heightened sympathetic activity. Minute ventilation is also bounded by individual fitness and is sensitive to body temperature and PA intensity, capturing the disproportionate increase in breathing rate at the ventilatory threshold. Thermoeffector functions are individualised for intrinsic characteristics, including heat acclimatisation, age, menstrual cycle phase, skin grafting, sympathetic blockade (i.e., spinal cord lesion), and severe energy restriction (i.e., anorexia nervosa). Finally, heart and rectal temperature are modelled independently and follow similar divergent patterns shown in empirical studies at rest and during PA.

title: Microbiome complexity shapes host transcriptional networks across the ileum-liver axis
content:
The microbiome plays an increasingly recognised role in development, metabolism and immunity across all segments of the small and large intestine, as well as more distant organs such as the liver. In the terminal ileum - a key site of nutrient absorption - the presence of microbes dictates the development of secondary lymphoid structures (Peyers patches), mediates bile acid metabolism, and impacts absorption. In part, coordinated regulatory networks in the gut impact liver function and immunity through gut-liver connectivity and the movement of immune cells and bioactive small molecules that includes bile acids and other bacterial metabolites.

We aimed to examine the extent of microbiome involvement in ileal transcription, where subtle changes in co-expression networks can be tuned by microbiome diversity, composition and function. We surveyed ileal transcriptomes across mouse models which vary in microbiome complexity ranging from germ-free (GF, n = 15), the Oligo-Mouse-Microbiota-12 (MM12, n = 15), and specific pathogen free (SPF, n = 15).

title: Oral microbiome and DNA virome profiling in pigs reveals age-associated dynamics and extracellular recovery of Streptococcus suis-associated phage lineages
content: The pig oral cavity is a critical interface for microbial transmission and herd health monitoring, yet its microbiome and virome remains poorly characterised. We performed shotgun metagenomic sequencing of oral fluids from pigs across 15 commercial farms in Ireland, using paired bulk and virus-like particles (VLP) enrichment to capture comprehensive microbial and DNA virome diversity. Microbial communities shifted progressively with age, with early post-weaning animals enriched in environmental genera such as Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus and later stages dominated by lactic acid bacteria and anaerobes. Only 20.6% of vOTUs could be assigned to a known genus, with the most abundant being Astrithrvirus, which increased with age. Both microbiome and DNA virome exhibited predictable, coordinated age-associated succession with strong cross-domain coupling supported by virus-host networks. Functional profiling of the microbiome revealed that predicted carbohydrate substrates tracked the dietary transitions, while accessory viral functions partitioned by lifestyle and host. The early post-weaning stage was characterised by high abundance of viral integration and excision functions, as well as elevated resistome diversity that was almost exclusively of prokaryotic origin rather than viral. Importantly, 26 of the 25,223 vOTUs identified were predicted to target Streptococcus suis, providing the first metagenomic catalogue of such phages from pig oral environments. These findings expand our understanding of oral microbiome-virome dynamics and establish a framework for integrated microbiome and viromics approaches that could enable therapeutic phage discovery and inform microbiome-targeted interventions in pig production systems.

title: ViruDB: An Assay-Aware Molecular Database and Endpoint-Adaptive Multimodal Learning Framework for Antibiofilm, Quorum-Sensing Inhibition, and Antivirulence Research
content: Antibiofilm and quorum-sensing inhibitory molecules have become increasingly attractive candidates to complement traditional antibacterial approaches, but the experimental evidence ranges from heterogeneous assays, organisms, methods of activity measurement, and chemical representation. We created ViruDB, a molecular evidence resource that is assay-aware, and tested an endpoint-adaptive multimodal learning framework for quantitative activity prediction. Curated collection of 8765 experimental evidence records for 3563 unique molecules: 2,959 quantitative observations, of which 2,345 were antibiofilm, 569 were quorum-sensing inhibition [QSI], and 45 were antivirulence. Molecular representations included 217 2D descriptors from RDKit, 2,048-bit ECFP4 fingerprints, molecular graphs, and some information about the biological context. A molecule- and scaffold-disjoint primary partition was used, which resulted in 2,339 observations in the training set, 265 observations in the validation set and 355 observations in the independent test set. ViruFusion-TaskExpert-MTL and an endpoint specific combination with classical regressors were selected by validation. The final predictor yielded an RMSE value of 0.5460 and an R2 of 0.4816 on the antibiofilm activity dataset (n=286) and an RMSE value of 0.5744 and an R2 of 0.4082 on the QSI dataset (n=67) in the reported frozen independent evaluation. Exploratory anti-virulence regression (n=2 test observations). The results validate quantitative, endpoint based prioritization under chemical novelty and highlight the significance of assay provenance, assay leakage control and external biological assay validation.

title: Integrative structural biology of a giant marine virus reveals architectural and functional complexity beyond icosahedral symmetry
content: Knowledge of giant virus diversity has expanded rapidly; however, isolated representatives remain scarce, and few have been examined at high resolution. Here, we characterized haptophyte-infecting Prymnesium kappa virus RF02 (PkV-RF02) using integrative structural biology. The ~3 [A] resolution structure obtained by block-based cryo-electron microscopy reconstruction shows a pseudoT=219 icosahedral shell built from over 20 different proteins and approximately 10,000 polypeptides, a multi-layered stabilization network reinforced by 20,000 disulphide bridges, two penton variants evenly distributed in the capsid, and a protein channel crossing the internal membrane. Cross-linking mass spectrometry defines the intricate capsid-membrane-core interaction network, which includes a second major capsid protein, a third penton variant, and multiple biochemical functions packaged within the virion. Phospho- and glycoproteomics reveal widespread post-translational modifications, with approximately 50% of proteins phosphorylated and uncommon methyl-N-acetylated viosamine glycans. This study provides a comprehensive structural and interaction map that highlights organizational and functional innovations underlying giant virus assembly.

title: Infant formula composition is linked to distinct patterns of early gut colonization
content: Early-life nutrition shapes the gut microbiota and can have long-term health implications. While infant formula feeding is widespread, it remains unclear how variations in its nutritional components shape microbiome colonization. Here, we reconstructed 62 components across the 17 infant formulas consumed during the first three months of life in 240 exclusively formula-fed infants in the Lifelines-NEXT birth cohort. Formula composition varied widely and several micronutrients, including vitamin E and iodine, were associated with species richness. Components were also associated with species-level colonization patterns. Higher iron content was associated with reduced Bifidobacterium breve and Bifidobacterium bifidum and increased Clostridium paraputrificum. Follow-up in vitro growth assays on infant-derived stool isolates showed that Bifidobacterium breve and Bifidobacterium bifidum tolerated iron limitation, while C. paraputrificum did not, consistent with the association signals. These findings show that infant formulas are not all alike and differences in component concentration affect microbiome colonization in early-life.

title: DRP1 Orchestrates RNA Virus Permissiveness Through Metabolic Reprogramming Independent of Mitochondrial Dynamics
content: Viruses reprogram host metabolism and mitochondrial dynamics to support replication, yet how these processes govern viral permissiveness remains unclear. Using SARS-CoV-2 alongside other RNA viruses JEV, VSV, and HCV, we identify DRP1 as a central determinant of the virus-permissive cellular state beyond mitochondrial fission. While RNA viruses induce pronounced mitochondrial fragmentation linked to enhanced permissiveness, MFN1 conferred potent antiviral protection independent of type I interferon. Targeting DRP1-associated functions pharmacologically suppresses viral replication, accompanied by decreased glycolysis and enhanced oxidative metabolism. Remarkably, genetic depletion of DRP1 itself potently restricts viral replication in both wild-type and MFN1-deficient cells despite persistent mitochondrial fragmentation in the latter, demonstrating that MFN1 and mitochondrial elongation are dispensable for antiviral restriction. Together, these findings identify DRP1 as a key regulator of viral permissiveness operating beyond mitochondrial morphology. By uncoupling mitochondrial morphology from antiviral regulation, our study highlights DRP1-associated pathways as promising targets for host-directed antiviral strategies.

title: The identification of 110 novel Mycobacterium species within 57,974 UK Health Security Agency clinical samples
content: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTMs) are a large diverse group of opportunistic pathogens. The accurate identification of species within this genus is vital as pathogenicity, epidemiology, and treatment differ substantially between taxa. Whole-genome sequencing has improved taxonomic resolution, however current reference databases are likely incomplete. We analysed 53,170 high-quality mycobacterial genomes from 57,974 UK Health Security Agency samples collected between 2010 and 2025, a collection more than four times larger than the 12,726 mycobacterial genomes represented in GTDB release r232. High-quality isolates were assigned by average nucleotide identity (ANI) to recognised species within the Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB) using a 95% ANI threshold. Isolates that fell below this threshold were clustered using a minimal dominating set approach to identify genomically coherent groups consistent with being candidate novel species. Phylogenetic analysis of all Mycobacterium species was used to place the observed UK diversity in a global context and assess the ecological structure within the genus. Of the 850 Mycobacterial species-level reference genomes in GTDB, 204 GTDB references received at least one provisional assignment. We identified 586 (1.1%) high-quality isolates that could not be assigned to any GTDB species. Genomic clustering identified 110 additional candidate species-level references, expanding the reference set from 850 to 960 (12.9%). These candidate species were broadly distributed across the phylogeny. Within the Mycobacterium genus we found strong evidence that phylogenetic structure is associated with human (Fritz and Purvis D = 0.10, p<0.001) and environmental sources (D = 0.34, p<0.001). Together, existing and novel reference genomes resolved the UKHSA collection into 275 species-level clusters, of which 110 (40.0%) were not represented by existing GTDB references. Furthermore, source associations differed substantially between phylogenetic clades ({chi}{superscript 2} = 364 for human and {chi}{superscript 2} = 258 for environmental association; both p<0.001). Rarefaction analysis of the 275 species observed in UKHSA clinical samples did not plateau, with Chao1 estimation suggesting that additional sampling may reveal further novel species (Chao1 = 461). This study provides a comprehensive analysis of genomic NTM diversity within a large national surveillance collection. Our findings suggest that NTM diversity remains incompletely characterised, and supports the value of continued surveillance and curation to improve bacterial reference databases.

title: Cross-species dissemination of diverse plasmid lineages and mobile resistance modules shapes carbapenemase co-production in Chilean Enterobacterales
content: Carbapenemase co-production among Enterobacterales is an emerging clinical challenge, yet the relative contributions of clonal expansion, cross-species plasmid dissemination, and movement of resistance modules remain unclear. We integrated national surveillance data with plasmid-resolved hybrid genomes to investigate these processes in Chile. Among 414 isolates carrying at least two carbapenemase families referred during 2018-2024, annual numbers increased markedly alongside broader taxonomic and geographic representation. Thirty isolates were selected to span variation in year, species, region, and carbapenemase profile. These represented 11 species from six genera and contained 149 complete plasmids, 57 of which carried carbapenemase genes. Of 63 carbapenemase gene copies, 62 were plasmid-borne, and 55 of the 57 carbapenemase-carrying plasmids were predicted to be conjugative or mobilizable. Complementary plasmid typing, whole-sequence clustering, structural comparisons, and pan-plasmidome analysis identified three recurrent lineages: IncX3/blaNDM-7, IncN/blaKPC-2, and IncHI2A/blaVIM-1. Their occurrence across multiple species and sequence types supported cross-species dissemination, while numerous minor groups and singletons revealed a broader repertoire of plasmid architectures and accessory genes. Related backbones carried variable resistance regions, and equivalent class 1 integrons and transposon-associated platforms occurred in otherwise unrelated plasmids, indicating modular redistribution of carbapenemase genes. In selected isolates, co-resident plasmids created resistance redundancy, brought recurrent carbapenemase plasmid lineages together, or coupled resistance and virulence within the same cell. Thus, co-production did not arise through a single route: bacterial clones, plasmids shared across species, and mobile resistance modules each contributed to its emergence. Complete plasmid resolution is essential to distinguish these processes and track their dissemination.

title: Hyphosphere Hunting Grounds: Fungal Hyphae Guide a Protist Predator to its Bacterial Prey
content: Interactions between microeukaryotes mediated by prokaryotic intermediaries remain poorly understood. Here, we show that the hyphae of a plant pathogen guide bacterivorous protists into bacterial habitats, transforming a fungal dispersal route into a potential hunting ground. Although fungal hyphae are established dispersal corridors for bacteria, their capacity to guide individual protist cells remains largely unexplored. Time-lapse imaging of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. vasinfectum Race 4 revealed bacteria and the flagellate Paracercomonas sp. moving bidirectionally along hyphae with significant axial alignment, despite contrasting motility regimes: rapid, superdiffusive bacterial movement and slower, subdiffusive protist movement. The ciliate Paracolpoda steinii also exhibited directional alignment along an inert glass rod, demonstrating that physical geometry can bias protist movement independently of fungal-specific cues. Across successive generational culturing of hyphal-baits, protist communities converged reproducibly toward Paracolpoda dominance, whereas bacterial assembly was largely stochastic, revealing contrasting assembly processes within the same habitat. In a dual-microcosm assay, fungal bridges enabled bacteria and protists to cross a 3 mm air gap, while the presence of P. steinii reduced bacterial arrival approximately 8-fold, consistent with predator-associated filtering. Together, these findings extend the fungal-highway concept beyond microbial transport, identifying pathogenic fungal hyphae as multi-kingdom ecological corridors where physical guidance, community assembly and predator-associated effects on dispersal intersect.

title: Viral genetic variation programs divergent neuroimmune states during rabies infection
content: Viral burden does not necessarily predict the extent or composition of the host immune response, reflecting the complexity of virus - host interactions. Rabies virus (RABV) provides a powerful model to investigate this question because genetically distinct RABVs differ in replication, immune evasion, and neuroimmune activation. Here, we performed integrated temporal proteomic and spatial imaging analyses of recombinant RABV, including pathogenic, attenuated, and a newly generated interferon-sensitive variant with disrupted phosphoprotein antagonistic activity. Following intracerebral infection of mice, viruses established distinct neuroimmune states that diverged over time in antiviral signaling, complement activation, and immune response. Notably, the pathogenic field viruses rDogA and rFox both exhibited substantial viral accumulation, but elicited markedly different central nervous system (CNS) responses, with rDogA inducing limited host immune engagement, whereas rFox triggered early and broad antiviral, complement, and immune recruitment programs. Disruption of phosphoprotein-mediated interferon antagonism in rDogA enhanced interferon-stimulated gene expression and antiviral effectors, restricting viral accumulation without inducing broad neuroimmune remodeling. Conversely, the attenuated glycoprotein-modified rSAD GASGAS elicited strong complement activation and T cell recruitment with little detectable viral levels, revealing a highly immunogenic neuroimmune state. Spatial profiling further identified virus-dependent patterns of myeloid, astrocyte-associated, complement, and lymphocyte responses across brain regions. Together, these findings demonstrate how viral genetic background and its modulation of host antiviral responses shape divergent neuroimmune states in which viral accumulation, antiviral immunity, and CNS immune activation are differentially coordinated.

title: Identification of two novel lipoteichoic acid synthases essential for viability in Clostridioides difficile.
content: Lipoteichoic acids (LTAs) are major components of the Gram-positive bacterial cell envelope that contribute to cell morphology, division, and resistance to antimicrobial stress. Clostridioides difficile produces a type V LTA composed of repeating GlcNAc-GlcNAc-glyceric acid subunits anchored to the membrane by a glycolipid. Here, we identify two previously uncharacterized enzymes involved in C. difficile LTA synthesis: LtaB, which is required for LTA production and cell envelope integrity, and LtaA, which influences apparent LTA polymer length and partially compensates for reduced LtaB activity. Loss of LtaB causes growth and morphological defects, including aberrant septation and cell lysis, while LtaB depletion in the absence of LtaA is lethal. LtaA and LtaB contain two distinct domains: an LTA synthase-like domain and a glycosyltransferase (GT) C-like domain. Site-directed mutagenesis of conserved residues shows that the GT-C-like domain of LtaB is critical for both LTA synthesis and viability, whereas mutations in the LTA synthase-like domain have little effect on viability and only modest effects on LTA chain length. Production of several LtaB homologs from related species restored viability and, in some cases, LTA synthesis when a C. difficile {Delta}ltaA mutant was depleted of LtaB. These findings establish LtaA and LtaB as distinct but functionally overlapping enzymes required for type V LTA synthesis in C. difficile.

title: maoP impacts biofilm formation via csgD in Salmonella Typhimurium
content: Biofilm formation is a key process in the life cycle of most bacteria and involves the formation of multicellular aggregates, frequently attached to a surface. Despite extensive research into the complex regulatory pathways controlling this process, many aspects are not fully understood. Originally named for its role in chromosomal organisation, MaoP has previously been shown to have an important impact on biofilm formation in Escherichia coli and Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium. Here we continued to explore how MaoP impacts biofilm formation in S. Typhimurium 14028S. We show that deletion of maoP significantly reduces biofilm formation through reduced production of the biofilm matrix components curli and cellulose, and that this is associated with a reduction in transcript abundance of the central biofilm regulator csgD. Comparison of the transcriptomes of WT and maoP deletion strain biofilms confirmed the substantial impact of MaoP on csgD and its regulon. To further explore how MaoP impacts biofilm formation we conducted a biofilm evolution experiment to select for suppressor mutants that had restored curli production in a {Delta}maoP background. Sequencing of these mutants identified single nucleotide polymorphisms upstream of csgD that increased csgD transcript abundance and recovered biofilm formation to wild-type levels. In conclusion, our findings suggest a pathway where MaoP is involved in the regulation of biofilm formation through the control of the central biofilm regulator CsgD.

title: Fungal abundance and community composition associations with environmental and operational factors within and between manufacturing facilities.
content: Fungal communities in manufacturing environments remain understudied despite their potential implications for product quality and occupational health. Surface swabs collected from 19 footwear factories in Vietnam between 2023 and 2025 were used to assess culturable fungal counts, genus-level diversity and community composition. Associations with operational factors and environmental conditions, including temperature, relative humidity (RH), CO2 and PM10, were examined by separating environmental variation into within-factory and between-factory components. Fungal counts were associated with both operational and environmental factors, with object type showing the strongest operational association. Higher PM10 tended to be associated with lower surface fungal counts within factories, while factories with higher average CO2 also showed lower counts. Alternaria and Neurospora were positively associated with within-factory RH, and Aspergillus showed a negative between-factory association with CO2. Community composition varied most strongly among factories, while environmental associations were limited to the combined effects of between-factory conditions at the community level. Overall, environmental indicators showed clearer associations with culturable fungal burden and individual genera than with overall community composition, indicating that fungal counts and community structure capture distinct aspects of contamination in manufacturing environments.

title: The ACDC domains of AP2-O3 and FD3 contribute to protein interactions and ookinete development
content: The Apicomplexan AP2 (ApiAP2) family of transcription factors are key regulators of Plasmodium spp. parasite development. In addition to containing AP2 DNA-binding domains, nine ApiAP2 proteins also encode an apicomplexan-specific ACDC domain whose function remains largely unknown. Here, we dissect the biological role of the ACDC domain from two female-specific regulators, AP2-O3 and FD3, using the rodent malaria model Plasmodium yoelii and the human malaria parasite P. falciparum. In Plasmodium yoelii, deletion of the ACDC domain preserved AP2-O3 and FD3 protein presence and nuclear localization without significantly affecting asexual growth or gametocyte production. However, deletion of these domains impaired the gametocyte-to-ookinete transition, reducing ookinete conversion efficiency. Proteomic and biochemical studies indicate that the AP2-O3 ACDC domain interacts with FD3, while the FD3 ACDC domain preferentially associates with full-length FD3. Transcriptomic data showed that over 80% of transcripts that increased after FD3 ACDC deletion were also higher following AP2-O3 loss, with female gametocyte marker expression largely unchanged. In Plasmodium falciparum, removing the FD3 ACDC domain did not affect female lineage-specific expression of FD3, nuclear localization of FD3, or the asexual growth and gametocyte maturation of parasites. Leveraging the high sequence conservation of ACDC domains across the Plasmodium genus, we conducted structure-based virtual screening of 283 compounds targeting the predicted PfAP2-O3 and PfFD3 ACDC interaction interface. Seven compounds ranked among the top candidate inhibitors for both domains, and the highest-priority ligand for each domain was further evaluated by molecular dynamics simulations. Collectively, our findings support a role for ACDC domains in ApiAP2 protein interactions and identify candidate compounds for future experimental evaluation as potential transmission-blocking leads.

title: Resistance evolution in a single species reorganizes community responses across a resource-antibiotic landscape
content: Rapid evolution in one species can restructure ecological communities, but how its effects vary across environmental conditions remains poorly understood. Here we mapped the consequences of antibiotic resistance evolution in Aeromonas caviae across 64 combinations of resource availability and antibiotic stress in three- and 16-species bacterial communities. Resistance evolution changed where community-state boundaries were located, with boundaries lost or gained depending on resource availability. The same evolutionary change increased diversity in some environments but decreased it in others. Species success was partly explained by growth traits at zero or low antibiotic concentrations and by intrinsic resistance at inhibitory concentrations. Resistance evolution reversed dominance between the two dominant species and changed which traits mattered. It also altered other species' responses below inhibitory concentrations, mostly between closely related species. Our findings show that the consequences of evolution depend on environmental context but can be partly explained by species traits.

title: Forecasting sockeye salmon migration timing and mortality under thermal stress
content: Pacific salmon hold high ecological, cultural, and economical importance, but climate change is constraining their survival and reproductive success. Warming rivers are one of the foremost threats, with many populations increasingly facing temperatures approaching or exceeding their physiological limits. Understanding and predicting these negative impacts can inform mitigation or offsetting measures. We used a 12-year dataset of 13801 individually-tagged fish to develop a detailed model of Okanagan sockeye salmon migration based on functional relationships with river temperature and flow. Okanagan sockeye are the largest of the last two self-sustaining sockeye populations in the Columbia River basin. Their abundance increased dramatically over the last two decades amid significant rehabilitation efforts. However, Okanagan sockeye migrate into one of the species' warmest inhabited regions in North America and are highly vulnerable to climate change. Our model revealed temperature thresholds associated with migration cessation and mortality near 21{degrees}C and 25{degrees}C, respectively. These temperatures are common during the migration period in the Okanogan River, which sockeye must ascend to reach the spawning grounds. We used the estimated functional relationships to parameterize forward simulations of Okanagan sockeye migration from 2006-2025, spanning all years where water and fish passage data were available. These simulations accurately predicted migration timing and survival through the Okanogan River, providing a forecasting tool for Canadian fishery managers to regulate harvest in Osoyoos Lake. The simulations also showed elevated mortality rates during warm years and highlighted the perils associated with brief periods of river cooling, which apparently trigger large influxes of salmon migrants who may subsequently be exposed to extreme temperatures and experience high mortality rates. Our work highlights the potential for functional models to provide detailed and accurate reconstructions and forecasts of Pacific salmon migration success, which managers will require as river temperatures increasingly exceed salmon physiological limits.

title: Pollinator response diversity and turnover buffer pollination networks from habitat loss in human-modified landscapes
content: Agricultural intensification and habitat fragmentation are major drivers of biodiversity loss, yet their effects on ecological interaction networks remain elusive. In plant-pollinator systems, many species disappear with habitat transformation, but network responses remain inconsistent across studies. We hypothesize that this mismatch arises because local observations often overlook the response diversity of the regional species pools. To test this, we compared observed plant-pollinator networks along a land-use gradient with expectations under hypothetical closed-community simulations. Using data from 30 sites in the Donana Protected Area (southern Spain), we found that spatially connected communities maintained a stable network structure despite habitat loss. This stability was driven by pollinator response diversity, leading to marked species turnover across sites. In contrast, simulated closed communities showed reduced buffering capacity and predominantly negative trends in network metrics such as pollinator richness, total visits, and plant link density. Our results indicate that network stability can emerge from spatial connectivity rather than purely local processes.

title: ADTSIM2.0: An updated simulation of American dog tick (Dermacentor variabilis Acari: Ixodidae) population dynamics
content: The American dog tick, Dermacentor variabilis (Say), is found across most of the central and eastern portions of North America, and is a known vector of human and veterinary pathogens. While this tick has been found throughout this region for decades, there is still little understanding of the drivers for the highly variable annual densities. To explore the relative effects of hosts, environmental conditions, and tick biology, we introduce ADTSIM 2.0, an upgraded version of the ADTSIM model that simulates the lifecycle of D. variabilis. The model uses a weekly time step and follows the life stages (egg, larvae, nymph, and adult), questing behavior, host-seeking dynamics, and survival rates under varying environmental conditions. The model includes calculations for tick interactions with small- and medium-sized mammal hosts and factors in critical environmental influences such as temperature on tick development and questing activity. It addresses the effect of questing behavior on tick longevity, emphasizing the trade off between survival and host-seeking. The results show that accurate estimates of both host densities and weather information are critical to predict local D. variabilis densities. This model provides the first step to building a tool for public health information, offering a framework for assessing tick control measures and is adaptable to add tick-borne pathogen dynamics for both human and animal diseases.

title: Biotic interactions buffer the effects of biodiversity loss on ecosystem functioning
content: Biodiversity loss generally impairs functions on which nature and societies depend upon. Yet, it is difficult to predict under which conditions losing biodiversity has larger effects on functions such as primary production or carbon retention. We present a theory that demonstrates that biotic interactions mediate the intensity of these effects. In species interaction networks with many or strong trophic links, biodiversity loss has weaker effects on functioning because alternative interaction pathways allow surviving species to compensate for species loss. In contrast, in networks with fewer or weaker links, ecosystem functioning is very sensitive to the extinction of species. Here, we identify interaction erosion as a hidden dimension of the biodiversity crisis that provides a unifying explanation for functional consequences of biodiversity loss across ecological contexts.

title: Complementary roles among traits in community assembly processes of benthic foraminifera
content: Organismal traits play a distinct role in shaping community assembly, yet they have received comparatively little attention in marine communities. Here, we focus on living benthic foraminifera, a diverse group of marine protists that inhabit the seafloor. Benthic foraminifera are protists that have evolved different test-construction strategies: either by selecting and agglutinating grains from their surrounding environment or by biomineralization. In addition, taxa exhibit distinct morphologies have been hypothesized to reflect microhabitat partitioning within sediments. Here, we investigate their metacommunity patterns by analysing a co-occurrence network covering the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. We found that test-construction strategies significantly explained the structure of the network, whereas the general test shape did not. We hypothesize that test-construction strategy act as a broader-scale filter on the regional species pool, whereas morphological differences may be more closely related to local-scale coexistence and habitat partitioning. This study supports the idea that different organismal traits have different roles in the community assembly process.
