title: Integrating partner violence into HIV prevention and care for women
content:
Nature Reviews Microbiology, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41579-026-01371-2

Intimate partner violence can undermine women’s ability to access and safely use HIV prevention and treatment worldwide. HIV services and research must move beyond documenting violence to adopt confidential, flexible, trauma-informed care, trained first-line support and feasible referral pathways that protect biomedical effectiveness when women’s autonomy is constrained.

title: Isotope niches differ ontogenetically among key rocky reef predators
content:
Abstract
Predator niche partitioning occurs based on access to prey and feeding ability, which can change spatially and temporally, potentially becoming specialized with predator size. Isotopic niche analysis infers differences in dietary composition or niche, elucidating ecological links between sympatric predators and size effects. However, comparisons among temperate reef predators are scarce. In southeast (SE) Australia, New South Wales, the sympatric Palinurid Sagmariasus verreauxi (Eastern Rock Lobster), Sparid Chrysophyrus auratus (Snapper), and Wrasse Achoerodus viridis (Eastern Blue Groper) are considered large, key predators that structure benthic reef communities, yet their relative isotopic and trophic niches are unknown. To investigate, we used δ13C and δ15N muscle values from these species from seven regions > 1250 km of SE Australian coastline. Bayesian isotopic niche analysis showed varied regional niche size and overlap within species for Lobster (0.74–3.27‰2, 5.87–51.03%) and Snapper (0.87–3.30‰2, 10.57–68.45%) but not Blue Groper (1.36–1.50 ‰2, 17.67–23.74%), suggesting diets differ spatially. At large body sizes, niches were ~ 50% smaller for Lobster and Blue Groper but ~ 15% larger for Snapper, suggesting diets differ ontogenetically. Between species, Lobster niche was ~ 30% larger than fishes suggesting lobsters have more varied diets. Our results indicate that Lobster and Blue Groper follow general predator models using more specific resources with size, while Snapper may not. Overall, we found low niche overlap between these species indicating different overall niches despite Lobster, Snapper, and Blue Groper being sympatric rocky reef predators.

title: Coastal Eddies as vectors for connectivity during the summer in the Levantine Sea
content:
Coastal Eddies as vectors for connectivity during the summer in the Levantine Sea
Yotam Fadida, Tal Ozer, Tal Ben Ezra, Michael D. Krom, Anat Tsemel, Tatiana Margo Tsagaraki, Eli Biton, Yaron Toledo, and Yoav Lehahn
Ocean Sci., 22, 3835–3862, https://doi.org/10.5194/os-22-3835-2026, 2026
The Levantine Basin is ultra-oligotrophic with strong coastal–offshore gradients of pytoplankton and nutrients. In summer, stratification limits exchange, but coastal mesoscale eddies transport coastal biomass and nutrients offshore. Using satellite, glider, HF (high-frequency) radar, and in situ data, we show that these eddies carry distinct coastal signatures, making them key episodic drivers of cross-shore exchange.

title: Assessing SWOT performance to measure waves and sea level variability over Rangiroa atoll, French Polynesia
content:
Assessing SWOT performance to measure waves and sea level variability over Rangiroa atoll, French Polynesia
Ewen Cottour, Guillaume Dodet, Clémence Chupin, Laurent Testut, Taina Postec, Lisa Maillard, Swen Jullien, and Frédéric Bouchette
Ocean Sci., 22, 3811–3833, https://doi.org/10.5194/os-22-3811-2026, 2026
We studied how water levels and waves vary across Rangiroa, a low-lying atoll island of the Tuamotu archipelago. Using the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) satellite data and in situ measurements, we tested how well the satellite can track conditions in and around the lagoon. The satellite captured key patterns and improved estimates of water levels. Our results show that it can help monitor flooding risks and better understand how waves and tides affect vulnerable atoll islands.

title: Constraint-Based Pan-Cancer Metabolic Modeling Identifies Medium-Robust Biomarkers and Broad-Spectrum Anticancer Targets
content: Background: Cancer metabolic reprogramming varies across tumour types and nutrient environments, complicating the identification of robust metabolic biomarkers and therapeutic targets. We developed a constraint based pancancer framework to identify medium robust metabolic alterations and broadly effective candidate enzyme targets. Methods: Transcriptomic profiles from 33 TCGA cancer types were integrated with Recon3D to reconstruct cancer and healthy tissue specific genome scale metabolic models. Parsimonious multiobjective metabolite flow variability analysis was performed under five nutrient conditions to classify differential rates of metabolite synthesis, uptake, and secretion. An extended Anticancer Target Discovery framework incorporating fuzzy multiobjective optimization was employed to evaluate candidate enzyme perturbations based on cancer cell inhibition, ATP suppression, preservation of healthy tissue metabolism, and robustness across nutrient conditions. Findings: The models predicted recurrent increases in cardiolipin-related lipid synthesis and aromatic amino acid metabolism, enhanced uptake of essential amino acids and choline, and elevated lactate secretion across multiple cancer medium combinations. CRLS1 emerged as the most broadly effective predicted enzyme target, satisfying the treatment criteria across all 165 cancer medium combinations, whereas PGS1 and PTPMT1 exhibited broad but incomplete coverage. These findings highlight mitochondrial phospholipid metabolism as a potential shared vulnerability across cancer types and provide testable candidates for metabolomic and experimental validation.

title: Fixed-confidence identification of combination interventions in stochastic gene-network models, with a benchmark and an application to acute myeloid leukemia
content: Mechanistic gene-network models are widely used to rank drug-target combinations. Each ranking rests on a finite number of noisy simulations, yet the confidence that the top-ranked set is truly best in the model is rarely stated. We formulate intervention search in a stochastic network model as fixed-confidence best-arm identification and give certified search: empirical-Bernstein confidence sequences that return an {varepsilon}-optimal intervention set with probability at least 1 - 2{delta} under any sampling rule, with successive elimination and batch-parallel LUCB as sampling rules. We compare them with uniform sampling, successive halving, greedy forward selection, sequential LUCB and UGapE, and ablate each design choice, on four networks (a BeatAML-calibrated AML network and three published cancer Boolean models; 1,275 to 5,488 candidate sets) under a protocol written before the runs. All 21 certified benchmark runs returned an {varepsilon}-optimal set (exact one-sided 95% lower bound 86.7%), as did all 4,560 and 1,980 replayed runs of the comparisons, using 6.4 to 19.0 times fewer simulations than uniform sampling with the same guarantee. Elimination and the variance-adaptive radius account for most of the saving (2.1 to 34.1 and 1.3 to 3.9 times). Sequential LUCB and UGapE use fewer simulations in total but are slow on parallel hardware; batch-parallel LUCB, with as many candidates per round as workers, was at most 1% slower than successive elimination in any setting and up to 3.2 times faster, and on the three published networks used 2.0 to 3.1 times fewer simulations. Applied to AML, a search over eight drug classes returns ibrutinib + midostaurin + an ERK-inhibitor class (model score 0.710 against 0.448 untreated), which is the best set in all 15 related calibrations of the network and exceeds additive and Bliss-independence expectations.

title: Effects of Zika Virus Non-Structural Proteins on the Innate Antiviral Response.
content: Innate immune pathways are therapeutic targets of prime importance, both for antiviral and neurodegenerative therapies. The Zika virus is highly evolved to manipulate these same pathways so expertly that half of infections go unnoticed. While the direct inhibition of immune effectors by ZIKV nonstructural proteins is well characterized, second order effects on immune responsive cellular functions are less understood. We induced the innate antiviral response in human microglia like cells, perturbed that response using 6 ZIKV nonstructural genes, and resolve systems level effects using scRNA-seq and hdWGCNA. We recapitulate known ZIKV bioactivity and identify specific suppression of the PA28 immunoproteasome by NS2B, demonstrating how ZIKV can shape tissue level neuroinflammation.

title: Genome-Wide Association Study Identifies Novel Genetic Variants Linked to Meropenem Resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae
content: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae have emerged as an urgent public health threat in recent years. Infections caused by carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae in particular are associated with high rates of mortality, especially in immunocompromised patients. Substantial carbapenem resistance remains unexplained in K. pneumoniae even after accounting for known resistance genes. To uncover unknown mechanisms associated with meropenem resistance, we performed a genome-wide association study (GWAS) in 1,705 K. pneumoniae clinical isolates with previously determined resistance profiles to meropenem . We conducted the GWAS by using an elastic net regression to control for genome-wide linkage disequilibrium and combined it with a conditional linear mixed model to control for the presence of genes known to confer carbapenem resistance. The resulting set of variants predicted to be associated with meropenem resistance mapped to genes broadly related to the plasticity of the genome. We developed a visualization tool integrating GWAS results with phenotypic data and polymorphic site information to aid in hypothesis generation, which allowed us to prioritize novel genomic candidates. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the combined approach in detecting novel genomic variants associated with meropenem resistance in K. pneumoniae, while controlling for strong bacterial population structure, to advance our understanding of the genetic basis of carbapenem resistance.

title: Testing the impact of gut microbiome rewilding on the health of captive bumble bees
content: Animals and plants are often raised in captivity for food, companionship, conservation, or research purposes, a practice which typically reduces the diversity of their microbiomes. This loss of microbial diversity may in turn compromise host nutrition, pathogen resistance, and reproduction. Microbiome "rewilding"--restoring microbes present in the wild, but lost in captivity--has been proposed as a way to ameliorate these effects. However, it has only been tested in a handful of taxa. We evaluated the efficacy of microbiome rewilding in bumble bees (Bombus), a group of ecologically and agriculturally important pollinators. In captivity, bumble bees retain host-specialized "core" gut bacteria, but lack the diverse environmental bacteria commonly present in the gut of wild bees. We inoculated captive B. impatiens colonies with five species of environmental bacteria isolated from wild B. impatiens. Rewilding did not affect bee survival, reproduction, or nutrition (glycogen or lipid levels). We conducted a second experiment with Arsenophonus, the environmental bacterium exhibiting the highest colonization rate in captive bees, to test its role in resistance against an opportunistic bacterial pathogen. While inoculation with gut material from captive bees (which is dominated by core bacteria) completely protected hosts from pathogen infection, Arsenophonus inoculation had no effect. These findings demonstrate that microbiome rewilding is not always effective for sustaining the health of captive hosts.

title: Role-Aware Line-Graph Neural Networks for Interpretable Prediction of Pairwise Microbial Interactions
content: Predicting how microbial species affect each other's growth is a key challenge in microbial ecology. Using one of the largest available pairwise interaction datasets, comprising 20 soil bacteria co-cultured under 39 carbon conditions (15{,}074 directional measurements), we predicted whether one species has a positive or negative effect on the growth of another from monoculture growth, metabolic profiles, and phylogeny. Existing machine learning approaches treat each measurement as an independent sample, although experiments that share a species under the same condition are biologically related. We therefore represented the data as a role-aware line graph: each node is one directional measurement, and two nodes are connected when, under the same carbon condition, they share the same effector or the same affected species. This allows graph neural networks (GNNs) to pass information between related interactions. Our role-aware GAT-SAGE model achieved an F1-score of 81.38% for one-way prediction, outperforming the 73.79% previously reported for Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). For two-way interaction types (mutualism, competition, and parasitism), GAT-SAGE reached a macro F1-score of 60.34%. This exceeded the 55.71% of a neural network without graph structure but was below the 64.24% of XGBoost. Mutualism remained difficult to predict for all models. Layer-wise relevance propagation showed that one-way effects depend mainly on monoculture growth, whereas two-way interaction types depend more on the carbon environment. Encoding the dependency structure of interaction experiments thus adds information beyond the features of each measurement and provides interpretable insight into microbial interactions.

title: Identification of three apicoplast transporters with crucial roles in the malaria parasite life cycle
content: Malaria parasites depend on an intriguing endosymbiotic organelle, the apicoplast, for survival throughout the life cycle. The apicoplast is enclosed by four membranes and transport of metabolites across these membranes remains poorly understood. Thus far, only twelve (putative) membrane transport proteins have been confirmed to localize to the organelle. We report a crucial function in the apicoplast of three previously uncharacterized members of the major facilitator superfamily of transporters in Plasmodium falciparum. MCP1 and UMF are essential for asexual blood-stage parasites and could only be deleted in the presence of an alternative pathway for producing isopentenyl pyrophosphate. Deletion of either gene resulted in disruption of apicoplast morphology and loss of the organellar genome, suggesting that both are required for apicoplast housekeeping. In contrast, MCP2 was dispensable in the blood stages yet essential for parasite development in the mosquito. Oocysts in the mosquito midgut lacking MCP2 were significantly smaller than wild-type oocysts and produced no sporozoites, similar to when apicoplast fatty acid metabolism is disrupted. Differences in apicoplast morphology became apparent five days after infection, with MCP2-deficient oocyst apicoplasts displaying a less extended, sometimes fragmented, network with thinner branches. Taken together, we identified three novel apicoplast transporters, with MCP1 and UMF being essential for asexual blood-stage development by supporting apicoplast housekeeping, and MCP2 being crucial for parasite growth in mosquitoes, possibly by facilitating fatty acid metabolism.

title: The blue dragon nudibranch (Glaucus atlanticus) shifts to less venomous prey in the Mediterranean, with no evidence of defensive microbial symbionts
content: Glaucus atlanticus ("blue dragon"), is an aeolid nudibranch that acquires chemical defense through sequestration of nematocysts from its primary prey, the highly venomous Physalia physalis ("Portuguese man-of-war"). In August 2025 hundreds of G. atlanticus individuals appeared near Alicante (Spain), prompting temporary beach closures due to concerns about potential envenomation. This unusual occurrence, in a region where P. physalis is typically absent, raises questions about the trophic ecology and defensive strategies of this species under novel environmental conditions. Here, we used COI metabarcoding of gut to characterize the diet of G. atlanticus and combined it with 16S rRNA gene sequencing of cerata, gut, mucus, and central dorsal epidermis to assess potential microbial transfer from alternative prey that could contribute to the synthesis of defensive compounds, given that the role of microbes in chemical defense of aeolid nudibranchs was not assessed previously. We detected a trophic shift toward alternative cnidarian prey, including Pelagia noctiluca and Porpita porpita, which are not considered highly hazardous. Microbiome comparisons with P. porpita, as well as comparison of core microbiomes across different body parts of G. atlanticus, revealed no evidence of prey-derived transfer of mutualistic bacteria. Instead, G. atlanticus harbored distinct microbial communities dominated by environmentally widespread taxa, including potential opportunistic pathogens, with no indication of symbionts associated with defensive functions. Altogether, these findings indicate that, despite trophic flexibility, G. atlanticus may have limited capacity to maintain its defensive mechanisms in the absence of its primary prey.

title: Bulk RNA-seq data of an Adherent-Invasive Escherichia coli Strain ZVL and Its exuR-Knockout Mutant
content: Adherent-invasive Escherichia coli (AIEC) is a subtype of pathogenic E. coli associated with Crohn's disease. AIEC strains are characterized by the ability to adhere to and invade epithelial cells, survive and replicate within macrophages. Despite many years of research, the mechanisms of virulence and pathogenicity still remain not fully understood. Previous studies have shown that the virulence-associated phenotype of some isolates can be reversibly eliminated by changing the growth medium, specifically by switching from M9 minimal medium supplemented with propionate to M9 supplemented with glucose. This phenomenon was also observed in ZVL, an AIEC isolate from our laboratory collection. Since certain sugar acids, particularly hexuronates, have been shown to contribute to gut colonization by other bacterial pathogens, their role in AIEC has not been reported in the literature. Therefore, we aimed to investigate whether the hexuronate degradation pathway influences the adhesion and invasion properties of AIEC. To this end, we generated a CRISPR-based deletion mutant lacking exuR, which encodes a transcriptional repressor of the Ashwell pathway, and performed bulk RNA sequencing of wild-type ZVL and the exuR mutant. Both strains were grown in M9 minimal medium supplemented with either glucose or sodium propionate. Caco-2 cell assays were used to assess bacterial adhesion and invasion under both growth conditions. Our results suggest that deletion of exuR affects the invasion phenotype following growth in propionate-supplemented medium.

title: Pentose phosphate pathway metabolites are induced and required for nucleotides by latent Kaposi's Sarcoma infection of endothelial cells
content: Kaposi's Sarcoma Herpesvirus (KSHV) is the etiologic agent of Kaposi's Sarcoma (KS). As a herpesvirus, KSHV has both latent and lytic phases and is predominantly found in the latent phase in KS spindle cells, the main proliferating cell of KS tumors. KS spindle cells express markers of endothelium. We previously found that latent KSHV infection of endothelial cells dramatically alters host cell metabolism including increased glucose uptake and glycolysis. The Pentose Phosphate Pathway (PPP), a shunt from glycolysis is often increased in cancer cells and some lytic viral infections. Here we found that KSHV increases intermediates of the oxidative half of the PPP in tert-immortalized microvascular endothelial cells. Chemical inhibition or knockout of an enzyme in the oxidative half of the PPP demonstrated the essential nature of the PPP during latent infection of endothelial cells. However, inhibition of the non-oxidative half has no effect on latently infected cells. The oxidative half of the PPP produces a substrate for nucleotide synthesis, ribose-5-phosphate. We found that both purine and pyrimidine synthesis are necessary for survival of KSHV latently infected endothelial cells but not for mock infected cells. Addition of exogenous ribose recovers much of the cell death induced by inhibition of the PPP, indicating that the PPP appears to be required for nucleotide synthesis. The requirement of nucleotide synthesis in latently infected cells raises the possibility that the PPP and nucleotides are needed for more than rapid viral replication during viral infection.

title: An Oropouche virus N-glycosylation mutation in the Gc protein head domain is associated with transmissible infection in Anopheles mosquitoes
content: The Oropouche virus (OROV) outbreak in South America raises concern about spreading to new foci. Although biting midges are primary OROV vectors in the Americas, we tested whether mutation and bottleneck selection could enable mosquito transmission. We used OROV240023 cultured in C6/36 cells to orally infect mosquito species. Infectious virus was detected in Aedes aegypti and Anopheles gambiae saliva, with the latter demonstrating faster dissemination at 7 days post-infection. Direct sequencing of virus from mosquito saliva identified a consensus nonsynonymous K614N substitution and a potential N-glycosylation site in the Gc glycoprotein involved in cell attachment. Bi-glycosylation of Gc has been reported for orthobunyaviruses infecting An. gambiae in East Africa. The K614N variant was a minor population (0.8%) in the input mosaic virus population used to infect mosquitoes. Virus isolated from mosquito saliva and subsequent C6/36 culture showed selection of the K614N variant. While the mechanism needs further elucidation, these findings suggest mosquito infection is possible, especially where vector populations are at higher density. Furthermore, the data warrant reconsideration of OROV240023 transmission risk beyond the Americas.

title: Live vibratome sectioning of human lung and cerebral organoids for infection studies with respiratory and neurotropic viruses
content: We present a robust, reproducible protocol for generating live, thin (300 micrometer) vibratome sections from human lung organoids and human cerebral organoids. The method preserves the native three-dimensional tissue architecture, cellular heterogeneity, and viability for at least 7 days in culture, providing a physiologically relevant platform for investigating respiratory and neurotropic virus infection. Following infection, samples can be fixed, cryoprotected, and embedded for downstream cryosectioning. These organoid sections support efficient analyses of viral entry, replication, and host responses. The technique is readily compatible with immunofluorescence, RNA in situ hybridization, spatial transcriptomics, live-cell imaging, and a wide range of advanced molecular and cellular assays. On average, five sections can be obtained from a single organoid, substantially increasing experimental throughput while reducing costs and biological variability. By combining the physiological complexity of three-dimensional organoid systems with the accessibility and scalability of tissue-section-based assays, this platform bridges a critical gap in respiratory and neuronal disease modeling. The protocol provides a versatile and high-resolution framework for studying respiratory and neurotropic viral pathogenesis, host-pathogen interactions, and therapeutic interventions in human lung as well as brain tissue.

title: Inhibition of Bacteriophage Infection by Natural and Synthetic DNA-binding Compounds
content: The arms race between bacteria and phages involves a wide range of immune and anti-immune systems on both sides. One of the long-known mechanisms of antiphage defense involves DNA intercalators such as daunorubicin and its analogues. Daunorubicin was also shown to inhibit bacterial growth as well as eukaryotic cell division, underlying its use in chemotherapy. Other DNA intercalators and minor groove binding dyes are widely used for nucleic acids staining, but have not been studied for their effects on viral infection. Here, we systematically investigate the effects of known intercalator and DNA-binding agents, including daunorubicin and Hoechst derivatives, on phage infection in Escherichia coli. Using a diverse panel of phages with various replication mechanisms we identify phylogenetic groups sensitive to DNA-binding dyes and determined which stage of the viral life cycle was inhibited. Our data suggest that the active antiviral compounds block early steps of infection without cells killing, arguing against an abortive infection mechanism and lethal membrane permeabilization suggested recently. Together, our results expand the list of small molecules that affect phage infection and reveal DNA binders that inhibit viral DNA entry and/or replication without affecting cell physiology.

title: PAannotate: Software for Exploring Pseudomonas aeruginosa Gene-Expression Associations from Transcriptomic Data
content: With the proliferation of transcriptomic data for Pseudomonas aeruginosa there is a need for software programs able to efficiently analyze both individual transcriptomes as well as large, publicly available compendiums of arrays. PAannotate is an R package and native macOS application capable of analyzing the Whiteley Lab database of 5,821 transcriptomes from 470 BioProjects. In the application, researchers can use recorded metadata such as strain, medium or treatment to select experiments or genes associated with particular expression patterns. Alternatively, selecting one gene of interest, a user can find other, coordinately regulated genes that move together across many environments, mutants, and treatments. PAannotate also allows users to select groups of genes and to use Gene Ontology and KEGG annotations and enrichment analysis to see whether those genes are associated with particular biological functions more often than expected by chance, determine whether a particular perturbation produces a reproducible response across studies, or find public experiments resembling your own experiment. Researchers can build and customize heatmaps and association networks. In one project, we have examined the P. aeruginosa transcriptomic associations with the genes encoding the Pf prophage present in P. aeruginosa strain PAO1. We found a strong negative correlation between PA0724, a Pf4 gene, and ccmG, a bacterial gene involved in energy metabolism. We identified that much of this relationship was reflected by a difference in whether the bacteria were grown with acetate or glycerol as their carbon source. This finding illustrates how PAannotate helps researchers investigate P. aeruginosa gene correlations.

title: Salmonella MgtC promotes polymyxin B resistance and systemic infection by activating LpxO-mediated lipid A hydroxylation
content: The intracellular pathogen Salmonella Typhimurium modifies the lipid A moiety of lipopolysaccharide through various lipid A-modifying enzymes, thereby acquiring resistance to host cationic antimicrobial peptides during infection. While regulation of these enzymes at the transcription level has been extensively studied, however, regulation at the activity level remains poorly understood. Here, we show that the Salmonella virulence factor MgtC interacts with LpxO, an enzyme that hydroxylates the 3'-myristoyl chain of hexa-acylated lipid A, identified through bacterial two-hybrid screening for potential MgtC interaction partners. MgtC binding to LpxO promotes lipid A hydroxylation in a concentration-dependent manner, and the Leu287 residue in the C-terminal helix of LpxO is required for this interaction. Substitution of Leu287 with Ala reduces MgtC binding without affecting intrinsic hydroxylase activity, consequently impairing MgtC-enhanced lipid A hydroxylation. This substitution decreases resistance to both the antimicrobial peptide polymyxin B and human serum, and attenuates virulence in a mouse infection model. These findings suggest that Salmonella exploits MgtC to promote LpxO hydroxylation activity, thereby enhancing survival inside the host.

title: Distinct chaperones coordinate the type III secretion system assembly and effector secretion in Vibrio parahaemolyticus
content: Many Gram-negative bacterial pathogens rely on the type III secretion system (T3SS) to deliver virulence factors or effectors into host cells. In Vibrio parahaemolyticus, the leading cause of seafood-borne gastroenteritis, one of the two T3SSs, the T3SS2, is essential for intestinal colonization and infection in the human body. While many T3SS2 effectors have been extensively characterized, the chaperones that guide their biogenesis and coordinate assembly of the T3SS machinery remain poorly understood. Here, combining comparative transcriptomic and proteomic approaches with functional analyses, we reveal that four T3SS2 chaperones exert non-overlapping control over distinct clients for pathogenesis. We further show that these chaperones form a hierarchical, multi-layered checkpoint system that ensures the temporal order of secretion, coordinating injectisome assembly, pore formation, and effector deployment. Our findings provide a quantitative framework for understanding the regulation of T3SS2, demonstrating that discrete non-redundant chaperone-mediated assembly is conserved across diverse Gram-negative pathogens.

title: A microbiota-dependent fitness locus promotes intraspecies competition and cell envelope resilience in gut bacterium Phocaeicola vulgatus
content: A central question in gut microbial ecology is how dominant bacterial species establish and occupy their niches amid inter- and intraspecies competition. Phocaeicola vulgatus (Pvu) is a Gram-negative anaerobe and prevalent member of the human gut microbiome that can integrate into established gut communities without antibiotic pretreatment, yet mechanisms underlying this competitive success remain poorly understood. Using in vivo transposon insertion sequencing, we identified a three-gene locus that promotes Pvu intraspecies fitness in the presence of a complex microbiota but is dispensable in germ-free hosts. The locus encodes a predicted HU/IHF superfamily histone-like DNA-binding protein (DifH), a hypothetical lipid-binding protein (DifS), and a FadL-like outer-membrane transporter (DifT). In vitro genetic and transcriptomic analyses implicated these genes in cell envelope resilience. Chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing revealed that DifH binds a specific repetitive DNA motif at its own locus and a limited set of additional loci involved in metabolism, envelope biogenesis, and cellular defense. Together, these findings identify a previously unrecognized fitness locus that promotes cell envelope resilience, enables intraspecies competition, and supports Pvu persistence within complex gut microbial communities. More broadly, these results uncover mechanisms by which this dominant gut commensal secures its niche and suggests avenues to therapeutically modulate gut microbiota composition.

title: Phage integrons are vaults of privatized counterdefense genes
content: Integrons facilitate the adaptation of microbes by capturing beneficial gene cassettes, including antiphage defense systems, but their role in phage adaptation remains unclear. Here, we identify reversed integron cassette organization in phages, with 96% of reverse-oriented cassettes lacking detectable homologs in surveyed bacterial and plasmid integrons. Phage cassettes are enriched in counterdefenses, including viral sponge-like proteins. Despite these differences, representative phage and bacterial integron integrases recombine cassette attachment sites from either source; however, exchange between oppositely organized phage and bacterial integron arrays misorients incoming gene cassettes relative to the recipient integron's promoter, posing an expression barrier. These findings establish integrons as a shared engine of the phage-host arms race, capturing defenses in bacteria and counterdefenses in phages, while cassette orientation buffers exchange between the two adaptive repertoires.

title: Acquisition of phthiocerol dimycocerosates enabled extension of fused mycomembranes for cellular cording in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
content: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and its pathogenic relative Mycobacterium marinum form virulence-associated serpentine cords. Using live imaging and cryo-electron tomography, we show that cording involves extensive outer membrane enmeshment, such that adjacent cells share a single outer membrane. Importantly, analysis of diverse non-cording Mycobacteriales species, including the poorly virulent saprophyte M. smegmatis, reveals some membrane enmeshment in the clumped colonies. Our analyses suggest that cording was acquired in two evolutionary steps. First, acquisition of the mycolic acid-rich envelope in Mycobacteriales enabled daughter cell membranes to fuse during division, generating membrane-connected clonal clumps. Subsequent acquisition of the virulence-associated outer membrane lipids phthiocerol dimycocerosates (PDIM) facilitated more extensive membrane fusion into cords. We show that PDIM moves freely through the continuous shared outer membranes of cords. Moreover, these in vitro observations of fused membranes in M. marinum were seen during zebrafish infection. Thus, mycobacterial cording relies on an ancestral fusion-based community architecture that PDIM refined into virulence-promoting cords.

title: PL25_M23: Salt-enhanced antibacterial activity of a plasmid-encoded SLT-M23 hydrolase from Virgibacillus salarius against Gram-positive bacteria
content: Antimicrobial resistance has intensified interest in peptidoglycan hydrolases as potential alternatives to conventional antibiotics. However, halophilic and halotolerant bacteria remain underexplored sources of these enzymes. Here, we characterized PL25_M23, a predicted 370-amino-acid, dual-domain cell wall hydrolase encoded on a candidate closed circular plasmid from Virgibacillus salarius PL25, a halotolerant Gram-positive isolate. PL25_M23 combines an N-terminal Slt35/lysozyme-like glycoside hydrolase fold with a C-terminal Peptidase_M23 domain containing the canonical HxxxD and HxH Zn2+-binding motifs characteristic of the M23 family. Although its closest characterized homolog, CwlP, shares limited sequence identity with PL25_M23, AlphaFold2 modeling and domain-restricted structural superposition support a CwlP-like, two-domain architecture. The predicted protein surface is enriched in acidic residues, a compositional feature commonly reported in halophilic proteins. Recombinant PL25_M23 reduced the viable counts of seven Gram-positive strains representing four genera, including methicillin-sensitive and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, by approximately 1.9-3.8 log10 CFU/mL at a concentration of 100 &microg/mL within 60 min. EDTA treatment reduced PL25_M23 activity, whereas Zn2+ supplementation restored antibacterial activity, resulting in reductions of 1.4-3.6 log10 CFU/mL and indicating that its antibacterial activity is sensitive to metal chelation. The extent of bacterial killing increased with NaCl supplementation in all salt-tolerant test strains, with an increase of 1.4 log10 CFU/mL. Together, these findings identify PL25_M23 as a divergent, plasmid-encoded hydrolase with antibacterial activity against the Gram-positive strains tested and establish it as a candidate for further biochemical characterization and evaluation as an enzybiotic.

title: Lateral interactions between antiparallel filaments drive self-assembly of the FtsZ ring in bacterial cell division
content: The Z-ring is the organiser of cell division in most archaea and bacteria, arriving early at mid-cell and recruiting downstream proteins. While FtsZ protofilaments and their treadmilling dynamics are well understood, how FtsZ assembles into condensed Z-rings remains unknown. Here we determined the Escherichia coli in-cell electron cryotomography (cryo-ET) structure of FtsZ to 6.9 [A] resolution, showing antiparallel double filaments with the C-terminus facing the membrane. Electron cryomicroscopy (cryo-EM) of purified E. coli FtsZ showed these double filaments self-assemble. Cryo-ET of cells showed ordering of FtsZ doublets into bands, which we revealed is regulated by the disordered N-terminal residues. Structures of purified Bacillus subtilis and Thermotoga maritima FtsZ demonstrated that antiparallel lateral interactions are a conserved feature. We describe how self-assembly of the Z-ring occurs through two types of lateral interactions and propose a new role for FtsZ treadmilling in reorganising antiparallel lateral interactions during cell constriction.

title: An RNase bacterial toxin family cleaves the anticodon loop across diverse tRNA isotypes
content: Characterized bacterial tRNase toxins typically recognize individual tRNAs or restricted tRNA subsets. Here, we identify TloR (tRNA loop-targeting RNase), a tRNase with an unusually broad substrate range but a strong positional preference for exposed tRNA loops. Comparative genomic analyses identified TloR homologs across diverse bacterial lineages, where they are frequently embedded in conflict-associated loci. Structural modeling supports assignment of TloR to the recently described BECR-like superfamily, and mutational analyses identify conserved histidines required for toxicity and RNA cleavage. TloR cleaved tRNA and inhibited protein synthesis in a reconstituted translation system without detectable degradation of ribosomal RNA or plasmid DNA. Small-RNA sequencing showed that toxin-induced fragments arise from tRNAs decoding 19 of the 20 amino acids, with fragment endpoints strongly enriched near the anticodon loop. Purified TloR directly cleaved an unmodified tRNA substrate, predominantly within the anticodon loop. TloR therefore defines a family of BECR-like tRNases that combines broad tRNA recognition with positional preference for exposed tRNA loops. Together, these findings establish broad but positionally constrained tRNA cleavage as a distinct targeting strategy for antibacterial RNases.

title: Cold atmospheric plasma for improved sustainability and fish welfare in recirculating aquaculture systems
content: Decontamination of water is mandatory for the cultivation of aquatic species in recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS). Avoiding economic and ecological losses while ensuring safe conditions is important for the future introduction of new technologies. Therefore, the implementation of cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) within RAS was examined for the first time. For the integration of this technology two equal RAS were set up, one using CAP, the other one ultraviolet light (UV) for water decontamination. Experiments with Rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) were performed for three weeks to compare CAP with UV as reference. The CAP device was switched on intermittently for 8 hours daily (with intervals of 10 min on and 30 min off), while two UV lamps were turned on continuously throughout the entire time of 3 weeks, which required more energy. Fish development was tracked by fish weight and stress levels (cortisol measurements). Values for pH, conductivity, oxygen, temperature, microbial load, microbiome and ion composition were also monitored. Microbial loads for both setups were reduced by four orders of magnitude. The biodiversity of the microbiome of the two technologies was similar with a beta-diversity between 19 and 25. Deviations within each setup were low with the alpha-diversity ranging from 2.23-2.93 (CAP) and 2.42-2.79 (UV). The water monitoring revealed similar results for pH value, conductivity, oxygen and temperature. No differences for the cortisol measurements and also the fish weight were determined. The results demonstrate CAP as a competitive and more energy efficient alternative to UV benefiting fish welfare and development in a similar way. The equal development of fish and water parameters and low energy consumption compared to UV makes CAP an energy efficient tool, likewise enhancing fish welfare.

title: A cell-based screen identifies host-directed inhibitors and nutrient-conditional antimicrobials against intracellular S. flexneri dissemination
content: Multidrug-resistant S. flexneri is a World Health Organization priority pathogen for which no universally licensed vaccine is currently available. Most antimicrobial screening platforms involve planktonic bacteria replicating in nutrient-rich medium, a condition that does not reflect the intracellular niche in which S. flexneri replicates and spreads and systematically excludes compounds whose activity depends on the host environment. Here, we screened the 1,581 compounds of the National Cancer Institute Diversity Set VII for inhibitors of S. flexneri dissemination in human colonic HT-29 monolayers by high-content microscopy. By applying sequential counter-screens, we identified six hits falling into two mechanistically distinct classes. Four compounds restricted dissemination without detectable antibacterial activity or host toxicity at the concentrations used. NSC310113 and Thiosangivamycin (NSC105827) implicate host matrix metalloprotease activity in cell-to-cell spread and host CDK2 in epithelial cell invasion. Two additional compounds, NSC45641 and NSC367428, were antibacte-rial only under nutrient-limited conditions and would have been described as inactive by conventional screening. NSC45641 is an adenine analog imposing a purine limitation reversible by adenine supplementation. The uracil analog NSC367428, whose activity requires the bacterial uracil phosphoribosyltransferase Upp, is consistent with perturbation of pyrimidine metabolism in both minimal medium and in HT-29 cells. Together, these findings demonstrate that cell-based dissemination screening of the NCI Diversity Set VII identified two classes of inhibitors that would likely be missed by conventional nutrient-rich medium screening, highlighting nutrient-conditional antimicrobials as promising starting points for developing treatments against intracellular pathogens.

title: Evaluating WGS-based methods as an in silico replacement of phage typing for historical continuity and host association in  Salmonella Typhimurium
content: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (STm) poses a significant burden on public health worldwide. The Anderson phage typing scheme has historically supported surveillance, outbreak investigations and source attribution through associations between phage types and animal hosts. However, limitations inherent to the scheme have led to the gradual replacement of phage typing by whole-genome sequencing (WGS)-based methods. In this study, we applied statistical and machine learning approaches to 1,329 high-quality STm whole-genome sequences to compare phage typing with hierarchical clustering of core-genome multilocus sequence typing (HierCC) and the single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) address. We observed low congruence (< 0.60) between phage typing and WGS-based approaches. Nevertheless, a random forest model using WGS-based subtypes as features was able to predict all phage types with high specificity ([≥] 0.94) and at least 80% recall for 10 of the 24 analysed phage types. These included phage types of human and veterinary epidemiological importance, including DT193, DT104, DT2, DT40, DT56, DT9, and DT99. We then assessed whether WGS-based subtyping methods could replace the host-association feature of phage typing. At higher distance thresholds ([≥] 100) WGS-based subtyping methods were more informative of animal host species and displayed stronger host-associations than phage types for 11 of the 12 animal hosts, with significantly stronger associations for ducks, finches, and pigs (all p < 0.05). Thus, despite low congruence between phage types and WGS-based subtypes, our random forest model accurately predicted several epidemiologically important phage types, including those important to public health and veterinary surveillance, supporting its potential as an in silico alternative for those phage types. Finally, our findings suggest HierCC and SNP address methods can capture the host-association information historically derived from phage typing.

title: Stomatal conductance and net photosynthesis depend on nitrogen supply in drought-limited boreal forest
content: Transition from cold limitation to drought limitation due to climate change is widespread in boreal forests. We explored in the scope of the Dry Boreal Forest Long-Term Nitrogen Fertilization Experiment (DryBoreal-LTNE) in southern boreal forests of Mongolia how N supply interacts with tree water and C relations in forests of Larix sibirica, which are naturally drought-limited. Using branches of mature L. sibirica subjected to N fertilization of 6.25-25 kg N ha-1 a-1, we conducted CO2/H2O gas exchange measurements to examine how N availability interferes with the climatic control of stomatal conductance (gs) in L. sibirica. We tested the hypotheses that gs increases with increasing N availability and that this increase can be translated into increased net photosynthesis (A) in L. sibirica even under the dry continental climate of Mongolia. We could confirm the first hypothesis and found that A decreased at low fertilization (6.25 kg N ha-1 a-1) probably caused by increases in respiration due to metabolic costs of intensified N uptake. A attained the highest values at 12.5 kg N ha-1 a-1, but declined at the highest fertilization level of 25 kg N ha-1 a-1. Our results demonstrate that research on the drought tolerance of boreal forests under climate change should not only focus on changes in temperature, vapor pressure deficit, and precipitation, but should take N availability into account, especially as N availability is thought to decrease in remote boreal forests due to elevated atmospheric CO2 concentrations and can be locally influenced by land use.

title: Elephant poaching continues in northern Botswana: spatial patterns and policy implications
content: Illegal killing for ivory is the primary threat to the endangered African savanna elephant (Loxodonta africana). Botswana has the world's largest elephant population and experienced little poaching during the continent-wide poaching outbreak of the early 2000's. In 2018, however, evidence of widespread elephant poaching in Botswana began to appear, with an estimated 385 elephants poached. Here, we update the status of elephant poaching in northern Botswana with new data collected in 2023-2026. We also used spatial models to determine the factors associated with elephant poaching locations and to better understand poacher behavior. From late 2023 through mid-2026, we located 202 poached elephants in a ~10,000 km2 area of northern Botswana, north and east of the Okavango Delta and mostly west of Chobe National Park. All poached elephants were believed to be adult males. Using point process models, we found that, depending on the method used to locate carcasses, poaching locations were associated with greater distance from roads, higher slope, lower distance to military posts, higher Enhanced Vegetation Index in the dry season, and greater distance from the Namibia border than random points. The poaching outbreak documented in 2018 was not transient: illegal killing for ivory appears to have continued. Because poachers are targeting adult males, their numbers could become depleted in our study area, which has implications for elephant social behavior, legal elephant hunting, and ecotourism. We encourage the government of Botswana to take immediate action against poaching, including improving monitoring and strengthening transboundary cooperation.

title: Effective Fungal SynCom Assembly in Wheat Depends on Field Cooccurrence Patterns
content: Plant-associated microbial communities can improve plant resilience to stress and as such are a promising avenue for the future of agricultural technologies to improve crop health. Ideally, synthetic microbial communities (SynComs) are simplified versions of real-world communities that can recapitulate their function. However, SynCom applications often have variable results, we hypothesize is due to the gap between the ideal and realized community. Understanding the mechanisms that support effective SynCom assembly is a key step to unlocking this resource. We investigated how fungal assembly mechanisms (priority, diversity) impacted wheat response to drought. The SynComs contained a single pioneer fungus applied first, followed by low diversity (3 fungi) or high diversity (9 fungi) community inoculations. Plants were then grown under drought or well-watered conditions. We measured plant phenotypic traits and realized fungal community. Realized communities contained a small set of the inoculated SynCom taxa and were not impacted by any treatment. To understand this outcome, we asked if fungal traits or field distributions could predict fungal persistence. We found that persistent SynCom taxa were those that were highly connected hubs in the field network, suggesting that fungi that cooccur and interact with many taxa are more likely to succeed in SynCom applications. Initial and realized SynCom composition influenced plant performance but not in a systematic way. This study highlights the importance of considering natural microbial communities during SynCom design to increase establishment and success of fungal taxa to improve crop stress tolerance.

title: Tree roots drive POM losses and transient MAOM gains across AM and ECM stands
content: Roots play a central role in soil organic matter (SOM) formation, stabilization and decomposition, yet how roots and soil properties modulate these dynamics is poorly understood. We used ingrowth cores to investigate how roots influence particulate organic matter (POM) and mineral-associated organic matter (MAOM) in forest plots dominated by arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) and ectomycorrhizal (EcM) trees in Indiana (IN) and New York (NY), USA. Additionally, we amended a subset of cores with nutrients or water (controls) to examine how nutrient availability affects root-induced changes in POM and MAOM at a moderately N-limited site (IN) and a strongly N-limited site (NY). We tested three hypotheses: H1) root-induced changes in SOM fractions differ between tree-mycorrhizal types, with EcM roots promoting POM losses and AM roots enhancing MAOM gains, H2) increases in nutrient availability reduce POM loss and enhance MAOM formation, with the greatest changes occurring at the most N-limiting environments (NY), and H3) root-induced changes in POM and MAOM fluctuate over time, as initial gains in SOM are offset by SOM losses. We found partial support for H1 and H2 and modest support for H3. For H1, POM-C losses outpaced MAOM gains in EcM-dominated plots (as hypothesized) but both SOM fractions were mostly unchanged in AM-dominated plots. For H2, nitrogen addition did not increase POM-C (as hypothesized), but it did increase MAOM-C modestly in AM plots and EcM plots at the more N-limited (NY). In support of H3, MAOM gains observed after 24 months had generally diminished by 35 months. This was especially true for MAOM-N at the NY site which declined by 13.4%. Together, our results show that roots can simultaneously accelerate losses from POM and promote MAOM accumulation, and that tree-mycorrhizal type, environmental context and time modulate these effects. Additionally, our study suggests that short-term studies of root-SOM interactions may provide an incomplete view of soil C persistence drivers in forests, which can change dynamically over time.

title: Recent trends show a 20 year decline in global biological invasion rates
content: Biological invasions are costly economically and environmentally. Despite international agreements to mitigate invasions, we have limited understanding of recent trends - the last two decades of invasion records have been typically excluded from analyses, given potential discovery and reporting lags. We use simulations to show discovery lags do not cause spurious recent declines, but reporting lags can do so. Using global empirical patterns, we estimated reporting lags caused up to a 94% underestimation of recent invasion rates. After controlling for these lags, our model estimated that the invasion rate accelerated at 1.5%/yr between 1970 and 2003 up to a maximum of ~650 species/yr, but has since declined to ~150 species/yr in 2020. Thus, for global trends, our analyses indicate that observed empirical declines are likely real and that lags cannot explain them, potentially suggesting that invasion policies have been effective.

title: Bacterial community patterns of the Antarctic stalked jellyfish Haliclystus antarcticus and antimicrobial activity from a gut-associated Oceanisphaera ostreae isolate
content: Host-associated microbiomes are increasingly recognized as important components of cnidarian biology, yet their diversity and organization remain poorly understood in non-coral lineages, particularly in polar environments. Staurozoans, or stalked jellyfishes, are a small and understudied group of benthic medusozoans whose associated bacterial communities remain largely unexplored. Here, we used 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing to characterize bacterial communities associated with the Antarctic stalked jellyfish Haliclystus antarcticus collected from two coastal sites in the South Shetland Islands, Byers Bay and Risopatron. We examined three anatomical compartments (gut, peduncle, and tentacles) to investigate patterns of bacterial community diversity and composition. Gut samples exhibited the greatest variability in richness-based alpha diversity, whereas peduncle and tentacle samples displayed more constrained diversity profiles. Across compartments, 47 amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) were shared, indicating a recurrent bacterial component within the host-associated communities. Gut samples exhibited the strongest differential-abundance signal, while genera such as Polaribacter and Planktotalea were identified as indicators of tentacle-associated communities. In parallel, we isolated and characterized a gut-associated bacterium identified as Oceanisphaera ostreae. Genomic and metabolomic analyses revealed diverse biosynthetic potential and multiple metabolite-related features. Preliminary bioactivity screening indicated antibacterial activity against Staphylococcus aureus, with no cytotoxicity detected against HCT-116 cells under the tested conditions. Together, these results provide the first characterization of the H. antarcticus microbiome, demonstrating anatomical and geographic variation in bacterial communities and identifying a cultivable bacterial associate with potentially relevant metabolic capabilities.

title: Winter agricultural practices matter : rice stubble cover and landscape feature diversity increase abundance of wintering farmland birds in the Camargue
content: Agricultural intensification has led to a decline of farmland bird populations worldwide. Most studies have focused on the role of practices on birds during the breeding season but little is known about the role of practices during winter. Here, we study the effect of different types of winter field cover and landscape features on wintering birds in the rice production area of the Camargue (Rhone delta, France). We conducted bird surveys in 86 organic crop fields during winter. We hypothesized that the type of field cover (rice stubble, bare ground, winter wheat, grasslands), and the type of landscape features (hedegrows, grass strips and reed strips) have an effect on the abundance and species richness of wintering bird communities at field level. Moreover, we hypothesized that the diversity of field cover types and landscape features at the landscape level have a positive effect on the abundance and species richness of wintering bird communities, in line with the landscape complementation hypothesis. Results show that at the field level, rice stubble fields accommodate higher bird abundance that fields with other cover types. Moreover, we show that this pattern is driven by a few gregarious and granivorous wintering species while others preferred grasslands. At the landscape level, we show that the diversity of landscape features increased wintering bird abundance. We also show species-specific responses to different types of landscape features with hedgerows, reed strips and grass strips affecting diverse species at both field and landscape levels. Overall, our results suggest that rice stubble provide important winter habitats for declining granivorous species, while maintaining a heterogeneous mosaic of landscape features benefits wintering bird communities. Finally, we quantify species-specific response to the surface of different landscape features, a key step to build-up dedicated agri-environmental schemes.

title: Iterative prioritisation of upstream and downstream passage remediation for the critically endangered European eel (Anguilla anguilla) at pumping stations
content: The European eel (Anguilla anguilla) is critically endangered and subject to regulations requiring safe passage at migratory barriers and water intakes, but remediation must be prioritised to maximise conservation benefits. This study developed a novel prioritisation framework for both upstream and downstream eel passage remediation in heavily modified and fragmented pumped river systems. Catchment area (habitat quantity), distance from the tidal limit and numbers of migration barriers downstream were used as baseline geospatial metrics for bi-directional passage data. Following this, eel presence/absence data was incorporated to separate sites into upstream and downstream passage prioritisations, with site-specific hydrological connectivity (downstream) and fish community richness (upstream) data further refining rankings. Prioritisation rankings were compared iteratively to assess the influence of combining variables. Eel presence/absence data substantially altered downstream passage priorities relative to geospatial metrics alone, with a maximum rank change of 96 and eleven sites changing by 50 or more places. For downstream passage, hydrological connectivity resulted in significant re-ranking of priorities. For upstream passage, including fish species richness as an indicator for habitat quality caused notable re-ranking of sites compared with geospatial metrics alone. The results demonstrate that prioritisation based solely on geospatial metrics risks overlooking important sites and, consequently, directing resources towards areas with limited conservation potential. The iterative, flexible framework presented in this study provides a transparent and transferable approach for informing eel passage investment within heavily modified drainage systems and could be adapted to other landscapes where anguillid eels are conservation priorities.

title: Tracing urban diet shifts into guppy stoichiometry in Trinidadian streams
content: Urbanization can alter dietary stoichiometry by changing the elemental composition of food resources or the mixture of resources consumers assimilate. However, the relative contributions of resource elemental quality and assimilated diet composition to dietary stoichiometry, and whether the resulting dietary differences are reflected in consumer body stoichiometry, remain poorly understood, particularly in omnivores. We sampled adult female Trinidadian guppies (Poecilia reticulata) and their food resources from paired high-urbanization (HU) and low-urbanization (LU) sites in three rivers of Trinidad's Northern Range. Combining hierarchical Bayesian stable-isotope mixing models with resource %C, %N, and %P, we reconstructed dietary stoichiometry, partitioned differences between urbanization levels into contributions from diet composition and resource elemental quality, and compared these with somatic stoichiometry. Under the primary mixing model, aquatic invertebrates contributed less to estimated HU diets (33.7 percentage points lower; 95% credible interval [5.0, 60.1]), whereas detrital contributions tended to be higher. Resource elemental composition showed no consistent differences between urbanization levels. Under this model, reconstructed dietary N:P ratios were lower in HU guppies (by 59.2% [10.0, 81.8]), while C:N ratios tended to be higher, and C:P ratios tended to be lower. Changes in assimilated source mixtures contributed more strongly than resource elemental quality to C:N and N:P differences. All of these contrasts depended on the estimated trophic discrimination factors, weakening under fixed literature values, with the C:N contrast reversing under two of them and the detrital contrast varying in direction. Guppy somatic tissues partly tracked these dietary differences. HU guppies tended to have lower somatic C:P and N:P ratios, in the same direction as their diets but of smaller magnitude. Somatic C:N showed no clear difference, and the dietary C:N contrast was itself uncertain. Our findings suggest that urbanization reshapes guppy dietary stoichiometry mainly through shifts in which resources they assimilate, and that guppies only partially pass these shifts into their bodies. Understanding the stoichiometric consequences of environmental change therefore requires considering not only what resources contain, but also which resources consumers assimilate.

title: Can a woody encroaching species affect woodlands? Impacts of eastern redcedar (Juniperus virginiana) overdominance on woodland understories and management scenarios
content: Eastern redcedar (Juniperus virginiana L., Cupressaceae; ERC) is rapidly expanding throughout the Great Plains. However, its effects on woodlands, particularly in the Northern Great Plains, are poorly understood, even as managers invest substantially in its removal. To fill this gap, along an ERC dominance gradient in a forest inventory plot in Nebraska, we assessed: (1) how woodland understory plant communities and environmental conditions varied and (2) where and how ERC management had the greatest benefits. Spatial neighborhood analyses showed that greater ERC canopy reduced woody seedling abundance, species richness, and species diversity relative other canopy species. No canopy species, including ERC, was associated with variation in herbaceous species richness. ERC dominance was unrelated to soil moisture, pH, or organic matter, but was associated with reduced understory light, suggesting that dense ERC foliage limits seedling establishment. Simulated management scenarios predicted that continued encroachment would shift the woody understory community toward disturbance-tolerant shrubs and away from canopy tree species, likely altering forest structural and species diversity and reducing habitat quality. ERC removal at low to moderate encroachment levels and from steep canyon habitats was associated with the greatest increases in seedling abundance and species richness, but also small declines in diversity, with implications for the complex decisions of when, where, and how much of this native species to remove. Our results indicate that ERC encroachment has reduced woody species diversity, and left unchecked, will likely continue to do so, with potentially cascading effects on higher trophic levels, biotic interactions, and ecosystem services.

title: Genomic data need a stronger equity framework | Science
content: In June 2026, the US Fish and Wildlife Service signed a memorandum of understanding with Colossal Biosciences, a for-profit genetic engineering company, to biobank and sequence threatened and endangered species, including species foreign to the United States (1, 2). Commercial sequencing companies have also collaborated with academic researchers to publish whole-genome data from many nonhuman primate species (3), which have later been used to predict tolerated variation in the human genome (4). Whether held privately, as in the recent agreement, or released openly, as required for peer-reviewed journal articles, genomes of endangered wildlife accrue commercial value for years after any conservation use has ended, with no guaranteed returns to the communities or national institutions in the source countries that protect the species. To ensure equitable benefit sharing, the terms of genome commercialization should be set before sequence data are generated.

title: Biocrust Type Modulates Soil Multifunctionality and Microbial Responses to Long‐Term Nitrogen Addition
content:
Long‐term nitrogen addition primarily enhanced soil multifunctionality (SMF) in cyanobacterial and moss crusts. Microbial responses were non‐linear and diverged at N3, with reduced community cohesion in cyanobacterial crusts, fungal richness and network complexity in lichen crusts and microbial richness in moss crusts. The dominant SMF regulators were soil pH, microbial network complexity and direct nitrogen effects combined with microbial richness, respectively.

ABSTRACT
Biological soil crusts (BSCs) maintain soil multifunctionality (SMF) in drylands, yet their responses to nitrogen (N) deposition and underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We conducted a 13‐year field N‐addition experiment in the Gurbantunggut Desert, China, using cyanobacterial, lichen and moss crusts exposed to six N‐addition levels (0, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 3.0 g N m−2 yr−1; N0, N0.3, N0.5, N1, N1.5 and N3, respectively). N addition enhanced SMF most in moss crusts, whilst its positive effect in lichen crusts diminished at higher N levels. Microbial responses were type‐specific, particularly under N3. In cyanobacterial crusts, microbial richness remained stable whereas bacterial community cohesion declined; in lichen crusts, fungal richness and network complexity decreased; and in moss crusts, microbial richness declined whilst network complexity and community cohesion remained relatively stable. Dominant pathways regulating SMF also differed amongst BSC types. SMF was primarily associated with soil pH in cyanobacterial crusts and microbial network complexity in lichen crusts. In moss crusts, N addition directly promoted SMF, whilst microbial richness and network complexity exerted additional positive effects. Overall, BSC type shapes SMF responses and regulatory pathways under long‐term N enrichment, highlighting the importance of biocrust‐specific mechanisms for predicting dryland ecosystem responses to increasing N deposition.

title: Mechanistic Transition From Phosphate Adsorption to Precipitation on Dolomite Under Calco‐Carbonic Equilibrium: Implications for Microbial Phosphorus Cycling
content:
Dolomite‐mediated phosphate retention involves adsorption and precipitation, controlling carbonate effects on P availability and microbial nutrient acquisition. Distinguishing their controlling conditions is therefore essential for understanding phosphorus immobilization and its implications for microbial nutrient cycling. Phosphate immobilization by dolomite is governed by interacting concentration, reaction time and temperature and provides mechanistic insights into phosphate bioavailability.

ABSTRACT
Dolomite can remove phosphate (PO43−) through surface adsorption and mineral precipitation, two mechanisms that differ in phosphorus retention, stability and bioavailability. Distinguishing their controlling conditions is therefore essential for understanding phosphorus immobilization and its implications for microbial nutrient cycling. This study investigates the critical conditions governing the transition between these two processes under calco‐carbonic equilibrium by adjusting PO43− concentration, reaction time and temperature. Kinetic experiment results showed a clear concentration–time and temperature‐dependent shift in the dominant removal mechanism. At 25°C and 35°C, adsorption predominated at initial phosphate concentrations < 10 mg L−1 within 48 h, whereas precipitation became dominant at concentrations ≥ 20 mg L−1 after 24 h. At 15°C, adsorption remained predominant below 30 mg L−1 for 72 h, while precipitation emerged at concentrations ≥ 50 mg L−1 after 48 h. IR and XPS spectroscopy indicated progressive phosphate association with the dolomite surface under precipitation‐favourable conditions. SEM provided evidence of phosphate‐bearing precipitate formation. Removal kinetics and Freundlich model further identified concentration‐ and time‐dependent transition thresholds. These findings demonstrate that phosphate immobilization by dolomite is governed by interacting concentration, reaction time and temperature, and provide mechanistic insights into phosphate retention and stability and informing dolomite‐based remediation strategies.

title: Issue Information
Distance‐ and Direction‐Dependent Effects of Macroalgae on Early Epilithic Bacterial Assemblages and Coral Settlement Processes
content:
By conditioning tiles in situ, this study showed that macroalgae shape epilithic bacterial assemblages, with strong effects 1 cm downstream. Settlement of coral larvae coincided with distance‐ and flow‐dependent bacterial shifts and responded to specific bacterial taxa. Recruit survival was consistently reduced near and downstream of Dictyota bartayresiana. This study demonstrates how macroalgae can structure coral settlement at the centimetre‐scales, a process likely mediated by epilithic bacterial assemblages.

ABSTRACT
While the expansion of macroalgae on coral reefs is a global concern, the spatial scales and mechanisms through which macroalgae inhibit coral recruitment processes and the role of epilithic bacteria in coral settlement remain inadequately understood. Using tiles preconditioned at three distances of two algal species in both up and down‐current directions, we show that macroalgae shape early epilithic bacterial assemblages, with strong effects 1 cm downstream of both algae. When exposing the tiles to larvae of two coral species in ex situ settlement experiments, the coral Acropora pulchra showed reduced larval settlement on cryptic surfaces of tiles conditioned 1 cm up and downstream of the alga Dictyota bartayresiana, whereas the coral Pocillopora acuta showed the opposite pattern. Specific bacterial taxa within the families Bdellovibrionaceae, Pirellulaceae, Flavobacteriaceae and Rhodobacteraceae were associated with P. acuta settlement with differences across algal species. When tiles with coral spat were returned to their initial positions on the reef, spat survival was consistently reduced closer to, and particularly 1 cm downstream of, D. bartayresiana. These results demonstrate that macroalgae influence coral settlement and post‐settlement survival at centimetre scales through distance‐ and flow‐dependent effects and indicate that these effects may be mediated by epilithic bacterial assemblages.

title: Experimental evidence that organo-mineral interactions regulate dissolved organic matter composition and lability across permafrost landscapes of northwestern Canada
content:
Experimental evidence that organo-mineral interactions regulate dissolved organic matter composition and lability across permafrost landscapes of northwestern Canada
Gabrielle K. F. Hatten, Steven V. Kokelj, Sophie Opfergelt, Duane G. Froese, Alejandro Alvarez, Joseph M. Young, and Suzanne E. Tank
Biogeosciences, 23, 8617–8638, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8617-2026, 2026
Sorption of organic matter (OM) to recently thawed permafrost sediments can critically alter OM fate. Using 32 sediment samples from a suite of diverse permafrost landscapes, we show that organo-mineral interactions “sort” dissolved OM, enriching the aquatic matrix in labile compounds and increasing biodegradation via shifts in OM composition and nutrient release. Sorption potential varied across and within regions and was tied to sediment characteristics, dictated by landscape history.

title: Wildfire‐Derived Molecular Tracers Reveal Post‐Depositional Transformation of Pyrogenic Signatures in Wildfire‐Impacted Boreal Soils Across a Post‐Fire Chronosequence
content:
Abstract
Wildfire is a critical ecological process in boreal ecosystems and the dominant source of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in boreal environments. However, the long‐term preservation and transformation of such compounds within boreal soils remain poorly constrained. Here, we investigated parent, alkylated (alk‐) and furan‐infused oxygenated (O‐) PAHs across litter, organic and mineral soil horizons collected along a north‐south transect in Western Canada spanning a post‐fire chronosequence from 1989 to 2022. Total parent PAHs concentrations decreased systematically with depth, with litter samples exceeding organic and mineral horizon samples. Likewise, the concentrations of alk‐ and O‐PAHs were highest in litter samples, followed by organic and mineral horizon samples. Litter samples preserved the most compositionally complete pyrogenic signature, including diagnostic low‐molecular‐weight (LMW) PAHs, which were absent from deeper horizons. Retene dominated the alk‐PAHs fraction, indicating combustion of resin‐rich conifers, while dibenzofuran dominated O‐PAHs, consistent with biomass‐derived furanic products and subsequent post‐depositional processing. The low to high‐molecular‐weight PAHs ratio declined from litter (0.65 ± 0.10) to mineral horizons (0.11 ± 0.12), demonstrating the preferential attenuation of LMW‐PAHs. Enrichment factor analysis revealed compound‐class‐specific vertical partitioning controlled by hydrophobicity, pyrogenic carbon retention and pedogenic transformation. Selected PAHs isomeric‐ratios showed coherent pyrogenic signatures for litter samples but increasingly altered signatures in deeper horizons. HYSPLIT trajectories, aerosol optical depth and precipitation climatology further revealed possible regional climatic controls on atmospheric PAHs deposition. Our findings demonstrate that boreal soils function as a dynamic geochemical archive integrating wildfire emissions, atmospheric redistribution and long‐term post‐depositional transformation, with important implications for interpreting PAHs‐based paleofire proxies in environmental archives.

title: Meltwater Pathways Control the Effect of Subglacial Discharge on Sub‐Shelf Melting
content:
Abstract
Increased ocean‐driven ice‐shelf melting is a major contributor to mass loss from the Antarctic Ice Sheet. When subglacial freshwater discharge (SFD) enters ice‐shelf cavities, it enhances local buoyancy and accelerates meltwater flow beneath ice shelves and increases melt rates. We adapt the meltwater‐layer model LADDIE to include SFD and show that it quantitatively reproduces the melt sensitivity to SFD of the more complex three‐dimensional ocean model MITgcm for the Thwaites ice shelf cavity. We then use the adapted LADDIE model to investigate the sensitivity of SFD‐enhanced melting to (a) background ocean conditions and (b) SFD release location. We focus on the Thwaites and Pine Island ice shelves, which experience substantial ocean‐driven melting and both receive SFD in their cavities, but have distinctly different geometries. Our results show that SFD‐enhanced melting is relatively insensitive to ocean conditions representing present‐day variability and projected 50‐year warming. Instead, it is strongly controlled by the SFD release location. Ice‐shelf geometry controls whether meltwater flow from the release site converges or diverges laterally across the ice base, shaping the magnitude and spatial pattern of additional melting. Divergent flow spreads buoyancy forcing over a larger area, producing stronger integrated melt enhancement than convergent flow, where forcing is concentrated. In the convergent‐flow case, however, local increases in melting are higher, which may be important for the ice‐dynamical response. These findings underscore the importance of accurately constraining the SFD release locations and resolving meltwater pathways when representing SFD‐driven melting in ice‐sheet projections.
