title: Anaerobic Oxidation of Methane Couples Sulfide Generation Promotes Mercury Sequestration in Gas Hydrate Sediments
content:
Abstract
The deep sea constitutes the largest marine mercury (Hg) reservoir on Earth, with gas hydrate‐cold seep systems emerging as critical, yet poorly constrained, hotspots for Hg cycling. While these systems host intense microbial activity and sulfide production that drive Hg methylation, demethylation and sequestration, the specific migration, transformation, and speciation of Hg within gas hydrate sediments remain elusive. Here, we present a systematic geochemical analysis of W19 drill core during the GMGS3 expedition from the Shenhu area, South China Sea to address this gap. The results reveal pronounced Hg enrichment (up to 122.0 ng/g) at the fossil sulfate‐methane transition (SMT), tightly coupled with enrichments of sulfur and sulfophilic trace elements (e.g., Mo, Sb, and As). Sequential leaching demonstrates that Hg is predominantly sequestered as highly insoluble Hg‐sulfide precipitation derived from anaerobic oxidation of methane (AOM), with this authigenic sulfide fraction accounting for up to 94.1% of the total Hg pool. Additionally, elevated Fe/Al ratio, Hg content, and Mo enrichment factor (MoEF) indicate Hg release driven by the reductive dissolution of iron‐manganese oxyhydroxides. Crucially, this sulfide‐mediated sequestration effectively arrests Hg(II) migration, and may simultaneously suppress microbial mercury methylation, identifying gas hydrate‐cold seep systems as previously unrecognized geochemical Hg barriers in the deep sea. These finding fundamentally advances the understanding of geogenic Hg fate in marine sediments and anticipating how climate driven destabilization of hydrate reservoirs may alter deep‐sea Hg mobilization pathways under future warming scenarios.

title: Migration Load, Competition and Metabolic Trade‐Offs Shape Spatial Divergence Through Eco‐Evolutionary Dynamics
content:
ABSTRACT
Evolutionary models predict that trade‐offs related to resource utilization promote local specialization and diversification in spatially heterogeneous environments. However, diversification is also influenced by ecological feedback mechanisms—such as frequency‐dependent resource use—and their interaction with migration. To investigate how spatial variation affects diversification, we conducted an evolution experiment exposing populations of Lactococcus cremoris to divergent selection on two carbon sources: fructose and galactose. Using a continuous culture system, we partitioned these resources into two isolated patches (allopatry), two patches with constant migration between them (parapatry) and one fully mixed patch (sympatry). Resource specialization and subsequent phenotypic diversification evolved in all treatments, revealing a metabolic trade‐off between fructose and galactose utilization. Compared to treatments without migration, spatial variation produced a distinctive temporal pattern: migration initially delayed specialization on galactose but later accelerated it. This temporal pattern emerged from eco‐evolutionary feedbacks operating through two mechanisms: (i) early in the experiment, higher population density in the better‐suited fructose patch increased the influx of maladapted immigrants into the galactose patch, slowing local adaptation; however, (ii) as strains adapted locally to galactose, population density increased in the galactose patch and density asymmetries weakened. Simultaneously, the competitive ability of immigrants declined as residents became increasingly specialized in their local resources, progressively reducing the effective migration rate and allowing accelerated divergence. Our experiment demonstrates how the likelihood and tempo of spatial divergence depend on the evolvability of phenotypic trade‐offs and their dynamic interaction with migration load and population density.

title: Do Co‐Occurring Species Share Common Drivers of Connectivity? Insights From a Multi‐Species Landscape Genetic Analysis of Alpine Ecosystems
content:
ABSTRACT
Landscape permeability can influence the maintenance of genetic variation and the capacity of populations to respond to environmental change. However, whether co‐occurring species respond similarly to landscape heterogeneity remains poorly understood, particularly on environmentally heterogeneous oceanic islands. We evaluated genetic structure, landscape‐mediated connectivity, and projected habitat change for eight alpine plant species (seven endemic and one native) across the two highest‐elevation mountain systems of the Canary Islands: Teide National Park (Tenerife) and Caldera de Taburiente National Park (La Palma). We characterized environmental differentiation, quantified fine‐scale spatial genetic structure (Sp), and tested resistance hypotheses based on topo‐climatic, wind, and ecological niche model (ENM)‐derived predictors using ResistanceGA. Environmental ordination revealed inter‐island differentiation driven primarily by precipitation, whereas within‐island variation was associated mainly with temperature and topography. Contrary to expectations, Sp did not differ between short‐ and long‐distance seed dispersers, suggesting that seed‐dispersal syndrome alone may not reliably predict fine‐scale genetic structure. Resistance patterns were strongly species‐ and island‐dependent, although wind and topography repeatedly emerged among the best‐supported predictors. Future ENM projections indicated substantial losses of suitable habitat for most species, together with upslope shifts and particularly severe contractions on La Palma. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of accounting for species‐specific responses when planning connectivity across multispecies high‐mountain systems, particularly as suitable habitats contract and shift under climate change.

title: Natural pH Gradients Uncover Genomic and Transcriptomic Bases of Ocean Acidification Adaptation in the Marine Calcifier Paracentrotus lividus
content:
ABSTRACT
Ocean acidification (OA) is reshaping marine environments at an unprecedented pace, yet whether and how populations can evolve tolerance—and through which molecular mechanisms—remains a central open question for predicting species persistence under future climate scenarios. Natural CO2 vent systems, where pH is chronically reduced by volcanic emissions, provide unique opportunities to study adaptive divergence under conditions that mirror future oceans. Here, we integrate population genomics, transcriptomics, and morphological data to dissect the molecular bases of adaptation to OA in Paracentrotus lividus, a marine calcifier inhabiting the Fuencaliente CO2 vent system (La Palma, Canary Islands). Using ddRADseq on 95 individuals sampled along a natural pH gradient (7.5–8.1), we identified 27,542 SNPs, including 232 candidate loci under pH‐driven selection. Despite negligible differentiation at neutral loci—confirming high gene flow—loci under selection revealed strong divergence across the gradient, with enrichment in genes related to ion transport, biomineralization, and acid–base regulation. Transcriptomic analyses revealed pronounced constitutive divergence between ambient (pH 8.1) and vent (pH 7.5) populations, consistent with long‐term molecular reprogramming of metabolic pathways. In contrast, acute experimental exposure of ambient individuals to low pH triggered a modest stress response centered on protein stabilization that did not converge with the constitutive transcriptional profile of vent‐adapted individuals, underscoring the distinction between transient plasticity and evolved tolerance. Together, our results show that adaptive molecular divergence can emerge at fine spatial scales despite extensive gene flow, and that resilience to OA is driven mainly by evolved molecular reprogramming rather than short‐term plasticity.

title: Molecular Signature of a Marine Heatwave in the Hypothalamus of a Wild Fish Species
content:
ABSTRACT
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are increasing in frequency, intensity, and duration, yet their physiological impacts on wild mobile ectotherms remain poorly understood compared with laboratory‐based studies. Here, we investigated hypothalamic transcriptomic responses to MHW exposure in the Salema porgy Sarpa salpa, a key herbivorous Mediterranean fish species inhabiting one of the fastest‐warming marine regions. Using a 2‐year field sampling design, we compared a heatwave year, 2023, with a relatively temperate year, 2024, at the same seasonal period (spring, summer, and autumn) and at the exact same coastal location in France. This design allowed us to disentangle seasonal transcriptional variation from MHW‐specific molecular responses. We first identified a strong and consistent seasonal signal in hypothalamic gene expression, largely driven by temperature and photoperiod. Seasonally regulated genes were primarily involved in metabolism, mRNA regulation, neuronal activity, and calcium signalling, suggesting seasonal adjustments in hypothalamic neuronal function and cellular metabolism in response to changing environmental conditions. After accounting for interannual variation and confounding factors, we identified 12 candidate MHW‐responsive genes. Among these, nine genes were consistently upregulated during the heatwave, including several heat shock protein genes: hspa1l, hsp47, hspa8, and hsp90aa1. These results reveal a pronounced hypothalamic cellular heat‐stress signature associated with MHW exposure, with limited transcriptional changes in genes involved in the hypothalamic–pituitary–interrenal stress axis. Our findings highlight the potential of hypothalamic gene expression to reveal molecular responses to extreme warming in natural populations and identify candidate molecular indicators for monitoring the biological impacts of increasingly frequent MHWs.

title: Differential Contributions of Heterogeneity and Stochasticity to Individuals' Life Histories Along the Slow‐Fast Continuum
content:
Individuals differ in lifespan and lifetime reproductive output because of chance (individual stochasticity) and because of fixed differences in quality. Simulating six species along the slow ‘fast continuum’, we show that stochasticity dominates: quality heterogeneity typically explains under 6% of the variance, peaking at intermediate paces of life. Where it matters, it acts through juvenile survival, maturation and fertility in fast species and through adult survival in slow species.

ABSTRACT
Life histories vary widely among individuals within populations due to individual stochasticity (unpredictable life events) and individual heterogeneity (consistent differences in vital rates among individuals). We develop a theoretical population model and use a novel multifactorial variance decomposition framework to investigate the relative contribution of individual stochasticity and heterogeneity to the variance in life history outcomes. We compare the results obtained for simulated populations along the slow‐fast life continuum of life histories. We show that individual stochasticity is the dominant source of variation. Yet, its relative amplitude depends on species' position along the continuum and on the vital rates exhibiting heterogeneity. In addition, we show that individual heterogeneity generates higher proportions of the variance when heterogeneity on several vital rates combines to produce differences in fitness among individuals. This suggests that demographic impacts of fixed individual heterogeneity depend on the pace of life and on how traits covary within populations.

title: We Lost It: Local and Global Drivers Have Caused up to 50% Local‐Scale Plant Biodiversity Loss Over the Last Century
content:
We resurvey 46 century‐old vegetation plots in Austria, rare baselines for Central European plant biodiversity, to evaluate effects of major biodiversity change drivers and use causal inference analyses to integrate causal structures from literature with historical vegetation, landscape and climate data. We show ~50% declines in plot‐level species richness over the past century, mainly driven by local factors, with macroclimate effects limited to plots without significant land use change.

ABSTRACT
Eutrophication, sea—and land use change, area loss, climate change and alien species are changing biodiversity in unprecedented ways, with magnitudes varying drastically across metrics and observational scales. We resurvey 46 century‐old vegetation plots around Graz, Austria to evaluate effects of these major biodiversity change drivers. These historical plots provide rare baselines for Central European plant biodiversity before 1950, and reveal ~50% declines in plot‐level species richness and ~30% declines in evenness over the past century. We use causal inference analyses of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to integrate hypothesised causal structures from literature with historical vegetation, landscape and climate data. Our analyses indicate that observed biodiversity loss was mainly driven by local factors (eutrophication, habitat loss, microclimate), with macroclimate effects limited to plots without significant land use change. These findings imply that targeted local management efforts could mitigate ongoing biodiversity loss, even in the absence of effective global‐scale policies.

title: Hippocampal representations differentiate reactive and anticipatory responses during foraging under threat
content: Adaptive behavior under threat requires balancing reward pursuit against the risk of harm. During approach-avoidance conflict, animals often pause at decision points, but whether these pauses reflect a unified process or distinct decision states remains unclear. Here, we replicate and extend findings from Calvin et al., 2025, by analyzing hippocampal activity in rats performing a pseudo-predator foraging task across two cohorts. We compared mid-track aborts (MTAs), mid-track continues (MTCs), and retreats. Behaviorally, MTAs and MTCs emerged from a shared pause state but diverged in outcome, whereas retreats reflected rapid escape following attack. Despite similar endpoints, retreats and MTAs differed in movement dynamics and neural activity. During retreats, hippocampal representations remained biased toward the attack location. In contrast, representations during MTAs shifted toward safe locations. During pauses, representations differed according to subsequent behavior: pauses preceding MTAs showed greater decoded probability near the attack region, whereas pauses preceding MTCs showed greater decoded probability to goal locations. These differences were present during the outbound approach, suggesting decision-related processes emerged early on in the journey. Together, these findings dissociate hippocampal representations associated with reactive escape from those underlying anticipatory, anxiety-like decision-making, suggesting that the hippocampus dynamically tracks behaviorally relevant features to guide decisions under threat.

title: Hydrodynamic Nonlinear Interactions in River‐Dominated Deltas: Wax Lake Delta (Louisiana, USA)
content:
Abstract
Understanding nonlinear interactions is essential for predicting storm surge, compound flooding, and coastal management. While individual forcing mechanisms are well studied, quantitative assessments of nonlinear interactions within shallow deltaic environments remain largely unexplored. Here, numerical experiments are conducted to quantify nonlinear interactions influencing water level and range, flow velocities, and momentum‐balance in Wax Lake Delta, a river‐dominated delta. Nonlinear interactions in the shallow delta can intensify water level variability to exceed the water depth, leading to inundation of floodplains that would remain dry under linear forcing; amplify peak velocities; and produce divergent effects across geomorphic zones—enhancing tidal range and velocity magnitude by more than a factor of two in sub‐aerial regions, while damping them in deeper channels and floodplains. Momentum analysis reveals the strongest nonlinear variability in pressure‐gradient, friction, and advective acceleration. Findings underscore the role of nonlinearity in shaping deltaic processes with implications for geomorphology and ecosystem function.

title: Skillful Global Ocean Emulation and the Role of Correlation‐Aware Loss
content:
Abstract
Machine learning emulators have shown extraordinary skill in forecasting atmospheric states, and their application to global ocean dynamics offers similar promise. Here, we adapt the GraphCast architecture into a dedicated ocean‐only emulator, driven by prescribed atmospheric conditions, for medium‐range predictions. The emulator is trained on NOAA's UFS‐Replay data set. Using a 24 hr time step, single initial condition, and without using autoregressive training, we produce an emulator that provides skillful forecasts for 10−15 $10 -\!15$ day lead times. We further demonstrate the use of Mahalanobis distance as loss that improves the forecast skill compared to the Mean Squared Error loss by explicitly accounting for the correlations between tendencies of the target variables. Using spatial correlation analysis of the forecasted fields, we also show that the proposed correlation‐aware loss acts as a statistical‐dynamical regularizer for the slow, correlated dynamics of the global oceans, offering a better background forecast for downstream tasks like data assimilation.

title: How Much Aerosol Over the Interior Tibetan Plateau Lies Below CALIPSO's Detection Threshold? A Multi‐Year Ground‐Based LiDAR Assessment
content:
Abstract
CALIPSO is the main source of aerosol profiles over the Tibetan Plateau, but its detection threshold over the clean plateau interior has not been tested against ground observations. We compare 336 cloud‐free nights and 411 cloud‐free days of ground LiDAR profiles at Yangbajing (4,284 m) with late‐mission CALIPSO profiles (2021–2023) within 100 km. Matching the frequency of ground extinction above a threshold to the CALIPSO aerosol‐bin frequency at 5–8 km gives an equivalent threshold of 13 Mm−1 (95% interval 8–20) at night and a higher, poorly constrained value by day. The night value agrees with a published threshold and with a noise‐limited model based on the local CALIOP Level 1B noise, and Level 1B signals contain aerosol in bins that Level 2 labels clear air. On 52% of cloud‐free nights (35%–67% across the threshold interval), more than 90% of the column optical depth above 4.9 km lies below this threshold.

title: Continental‐Scale Dynamic Flood Routing via Graph Fourier Neural Operator
content:
Abstract
Accurate and timely flood forecasting for large river networks (or “graphs”) requires fast routing. Muskingum–Cunge (MC) routing captures nonlinear flood dynamics but its sequential time stepping can create barriers to near‐real‐time warnings and hybrid training. Linear time‐invariant (LTI) spectral methods are fast but miss flow‐dependent celerity effects. We present River‐GFNO, a graph‐structured, space‐time‐decoupled surrogate that approximates MC as a learned mixture of linear regimes, each solved spectrally in parallel. A temporal convolutional neural network blends regimes based on routed discharge, capturing nonlinear flood propagation while closely conserving mass. Applied to the Mississippi River Basin, River‐GFNO achieves overall median outlet Nash‐Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) = 0.995, reduces NRMSE by 45%–81% over LTI for medium‐to‐large subgraphs and runs 25–155× faster than differentiable MC. Appropriate trunk–leaf decomposition is crucial for accurate cascaded inference across the network, including arid regions where LTI fails. This scheme enables continental‐scale knowledge learning on river networks.

title: SST Warming Patterns Modulate the Amplitude of Interannual Variability of Australian Monsoon Rainfall Under Global Warming
content:
Abstract
Interannual variability of Australian monsoon rainfall (AUMR) plays an important role in regional and remote climate, yet its future change remains highly uncertain. Using large‐ensemble atmospheric model simulations with multiple sea surface temperature (SST) warming patterns, we investigate the warming response of AUMR variability and its uncertainty. While AUMR variability is primarily driven by atmospheric internal variability rather than SST anomalies, its amplitude is strongly modulated by SST warming patterns. Weaker SST warming around the Maritime Continent relative to the western Pacific is associated with stronger monsoon westerlies and more effective wind–evaporation feedback over the Indian Ocean, likely resulting in larger AUMR variability. Similar relationships in coupled model simulations suggest that this mechanism contributes to uncertainty in projected AUMR variability, highlighting the importance of SST warming patterns.

title: Multidimensional Soil Degradation and Contrasting Functional Recovery After Fire
content:
Abstract
Fires are intensifying globally, yet post‐fire erosion, soil degradation, and mitigation outcomes are typically studied in isolation, limiting an integrated understanding of fire‐driven soil degradation and recovery. Here, we synthesize 9,390 observations from 366 studies to quantify fire‐induced changes in hydrological, structural, chemical, and biological soil properties, and assess the effectiveness of post‐fire mitigation in alleviating post‐fire disturbances. Fire induces coordinated degradation of soil structure, nutrients, and microbial properties, while disproportionately increasing sediment yield relative to runoff. Runoff and sediment recover within 3–4 years, whereas many soil functional properties show slower and more variable recovery, with structural and nutrient indicators showing greater degrees of recovery than microbial and biochemical functions. This synthesis reveals coordinated but asynchronous patterns of soil degradation and recovery. The contrast between relatively rapid erosion control and more limited soil functional responses highlights a fundamental constraint on post‐fire ecosystem resilience under intensifying fire regimes.

title: Emulator‐Expanded Projections Reveal Structure in Antarctic Sea Level Uncertainty
content:
Abstract
Antarctic Ice Sheet projections remain the largest source of uncertainty in future global sea level rise, but the number of available projections is limited by the high cost of ice sheet simulations. Here we use a machine learning emulator to explore a greatly expanded set of Antarctic sea level projections spanning four times more CMIP6 climate model forcings, twice as many emissions pathways, and a broader set of ice sheet model configurations. Expanding this space does not substantially change Antarctic median contributions implied by the original ensemble. However, the expanded ensemble reveals structured uncertainty: late 21st century variability is dominated by climate model forcing differences, while ice sheet model choice and initialization contribute more strongly early in the projections. By separating epistemic (emulator) and aleatoric (conditional variability in training data) uncertainty, we identify ocean‐forcing treatments, ice‐shelf fracture experiments, and initialization strategies as priority targets for future simulations and climate assessments.

title: Reduced Elastic Anisotropy of New Hydrous MgSiO4H2 Polymorphs in the Lower Mantle
content:
Abstract
Phase H (MgSiO4H2) is a dense hydrous magnesium silicate that may carry water into the deep mantle and influence seismic heterogeneity in subducted slabs. Recent studies identified two new MgSiO4H2 polymorphs, α‐ and β‐MgSiO4H2, as promising structures for phase H, yet their elastic properties remain unknown. Here, we calculate their elastic properties using first‐principles methods. α‐MgSiO4H2 exhibits seismic velocities comparable to those of the initially proposed P2/m structure, whereas β‐MgSiO4H2 is distinctly slower, especially for shear waves. Dehydration of α‐ and potentially metastable β‐MgSiO4H2 may cause abrupt velocity jumps that may contribute to mid‐lower‐mantle seismic discontinuities. Both new polymorphs are substantially less anisotropic than P2/m‐MgSiO4H2, with reductions up to ∼50%, while remaining more anisotropic than most major lower‐mantle minerals. These results call for re‐examining the seismological role of phase H in light of the elasticity of the new polymorphs rather than the exceptionally anisotropic P2/m model.

title: Diagnosing Upper‐Ocean Vertical Exchange From SWOT Sea Surface Height via Knowledge Distillation
content:
Abstract
Upper‐ocean vertical velocity (w) redistributes heat and biogeochemical tracers, yet it remains challenging to observe directly or infer reliably from surface data alone. Machine‐learning (ML) offers a pathway to estimate w, but most existing ML approaches are driven by surface signals. This surface‐centric approach inherently limits accuracy, as vertical velocity is dynamically linked with subsurface information. Here, we propose Density‐Aware Network (DenA‐Net) that utilizes knowledge distillation to guide the network toward subsurface signals implicitly contained in sea surface height (SSH). At inference, DenA‐Net reconstructs three‐dimensional w fields from SSH alone. DenA‐Net increases w correlation by 72% compared with a conventional deep neural network on daily‐mean simulation fields. Applying DenA‐Net to SWOT SSH alongside collocated Argo profiles, we provide observation‐based estimates of w, vertical heat transport, and mixed‐layer vertical heat advection. This framework provides a practical pathway for satellite diagnostics of upper‐ocean vertical exchange and its impacts on heat budget.

title: Better Together: Combining EMIT Spectroscopy With Traditional Geologic Mapping
content:
Abstract
Data collected from NASA's Earth Surface Mineral Dust Source Investigation (EMIT) provides one of the first opportunities to use imaging spectroscopy to map geologic units from space. Based on the hypothesis that there exist predictable linkages between geochemical characteristics of the bedrock geology and the spectra of the land surface, we used EMIT imagery coupled with the geologic map of the McDermitt Caldera, NV, to train partial least squares discriminant analysis models for differentiating geologic units. Model validation showed mixed but consistent outcomes, with some units predicted with up to ∼90% accuracy. Consolidating geologic units based on their chemical compositions and textural similarities helped increase classification accuracy overall, but some units remained poorly predicted. When available, we found remarkable improvement of poorly predicted units through the inclusion of vegetation spectra that were originally omitted. This suggests that reflectance spectra of vegetation are influenced by the unique chemical composition of subsurface bedrock.

title: Facilitation of Magnetic Reconnection by Energetic Anisotropic Ions Through Alfvén/Ion‐Cyclotron Assisted Tearing Mode
content:
Abstract
Magnetic reconnection can convert magnetic energy into particle energy in space plasmas and is often regulated by kinetic‐scale ion dynamics, yet the role of energetic and anisotropic ions in the reconnection remains incompletely understood. In this study, we investigate how such energetic and anisotropic ions affect the reconnection. We find that ion temperature anisotropy strongly modifies the early nonlinear evolution of the reconnection. In anisotropic cases, the background ions excite Alfvén/ion‐cyclotron (A/IC) fluctuations at sub ion‐cyclotron frequency range. These ion‐scale wave modes enhance the magnetic fluctuation spectrum, which may be linked to interactions with the primary tearing mode. Consequently, the anisotropic cases enter the fast reconnection phase earlier and achieve larger peak reconnection rates than the isotropic one. These results suggest an A/IC‐assisted tearing mode pathway accelerates reconnection onset and enhances reconnection efficiency. Our findings provide a kinetic mechanism linking ion‐scale temperature anisotropy to reconnection dynamics.
