Spectral analysis of gene-dependency networks reveals emergent organization across scales in CAR T biology
content: CAR T-cell infusion products are commonly characterized in terms of their cellular populations and transcriptional programs, but these descriptions do not fully capture how a product is organized as a system. We analyzed single-cell RNA sequencing data from the infusion products of 163 patients across eight cohorts to investigate how system-level transcriptional organization relates to both clinical outcome and how cellular features vary together across patients. For each patient, we constructed a gene-dependency graph using mutual information between the binary detection states of each gene pair across infusion cells. To characterize each patient's network architecture, we define spectral organization, O{lambda}, a measure of the relative persistence of collective patterns of gene dependence in the network. Using hierarchical Bayesian survival models, we assessed the associations of both O{lambda} and various established cellular features with treatment outcome. Higher spectral organization was associated with a higher hazard of treatment failure in both a continuous model (hazard ratio per standard deviation, 1.45, 95% credible interval 1.07-2.19) and a smooth transition model (hazard ratio comparing the high and low regimes, 2.03, 95% credible interval 1.10-3.53). When we investigated how cellular features covary across patients, we found that correlations among both T-cell programs and cell type proportions aligned more coherently with treatment failure risk in the high O{lambda} regime compared to the low regime, revealing a systems-level pattern that helps explain the clinical relevance of spectral organization. Gene set enrichment analysis further showed that more persistent architectures were associated with inflammation and cellular interaction pathways, whereas lower spectral organization was associated with biosynthetic and genome maintenance pathways, consistent with the hypothesis that the organizational state of an infusion product reflects its capacity to reconfigure in response to CAR T treatment. Altogether, our findings identify spectral organization as a property of the infusion product as a whole that connects gene-dependency architecture within individual products to the collective variation of cellular features across patients. This framework therefore motivates studying CAR T biology from a systems perspective alongside established descriptions of cellular state.

title: Subsequent Phases of Gene Expression Leading to Commitment and Differentiation in a Eukaryotic Cell
content: Cell differentiation requires the specific control of gene expression for each cell type. However, the mechanism by which robust developmental outcomes arise from inherently noisy single-cell dynamics remains unclear. To address this question, we performed a formal analysis of longitudinal time series during the commitment and differentiation of giant single cells. We tracked how the discrete expression states of individual genes changed relative to each other. Despite marked variability in timing and trajectories from cell to cell, we identified reproducible temporal motifs and quantified the strength of temporal correlations among early- and late-regulated genes. Notably, a core gene set exhibited the same relative temporal order in establishing stable or transiently stable expression states in most cells. This suggests that a well-defined gene expression program emerges amidst apparent stochasticity. These results support a model in which induction to differentiation proceeds via a cascade of partially concurrent, discrete genetic switching events that collectively produce gradual, continuous shifts in expression at the population level. This framework reconciles apparently stochastic single-cell behavior with reliable developmental outcomes and suggests general principles for the temporal organization of gene regulation during differentiation. Furthermore, it provides analytic tools that can be broadly applied to longitudinal single-cell datasets to design temporally precise interventions in development and disease.

title: A spatial transcriptomic map of subcutaneous adipose tissue aging in male mice
content: Aging alters adipose tissue composition and function, but the spatial organization and gene expression dynamics during lifetime remain incompletely characterized. Here we profiled spatial transcriptome-wide changes in the aging male murine inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT). We describe ten different cell type clusters and three distinct adipocyte states. Further, we detected lipid-associated macrophages (LAMs), the cell type-enriched cluster with the largest number of genes upregulated in old age. LAMs that engage in local crown-like structures (CLS) are associated with pro-inflammatory niche programs at old age while LAMs outside of CLS are enriched in metabolically active transcriptional programmes at young age. LAM spots show reduced predicted lipid oxidation and glycolytic activity with age. Independent validation confirmed functionally reduced glycolytic capacity in aged female and male LAMs. Together, our study provides a deeply sequenced spatiotemporal resource for investigating adipose tissue aging biology, and for prioritizing spatially defined macrophage niches.

title: Tritrophic Interactions among Crapemyrtle, Crapemyrtle Aphids, and the Green Lacewing Chrysoperla rufilabris (Burmeister)
content: Tritrophic interactions can have considerable impact on biological control systems, therefore, it is imperative to consider these interactions when implementing or evaluating biological control agents. Crape myrtles, Lagerstroemia indica L. x L. fauriei L., are important non-native ornamental plants from Asia that are widely planted and a major woody landscape species in the southern U.S. Six alkaloids have been identified from L. indica, mostly in the seeds and leaves. Crapemyrtle aphids, Tinocallis kahawaluokalani (Kirkaldy), are host specific to crape myrtle and have been shown to be important prey for many native beneficial insects including coccinellids, mirids, and green lacewings. The crapemyrtle aphids occur in different densities per leaf on crape myrtle cultivars and some native beneficial insects cannot fully develop by feeding solely on these aphids. Moreover, no parasitoids of crapemyrtle aphids are known. This information suggests that plant chemistry is involved in tritrophic interactions between this plant, its herbivores and their natural enemies. The purpose of this study was to investigate the suitability of crapemyrtle aphids as a food source for the green lacewing Chrysoperla rufilabris (Bermeister). Experiments were conducted to test the effects of crapemyrtle cultivar, mature plant height, and source of germplasm on the life history characteristics of C. rufilabris. Crapemyrtle aphids were reared on seven cultivars of crapemyrtle, including Apalachee, Natchez, Sioux, Tuscarora, Lipan, Carolina Beauty, and Byers Wonderful White. Aphids from each cultivar were fed exclusively to green lacewing larvae from egg to adult eclosion. Survivorship by cultivar treatment was determined for developmental stages and growth parameters. Cultivar did not affect larval survival but did affect pupal and total survivorship. Length of pupation was extended by aphids feeding on mid mature height cultivars. Dry mass of larvae and adults were also affected accordingly. Males had lower dry mass than females. Lacewings fed on aphids from tall mature height cultivars developed higher dry mass.

title: Multi-omics analysis reveals how the natural compound bostrycin induces iron starvation and ferroptosis
content: The development of novel anticancer drugs remains urgent due to limited efficacy of existing therapies. Natural products are a rich source for discovery of anticancer agents, yet their mechanisms often remain elusive. Bostrycin, a fungal anthraquinone with broad cytotoxicity, is one such compound. Here, we combine global and nascent proteomics with metabolomics to elucidate the mechanism of bostrycin-induced cell death. We show that bostrycin induces ferroptosis, and use thermal proteome profiling to identify thioredoxin reductase 1 (TXNRD1), a key enzyme in glutathione metabolism and redox control, as bostrycin's primary direct target. Bostrycin triggered an iron starvation response and reduced iron-sulfur cluster-containing proteins, consistent with impaired cysteine availability. While the resulting iron overload likely triggered ferroptotic death, this coincided with broader disruption of redox balance, glutathione metabolism, and energy pathways. These findings establish bostrycin's mechanism of action and identify it as a ferroptosis-inducing agent acting distinctly from canonical inducers.

title: A spatiotemporal perturbational atlas of the post-pneumonectomy lung
content: Perturbational spatial atlases have begun to map regenerative dynamics in a variety of tissues, yet lung remodeling has not been characterized at comparable spatial and temporal resolution. Post-pneumonectomy lung regeneration (PPLR) provides a tractable mammalian model for tissue regeneration that can be studied in situ. Here, we present a spatiotemporal perturbational atlas of PPLR in Rattus norvegicus, combining single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq), high-resolution spatial transcriptomics (10x Genomics Xenium), and NICHES-based spatial tissue connectomics. We observe three distinct tissue architectures at successive timepoints after pneumonectomy, each characterized by coordinated shifts in local cellular composition and intercellular signaling. At Day 3 (D3), a line of interstitial macrophages colocalizes directly beneath an intact mesothelium among active mechanotransductive and inflammatory signaling. We also observe the unexpected appearance of a transitional remodeling cellular community at D7 which appears largely absent at later timepoints, marked by fibrosis- mimetic signaling. At D14, an alveologenic architecture at distal lung tissue displays a connectivity signature consistent with active de novo growth, distinct from baseline homeostasis. Our findings establish a spatiotemporal map of multicellular architecture during regenerative lung remodeling and introduce a generalizable framework for spatial connectomic analysis to be used in perturbational tissue systems biology.

title: Toxoplasma gondii-induced NETs are mediated by CR3 engagement and the vital non-lytic NETosis pathway
content: Approximately one-third of the global human population harbors an infection with the protozoan parasite Toxoplasma gondii. The immune system exploits neutrophils and one of their effector mechanisms, neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), as an attempt to capture and neutralize T. gondii. NETs, composed of DNA, myeloperoxidase, citrullinated histone 3, and elastase, play a dual role in pathogen entrapment and amplification of the immune response. Traditionally, NET release was considered to result in neutrophil cell death. However, studies have identified an alternative process, vital NETosis, that allows NET formation while maintaining cell viability. Although T. gondii induces NET formation, the associated molecular mechanisms are not fully understood, and the neutrophil fate is unknown. In this study, the promyelocytic cell line HL-60 was differentiated into neutrophil-like cells (NLCs) and infected with type I (RH) or type II (PA7) T. gondii. Extracellular DNA was found in increasing concentrations over time in both type 1 and type 2 T. gondii-infected NLCs. Immunofluorescence staining for DNA and citrullinated histone 3 at 4, 6, and 16 hours post-infection confirmed NET formation by confocal microscopy. Cell viability at 16 hours post-infection was assessed by live/dead staining and extracellular ATP measurement, revealing that most NET-releasing neutrophils retained membrane integrity, consistent with vital NETosis. Additionally, immunofluorescence microscopy at 15 and 30 minutes further confirmed the fast release of nuclear DNA, a hallmark of vital NETosis. The use of opsonin-containing human serum and an anti-CD11b blocking antibody identified complement receptor 3 (CR3) as a receptor mediating T. gondii-induced vital NETosis. These findings demonstrate that T. gondii triggers vital NETosis in neutrophils through a CR3-dependent mechanism, advancing our understanding of the innate immune response to this globally prevalent parasite and laying the groundwork for future investigations into the molecular pathways that may be therapeutically targeted to support neutrophil-mediated immunity during infection.

title: Strain-resolved metagenomics shows gut microbiome signatures in a case-control study of Malawian children with zoonotic schistosomiasis
content: In 2024, Mangochi District, Malawi, we identified unexpected cases of zoonotic schistosomiasis associated with faecal egg excretion of Schistosoma haematobium, Schistosoma mattheei and hybrids thereof (S. haematobium x S. mattheei). Schistosomiasis is associated with gut microbiome alterations, but these associations remain unexplored in zoonotic schistosomiasis. Whether people with schistosomiasis are colonised with more closely related gut bacterial strains than people without schistosomiasis is also unclear. To better understand these patterns, we conducted a case-control study, using strain-resolved metagenomics to analyse faecal samples from 36 children: 12 with zoonotic schistosomiasis (S. haematobium and S. mattheei), 12 with "classic" urogenital schistosomiasis (S. haematobium only) and 12 uninfected controls. Microbial diversity, taxonomic composition, metabolic pathways and antimicrobial resistance gene profiles did not differ significantly between groups. However, Brachyspira, particularly Brachyspira aalborgi - an organism often associated with intestinal spirochaetosis - was more abundant in children with zoonotic schistosomiasis. We found no evidence of closely related B. aalborgi strains shared between participants, suggesting that localised B. aalborgi transmission networks are unlikely to explain the enrichment. In contrast, phylogenetic profiling across 143 other bacterial species revealed greater strain similarity between the gut microbiomes of children with any type of schistosomiasis than between those of controls. Broadly, we demonstrate the scientific value of strain-resolved metagenomics for investigating linked bacterial and schistosome exposures where local water, sanitation and hygiene infrastructure is inadequate. Future inclusion of livestock and environmental samples could be used to better identify where transmission pathways overlap, providing evidence to inform integrated disease surveillance and control.

title: Dynamic interactions of the coronavirus PEDV nucleoprotein with its viral partner nsp3 and RNA
content: Summary While coronavirus genome replication and transcription occur inside double-membrane vesicles (DMVs) in infected cells, nucleocapsid assembly of genomic RNA takes place at their cytoplasmic (external) face. Neosynthesized viral mRNAs (including genomic RNA) are exported from the DMV through nsp3/nsp4 pores and genomic RNAs are believed to be selected for encapsidation through an essential interaction of the nucleoprotein N with the amino-terminal domain of nsp3. Here, we describe the interaction play between the N of porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV, an alphacoronavirus) with the N-terminal domain of nsp3 and with RNAs. While N interacts with the N-terminal domain of nsp3 with a dissociation constant (KD) of about 150 nM, it binds to diverse small RNAs, displaying an affinity in the pM range for a short RNA (RNA[8mer]). This RNA and a 60-nt long RNA hairpin were both able to fully displace nsp3 complexed with N. In contrast, nsp3 was not able to dissociate RNA from N-RNA complexes. Using truncated forms of N and of the N-ter domain of nsp3, we showed that the RNA binding site does not fully overlap the nsp3 binding site on N. These results suggest that the interaction play between N, nsp3 and RNA is unidirectional, allowing to propose a mechanistical model for genome encapsidation, model in which N is first recruited by nsp3 at the cytoplasmic face of the DMV to bind to nucleotide stretches of (genomic) RNA exiting from the nsp3/nsp4 channel and concomitantly to dissociate from nsp3.

title: CurveKinetix: A user-friendly application for analysis of biological time series data
content:
Of interest to many biologists is how organisms change over time: their growth, their

response to a stimulus, their movement. How quickly a process starts, accelerates,

slows, or changes direction, often carries critical biological information for hypothesis

testing. Extraction of these parameters, however, requires computational expertise or

reliance on existing software not designed for the needed analysis. We present here

CurveKinetix, a graphical user interface application that helps researchers extract

quantitative parameters from time series data without writing code. Users can quickly go

from instrument data files to estimation of parameters using three complementary

methods to visualized data customization and export.

We exhibit CurveKinetix's utility in two case studies. In the first, we show expression of

an operon correlates with slowing of population level growth. In the second, we

enumerate viral fusion dynamics, demonstrating CurveKinetixs framework can be

applied to a range of biological questions.

By making flexible quantitative analysis straightforward, CurveKinetix helps

experimentalists extract more information from their data and supports clearer, more

rigorous interpretation of time-resolved experiments.

title: Olfactory epithelium local proteomic during SARS-CoV-2 infection in hamsters
content: SARS-CoV-2 has been extensively studied since its recent emergence. It has proven to be an excellent model of respiratory virus impact on nasal epithelium for its massive impact notably on the olfactory epithelium using the hamster animal model. We and others have previously observed that following infection, the nasal epithelium is massively infiltrated by innate immune cells followed by desquamation leading to release of cellular debris in the lumen of the nasal cavity. This impact varies spatially in the nasal cavity, the anterior part being infected early mainly in the respiratory epithelium followed by the olfactory epithelium in the posterior part. In order to better understand the impact on host cells, we decided to use laser microdissection to analyse the proteomic of restricted area of infected epithelium taking into account this spatial variation. We observed that protein levels are mostly decreased following SARS-CoV-2 infection at 2 days post-infection which contrasts with many genes having a stable expression level. Using available scRNASeq library, we could associate the variation of protein levels to the various cell types of the nasal cavity epithelium and our findings are consistent with a destruction of most epithelial cells and the infiltration of innate immune cells. Overall, our study confirms that SARS-CoV-2-host interactions lead to profound alteration of genes expression and that while most studies heavily rely on mRNA levels, it may be decorrelated to protein levels. Our approach offers an alternative to study host-virus interactions using spatially restricted proteomic.

title: Calcium Signaling and Glycerol-3-Phosphate Metabolism Coordinate Extracellular Vesicle Biogenesis in Cryptococcus neoformans
content: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are increasingly recognized as important mediators of fungal physiology and host-pathogen interactions, but the mechanisms governing their biogenesis remain poorly understood. Here, we combined time-course RNA sequencing with genome-wide genetic screening to define the regulatory network controlling EV production in the human fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans. Transcriptomic analysis identified an EV-associated regulon enriched in genes involved in vesicular trafficking, cell wall remodeling, lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function and ion homeostasis. Our screen further identified diverse regulators of EV production, highlighting endosomal trafficking, mitochondrial metabolism and calcium homeostasis. Cell viability was only weakly associated with EV production, arguing against cell lysis as the primary mechanism of EV release. Genetic and pharmacological analyses established calcium-dependent calcineurin signalling as a major regulator of EV production. We identified the calcineurin target Had1 as a positive regulator of EV production and demonstrate that Had1 functions as a glycerol-3-phosphate phosphatase. Loss of HAD1 caused glycerol-3-phosphate accumulation and extensive remodeling of cellular phospholipids, accompanied by a marked reduction in EV production. Together, these findings identify a calcium-calcineurin-Had1 pathway linking intracellular signalling and lipid homeostasis to fungal EV biogenesis.

title: Global evolutionary and spatiotemporal transmission dynamics of human respiroviruses and orthorubulaviruses
content: Human parainfluenza viruses (HPIVs) cause recurrent epidemics and are a major cause of hospitalization worldwide. However, the evolutionary and transmission dynamics driving HPIV persistence remain unclear. We analysed 1,161 archived samples representing four HPIV types from seven countries using genomic sequencing and Bayesian phylodynamic inference. We show that Respirovirus (HRV-1 and HRV-3) displayed greater fluctuations in genetic diversity whereas Orthorubulavirus (HOV-2 and HOV-4) showed more gradual changes. Despite comparable evolutionary rates, the four HPIV types exhibited contrasting lineage dynamics. HRV-1 showed prolonged lineage persistence, HRV-3 underwent greater lineage turnover, and HOV-2 and HOV-4 maintained fewer co-circulating lineages. Positive selection was more pronounced in respiroviruses, particularly in the phosphoprotein gene, while positively selected sites overlapped predicted hemagglutinin-neuraminidase B-cell epitopes. Phylogeographic analyses revealed repeated interregional introductions, bidirectional transmission, and regional persistence exceeding a decade for some lineages. These findings identify distinct evolutionary and transmission dynamics underlying HPIV persistence and inform the development of broadly protective vaccines and therapeutics.

title: A tricomponent mRNA pertussis vaccine elicits superior protective immunity over licensed acellular pertussis vaccine against emerging antibiotic-resistant variants
content: Pertussis remains a major global health burden and has been resurging rapidly over the past decade. The causes of pertussis re-emergence are multifactorial, including vaccine-induced pathogen evolution, antimicrobial resistance, and crucially suboptimal protective immunity elicited by the widely used acellular pertussis vaccine (aPV). In this study, we developed a tricomponent mRNA pertussis vaccine formulated with lipid nanoparticle (LNP), designated mPervax, which encodes inactive pertussis toxin subunit 1 (PTS1), truncated filamentous hemagglutinin (FHA) and pertactin (PRN). Compared to a commercialized Tetanus-diptheria-pertussis vaccine Boostrix, mPervax induced stronger and broader innate immune activation, superior antigen-specific Th1-type CD4+ T and Tfh cell responses, and robust B. pertussis-specific antibody responses with remarkably increased magnitude and functionality. In addition, mPervax conferred an efficient maternal antibody-mediated protection in offspring mice and reshaped the immune profile established by primary Boostrix immunization towards a Th1-phenotype when used as a heterologous booster. Furthermore, upon bacterial challenge, mPervax outperformed Boostrix not only against the WHO reference strain 18323, but strikingly provided effective protection against emerging antibiotic-resistant clinical isolates that are deficient in PRN and/or FHA. Collectively, these data demonstrate that the mRNA pertussis vaccine is superior to Boostrix in multiple contexts, and therefore holds promise for next-generation pertussis vaccine development.

title: Elucidating and Overcoming Lignin-Mediated Growth Suppression in Anaerobic Fungi
content: Native to the gastrointestinal tract of herbivores, anaerobic gut fungi (AGF) (Neocallimastigomycetes) have evolved highly efficient enzymatic machinery for lignocellulose degradation. While AGF are capable of degrading lignocellulose, they more readily degrade its cellulose and hemicellulose components. Lignin is the most recalcitrant component of lignocellulose that serves as both structural support and a microbial defense strategy within plants. In this study, a negative correlation between AGF growth and substrate lignin content was quantified, ranging from pure cellulose to the lignin-rich substrate eucalyptus. Based on this observation, we investigated the impact of lignin on AGF viability and concluded that lignin delayed and slowed AGF?s growth trajectory, with IC50 ranging from 10.7 ? 16.3 mg/mL, and specifically that lignin-rich substrates decreased overall growth. Meanwhile, lignin acted as an AGF deterrent, likely by preventing access to essential sugar-based polymers and lowering overall nutrient bioavailability. However, AGF growth was restored following glucose supplementation on otherwise growth-limiting woody substrates. Through experimental, sequential serial batch culture challenge, we successfully adapted one strain of AGF (Neocallimastix californiae) to grow on lignin-rich eucalyptus. This study supports the industrial valorization of lignocellulose using AGF by elucidating the relationship between the major bottleneck, lignin, on fungal growth. It also provides a strategy for optimizing fungal strains selected for growth in nutrient-deficient and lignin-rich environments.

title: Explaining an early ground-nesting bee emergence with climate and occurrence data: Temperature, not precipitation, advances onset
content: Understanding the drivers of bee phenology is important for predicting how climate change may alter the temporal overlap between bee activity and plant flowering, with consequences for pollination. We documented unusually early emergence of Melissodes tepidus timberlakei Cockerell, 1926 at a perennial nesting site in spring 2026 and examined the relationship between emergence and climatic conditions with (1) five years of nesting observations at a single site, and (2) 119 years of M. tepidus occurrence records from across the western United States. We found that warming temperatures were associated with earlier emergence, whereas precipitation was not, and we emphasize the utility of monitoring ground nests to understand emergence drivers in bees during ongoing climate change.

title: Transitory Invasion Graphs
content: Invasion graphs map community assembly by linking communities that contain stable equilibria through successful invasions. By design, they leave aside transient communities that arise when species arrive before a community settles. Transitory invasion graphs (TIGs) complement this framework by recording every observed community, stable or transient, weighted by its frequency. In 500 simulated competitive communities of 5 - 25 species, assembly expanded through many transient communities, then contracted onto a few attractors. Competition limited the expansion: stronger interactions produced fewer communities but more transitions among them. The contraction reflected the attractor type: stable-equilibrium communities settled on the endpoints predicted by invasion graphs, whereas cyclic and chaotic communities kept turning over, most often through communities away from those endpoints. Repeated invasion attempts also rescued species with negative invasion growth rates and occasionally displaced uninvadable equilibria. Together, invasion graphs and TIGs reveal both where assembly can end and what is observed along the way.

title: Quantifying and interpreting the inverse coefficient of variation from minirhizotron-derived root dynamics
content: 1. The inverse coefficient of variation (/{sigma}) is widely used to quantify temporal invariability of ecosystem functioning. However, most studies have focused on aboveground biomass production, while belowground processes remain understudied. Minirhizotrons enable repeated observations of root dynamics, but the resulting data differ fundamentally in their temporal structure from measurements obtained through aboveground biomass harvests, sequential soil coring, or ingrowth cores. This raises questions about whether inverse CV estimates depend on the metric used to represent root dynamics and on when and how frequently observations are made. 2. Using a five-year minirhizotron dataset, we quantified the inverse CV from standing root abundance and two change-based metrics (net change and rate of change in standing root abundance). Standing root abundance was quantified from individual imaging sessions, whereas change-based metrics were derived from differences between successive sessions. We compared their inverse CV estimates using all 45 imaging sessions, monthly observations (n = 35), and annual observations (n = 5). For annual observations, we compared measurements taken before the aboveground biomass harvest and at peak root abundance. 3. Inverse CV estimates differed between standing root abundance and change-based metrics, and correlations were weak and often negative. Estimates also differed across measurement frequencies and timings, with responses depending on the underlying metric. Together, these results show that inverse CV estimates depend on how root dynamics are represented and sampled. 4. We propose that the inverse CV does not always represent invariability and that its interpretation depends on the metric used to represent root dynamics. For standing root abundance, it reflects pool invariability. For change-based metrics, we suggest interpreting it as directional consistency of root gains or losses. This distinction may extend to other ecosystem fluxes that can be positive and negative, such as carbon or energy fluxes. 5. Synthesis. Our findings challenge the assumption that applying the same formula (/{sigma}) ensures comparability and emphasize the need to align the underlying ecological questions and quantities when comparing invariability across ecosystem realms or studies.

title: Resonance-organized phase-locking, extinction and phase-dependent rescue in periodically forced populations with delayed Allee effects
content: Population persistence under environmental fluctuations depends not only on the magnitude of external disturbances but also on their interaction with endogenous population dynamics. However, how environmental resonance interacts with delayed density dependence and Allee effects to determine extinction risk remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate a periodically forced Hutchinson-type population model incorporating delayed density regulation and a strong Allee effect. Through numerical simulations, Lyapunov exponent analysis, and bifurcation continuation, we characterize the organization of population dynamics and extinction across environmental forcing frequencies and amplitudes. We find that extinction vulnerability is strongly organized by resonance between endogenous population oscillations and environmental forcing, with the lowest forcing amplitudes required for extinction occurring near the principal 1:1 resonance. The parameter space exhibits a hierarchy of frequency-locking regions consistent with Arnold tongues, including structures bounded by saddle-node bifurcations of periodic orbits. We further demonstrate that the carrying-capacity-to-Allee-threshold ratio governs the emergence of intrinsic oscillations through a Hopf bifurcation, fundamentally reorganizing the population's response to environmental forcing. Counterintuitively, lowering the Allee threshold can increase extinction vulnerability by strengthening destabilizing delayed feedback. Finally, we identify a history-dependent rescue mechanism through which populations can recover after temporarily crossing below the nominal Allee threshold. Successful recovery events exhibit systematic phase dependence relative to environmental forcing. Together, these findings demonstrate that extinction risk cannot be inferred from environmental severity, population abundance, or dynamical regularity alone. Instead, persistence emerges from the interaction between environmental timescales, endogenous oscillations, and history-dependent opportunities for recovery.

title: Environmental drivers of abundance and later seasonal activity of a salt marsh mosquito
content: 1. Climate and environmental change are altering the seasonal dynamics of insects worldwide, yet long-term datasets remain scarce for mosquito vectors in temperate regions. Consequently, the environmental drivers and phenological responses of mosquito populations are still poorly resolved in northern Europe. 2. Here, we test whether the seasonal timing and abundance of a specialist coastal mosquito are jointly shaped by climatic and tidal drivers, and whether its activity period has extended over a 14-year monitoring record. 3. We analysed a 14-year dataset (2012-2025) of the salt marsh mosquito Aedes detritus - one of the most common saltmarsh mosquitoes in Europe - collected from four British coastal wetland sites. Weekly catch data from the full time series were used to assess long-term phenological trends, while generalised additive models were applied to site-month aggregated observations from the consistent four-site trapping period (2019-2025) to identify climatic and tidal drivers of abundance. 4. Across the full 14-year record, the late-season peak and the end of the activity period (the 90% activity week) shifted later by 0.52 and 0.76 weeks per year, respectively (equivalent to fitted shifts of approximately 7 and 10 weeks), with no corresponding advance in the spring onset. This delayed autumn activity was robust to sampling-window and moving-window controls. 5. Adult abundance showed a pronounced bimodal seasonal pattern, with a smaller peak in late spring and a larger peak in mid-autumn. After accounting for seasonal structure, rainfall at a one-month lag and tidal surge were both positively associated with mosquito abundance. The size of the spring peak was correlated with rainfall, but the size and timing of the autumn peak were not. 6. These findings provide evidence that the seasonal activity of a salt marsh mosquito is extending later into autumn. We show that its population dynamics reflects a combination of climatic and tidal drivers whose relative contributions will require longer or more finely resolved records to disentangle fully. Sustained, long-term, full-season monitoring of coastal mosquito populations would therefore be important for understanding their responses to climate change. We recommend extending mosquito sampling in salt marsh areas into late autumn to better assess future risks associated with mosquito-borne pathogens.

title: Reconciling multiple views of global marine plankton diversity
content: Marine plankton diversity influences key ecosystem properties, including primary production and carbon export, and is monitored using diverse observation systems. Yet, it remains unclear whether global diversity patterns from different observation streams converge, and whether potential commonalities can guide monitoring, modelling, and conservation. Using a habitat modelling (CEPHALOPOD), we compare plankton diversity patterns across observation types and metrics, relating global open-ocean surface diversity from 330,000 observations of occurrence, abundance, biomass, and relative metagenomic reads to environmental climatologies. We find that diversity patterns converge on a latitudinal diversity gradient, with tropical oligotrophic gyres, western boundary currents and the Info-Pacific archipelago emerging as diversity hotspots. Occurrence-based estimates indicate higher diversity in eastern boundary upwellings than estimates accounting for community dominance, showing how multiple observation types provide complementary views of diversity. Surface ocean temperature, primary production, and physical transport emerge as remotely observable diversity proxies that can guide in situ sampling. Finally, diversity-ecosystem functioning relationships depend on the observation system: occurrence-based estimates highlight how diverse species can support production through complementary ecological roles, whereas abundance-, biomass-, and metagenomic-based estimates better reflect how dominant species contribute to processes such as carbon export. These findings can guide monitoring, modelling, and conservation under climate change.

title: Using Mixture Density Networks to Predict Plot-level Environmental Factors from Tree Secondary Metabolites
content: Tropical forests contain remarkable phytochemical diversity, but the relationship between diverse plant metabolites and underlying climatic and environmental variation remains poorly understood. Mixture density networks (MDNs) offer a flexible approach for predicting variables with multimodal distributions. Traditional regression models produce single-value predictions, which may fail to capture the full variability of widely distributed variables. We evaluated the performance of an MDN model on a Panama metabolomics dataset, in which each metabolite occurs across multiple forest plots, resulting in environmental variables with multiple associated values. The MDN recovered the overall range and broad shape of environmental distributions, although feature-specific predictions often converged toward shared distributional patterns. These results suggest that mixture density networks can capture coarse environmental structure from metabolomic representations, while also highlighting challenges associated with limited environmental variation and sparse observations.

title: Coral monitoring with environmental DNA captures community restructuring after mass bleaching mortality
content: Marine heatwaves are restructuring coral reefs, but monitoring coral community change across impacted habitats and reefs remains expensive and logistically challenging. Metabarcoding of seawater DNA represents a potential solution to the issue of scale, but technical challenges and a lack of ground truthing with conventional measures of coral community structure have limited its application. In early 2025, Mermaid Reef in the Rowley Shoals, a remote oceanic atoll in northwest Australia, experienced unprecedented heat stress resulting in widespread coral bleaching and mortality. Using photo-transect data alongside seawater eDNA samples, we quantified changes in coral cover and community assemblage before and after the heatwave and compared results of the two monitoring methods. Photo-transect data showed sharp reductions in live coral cover, particularly in Acropora, the dominant pre-bleaching genus. eDNA data mirrored these shifts, and Acropora sequences dominated pre-bleaching samples but declined strongly after bleaching, while several less abundant genera increased in relative read abundance. Across sites and timepoints, eDNA reads corresponded to photo-transect cover, and multivariate assemblage patterns strongly aligned between the two methods. These results demonstrate that seawater eDNA metabarcoding can provide rapid detection of community restructuring on coral reefs and can augment existing monitoring frameworks.

title: Spectral tuning of proton-pumping rhodopsins underscores distinct light adaptations in polar diatoms
content: Resource limitation constrains primary production across vast regions of the global ocean. Diatoms often persist under these conditions, despite their relatively large size and nutrient quotas compared to other phytoplankton phyla. This trend is particularly pronounced in the variable light and iron-depleted waters of the Southern Ocean. Proton-pumping rhodopsins (PPRs) have emerged as an important adaptation underlying this success, allowing diatoms to energetically supplement chlorophyll-based photosynthesis with retinal-based phototrophy, particularly under iron stress. While PPRs are increasingly recognized as a driver of diatom resilience under iron depletion, the extent to which coinciding environmental factors, such as light, shape this adaptation remains unresolved. We performed an in vitro study to investigate how variations in iron availability and light spectra synergistically shape PPR physiology in two ecologically relevant Southern Ocean diatoms: Pseudo-nitzschia subcurvata and Synedra hyperborea. Integrative biochemical and bioinformatic approaches identified two distinct evolutionary strategies for rhodopsin-mediated light acquisition. While P. subcurvata employed a specialist approach with two PPRs utilized under different wavelengths of light (green v. blue/red), S. hyperborea adopted a generalist approach with expression of a single PPR under both light treatments. Structural analyses of PPRs revealed hallmarks consistent with xanthorhodopsins, while coordinated transcriptional and pigment analyses suggest the blue-absorbing xanthophyll diadinoxanthin functions as a secondary light-harvesting chromophore. Collectively, these findings expand the ecological light niche of diatom rhodopsins, reveal previously unrecognized diversity in eukaryotic rhodopsin strategies, and suggest spectral tuning of proton pumping rhodopsins will enhance diatom fitness within the climatically altered light climate of the Southern Ocean.

title: Out of the wild: lab-reared bumble bees lack environmental bacteria and fungi
content: Social bees, including bumble bees, host a community of microbes in their gut consisting of core bacterial taxa as well as non-core bacteria and fungi. Bumble bee research colonies from commercial suppliers are often utilized in research characterizing and examining the functions of bee microbiomes. However, commercial rearing conditions have the potential to shift the microbiome associated with bees, calling into question whether results obtained using commercial colonies are applicable to wild bees. Here, we examine differences between the microbiome of commercially-reared and wild caught bumble bees of three species (Bombus impatiens, B. terrestris, and B. vosnesenskii) using amplicon sequencing and qPCR to characterize bacterial and fungal communities within bee guts. We found that while all bee species hosted some microbes belonging to the core bumble bee gut community, microbial community composition and diversity varied between species and sources, with wild individuals lacking some groups of core bacteria and hosting a greater diversity of non-core bacterial and fungal taxa. This work highlights the presence and potential dominance of non-core microbial taxa within wild bumble bee gut communities, especially early in the colony life cycle. Overall, we conclude that rearing conditions can shape the composition of bumble bee microbiomes, and research on commercial colonies alone may overlook environmental taxa commonly associated with bees.

title: Trade-off between resource excretion and reliance maintains biodiversity of a cross-feeding mutualism
content: Microbial mutualisms, in which species exchange resources through cross-feeding, are common in nature. Yet the stability of mutualistic interactions is debated, and cross-feeding communities are vulnerable to cheaters that benefit from the excretions of others but reduce or cease their own excretion of resources, which can lead to community collapse. Here, we demonstrate with a mathematical model that in addition to decreased excretion, increased reliance on cross-fed resources can also lead to community collapse. In a two-species model of bacteria that metabolizes lactose and provides yeast with galactose, in exchange for amino acids from yeast, we show that the set of excretion and reliance parameters that maximizes biomass is adjacent to a region of community collapse in the phase diagram. By expanding the model to include multiple bacterial auxotrophs competing for lactose and either separate or overlapping amino acids, we also demonstrate that a trade-off between reliance and excretion can enable coexistence within the bacterial mutualist guild. Finally, we show that intraguild coexistence of bacteria favors yeast, increasing biodiversity but decreasing total community biomass. Our results argue that the question of cheaters should be paired with analysis of reliance on mutualistic exchange, and that both of these parameters modulate biodiversity and the stability of mutualisms to collapse.

title: Sodium-enriched nectar increases seed set in low diversity prairies
content: Plant-pollinator interactions depend on floral traits and background plant community properties, yet the role of nectar micronutrients in these interactions is poorly understood. Sodium is a micronutrient of particular interest because although plants need little to no sodium, animal pollinators require it. It is unknown whether sodium-enriched nectar increases plant fitness in animal-pollinated plants and how this may be affected by the broader plant community. To test this, we grew black-eyed Susan (Rudbeckia hirta) plants in sodium-enriched or control soil. We placed pairs of sodium-addition and control plants in prairies seeded with high or low diversity and measured seed set and germination rate. In a supplementary experiment, we explored differences in floral visitation. We found that black-eyed Susan plants grown in sodium-enriched soil had sodium-enriched nectar. Seed set increased in sodium-addition plants in prairies seeded with low diversity but not in prairies seeded with high diversity. Germination rate was not affected by sodium addition. Altogether, our study highlights the importance of considering both micronutrients and context dependency in understanding plant reproduction and complex species interactions.

title: Belowground Herbivory Shapes Carbon Release from Tree Roots and Its Retention in Soil
content: Belowground root inputs contribute to stable soil organic carbon (SOC) significantly more than aboveground plant inputs. Yet, current understanding of the role of belowground root herbivory in ecosystem C cycling is remarkably weaker than that of aboveground herbivory and litter inputs. Here, we experimentally exposed roots of co-occurring mature hickory (Carya) and maple (Acer) trees, in a temperate hardwood forest, to increasing herbivory pressure by ubiquitous root-feeding soil nematodes. We investigated responses and underlying mechanisms of root C exudation as well as downstream indirect effects of root herbivory on mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC) pools. Increased root herbivory promoted C exudation, which was strongly associated with increasing root necrosis and resulted in indirect positive effects on MAOC. Importantly, these direct and indirect effects were larger in magnitude and only significant in hickory but not maple. Instead, the latter appeared to channel herbivory response toward diversified chemical defense signaling rather than bulk exudate release, while more extensive root damage and increased exudation rate with less compositional change of hickory suggested a greater role of passive exudate release through leaking wounds in roots. Taken together, these findings indicate divergent eco-physiological mechanisms and ecosystem C consequences of root herbivory in mature hickory and maple trees, and show that changes in exudate quantity rather than chemical composition impact soil C. This study extends field-based causal explanation of root C inputs and retention in soil by highlighting the role of root-feeding animals in regulating rhizodeposition, and offers a basis for integrating belowground herbivory into multitrophic biogeochemistry.

title: Nutrient and host availability drive the evolution of viral plasticity
content: Viruses of microbes inject their genome into host cells, take over host metabolism, and produce progeny virions that are released into the environment upon lysis. Environmental and host conditions shape viral traits, including the intracellular maturation rate of virions and the time between infection and lysis. The dependence of viral traits on environmental context, i.e., phenotypic plasticity, would appear to be inevitable for obligate intracellular parasites, which depend on host metabolic activity for replication. However, viruses, including viruses of microbes, encode genes that can decouple their replication from the host metabolic state. Here, we present a trait analysis and modeling framework to investigate how plasticity in maturation and lysis rates influences viral growth, invasion, and coexistence. First, analysis of experimental viral trait data shows support for high maturation rate plasticity and intermediate lysis rate plasticity across virus-microbe pairs. Next, leveraging an eco-evolutionary model, we find that viruses with high maturation rate plasticity outcompete other viruses when nutrient inflow is high or variable but not when nutrient inflow is low and stable. In addition, we find that high lysis rate plasticity maximizes viral invasion fitness and growth when nutrient density is high and susceptible cell density is low, or when environmental conditions are highly variable. These findings suggest that while plasticity is evolutionarily advantageous in a broad range of environments, decoupling viral traits (including both maturation and lysis rates) from host metabolism can be advantageous, even if costly, in environments with low resource inflow. Finally, we find that variation in plasticity can facilitate coexistence between viral types given a shared, susceptible host population. Overall, these results highlight the adaptive value of (de)coupling viral traits from environmental and host state and suggest new directions for exploring the link between plasticity and diversity for virus-microbe communities.

title: Environmental and anthropogenic drivers of Culex pipiens biotype pipiens overwintering phenology
content: Background: Culex pipiens biotype pipiens (Cx. p. pipiens) is the primary vector of West Nile and Usutu viruses in Europe and overwinters as adult females in shelters, such as cellars. However, the localised environmental and anthropogenic drivers regulating adult behavioural plasticity and the timing of entry into and exit from these overwintering sites remain poorly understood. Methods: Over two consecutive winters (2023-2025) in Northwestern Germany, we monitored the overwintering period of Cx. p. pipiens across an urban-rural gradient using custom interception traps at the entry points (e.g. windows) of overwintering sites (e.g. cellars). We modelled the days of the year at which 10%, 50%, and 90% of cumulative populations entered or exited shelters (Q10, Q50, Q90), against satellite-derived land use and artificial light at night (ALAN), environmental temperature, indoor temperature and relative humidity, cumulative degree-days (CDD), and wing size. Results: In autumn, early entry (Q10) was delayed by 24.1{+/-}7.7 days in semi-urban allotment gardens compared to rural sites. At late entry (Q90), land use effects disappeared, and non-linear deviations from seasonal mean environmental temperatures shaped entry across land uses, while increasing ALAN delayed entry (0.64 days per unit increase). Entry probability increased with cumulative cooling degree-days below 18 {degrees}C. In spring, exit timing was independent of land use but driven by the indoor microclimate. Early exit (Q10) was advanced by higher minimum indoor temperatures (2.35 days per 1 {degrees}C) and higher minimum relative humidity (0.57 days per 1%), with additive land use effects driving earlier emergence in urban than in rural sites. Conversely, higher minimum relative humidity delayed late exit (Q90). Spring exit was best predicted by CDD above 0 {degrees}C. Finally, larger wing centroid size did not affect overwintering survival but delayed spring exit in Cx. p. pipiens. Conclusion: Adult Cx. p. pipiens exhibit behavioural plasticity, shortening their overwintering period in human-altered landscapes. Delayed autumn entry, paired with earlier spring exit driven by urban warming and low thermal thresholds, extends seasonal vector activity. Integrating these complex anthropogenic and microclimatic drivers into surveillance frameworks is vital for predicting early-season pathogen persistence and optimising targeted interventions. Keywords. Cx. pipiens biotype pipiens, phenology, overwintering, land use, artificial light at night, urban heat island

title: Asymmetric dispersal alters extinction dynamics in a two-patch metapopulation under an Allee effect
content: This paper investigates a two-patch metapopulation model with asymmetric dispersal, motivated by the directional transport of organisms between populations by aquatic currents. We consider a system of ordinary differential equations in which dispersal is population-conserving but directionally asymmetric, and each patch is subject to a strong Allee effect: Populations below a critical threshold decline toward extinction, whereas those above the threshold persist and approach their carrying capacities. We analytically prove the convergence of solutions to equilibria, and identify parameter regimes in which positive equilibria necessarily exist. We then numerically explore the one- and two-parameter steady-state bifurcation structures with respect to combinations of asymmetric dispersal rates and the Allee threshold. In particular, for sufficiently high Allee thresholds, we identify broad parameter regions in which the extinction equilibrium is the unique equilibrium of the system. These extinction regions arise from the interplay between asymmetric dispersal and the Allee effect and, notably, are absent in the corresponding population-conserving dispersal model without an Allee effect. Our results demonstrate that, through 'rescue' effects and emergent extinction regimes, directional dispersal can fundamentally help or hinder population persistence in systems subject to the Allee effect, highlighting important implications for the conservation and restoration of endangered species experiencing asymmetric dispersal.

title: Country‐Scale Isoscapes of Leaf Carbon and Nitrogen of Brazilian Tree Species
content:
Abstract
Stable carbon and nitrogen isotope compositions of plant leaves provide insights into interactions between vegetation and its environment. In C3 plants, preferential assimilation of 12C over 13C during photosynthesis produces a measurable foliar δ13C signal. Comparing foliar δ13C with atmospheric δ13C allows carbon isotope discrimination (Δ13C) to be quantified. Foliar δ15N, in turn, reflects nitrogen sources, transformations, and plant uptake. However, tropical regions remain underrepresented in global isotope data sets. Here, we developed country‐scale isoscapes of Δ13C and bulk foliar δ15N for C3 trees across Brazil at 1‐km resolution. We analyzed approximately 6,440 leaf samples grouped into 188 georeferenced clusters across major Brazilian biomes. Climate, soil, and vegetation covariates were used to perform regression kriging (RK) and random forest (RF) modeling approaches. RF outperformed RK for Δ13C and showed comparable performance for δ15N, yielding cross‐validated R2 values of 0.47 and 0.51, respectively. Key predictors of Δ13C included precipitation of the wettest quarter, aridity, vapor pressure, relative humidity, and soil pH. The most important predictors of foliar δ15N were mean annual precipitation, precipitation of the wettest month, potential evapotranspiration, relative humidity, and soil δ15N. The isoscapes reveal spatial gradients consistent with ecological and physiological expectations and constitute the first country‐scale framework for foliar isotope variation in Brazil. They provide spatial baselines for evaluating carbon─water interactions and nitrogen cycling in land‐surface and Earth system models, and may also support applications in wildlife forensics and the provenance assessment of plant‐derived products.

title: The Impact of Marasmius oreades Fairy Rings on Soil Physicochemical Properties and the Microbiome
content:
In their paper entitled ‘The impact of Marasmius oreades fairy rings on soil physicochemical properties and the microbiome’, van Zandvoort, Vonk, Tack and Johannesson* showed that the colonization of M. oreades caused a transient change in hydrophobicity, pH, nitroge and carbon. During colonization, M. oreades was dominant, decreasing fungal diversity and evenness and altering the fungal community composition. The bacterial diversity and evenness were not variable, but the bacterial community after colonization was significantly different from before colonization.

ABSTRACT
Fungal fairy rings are formed by a circular, underground, mycelial network growing radially outward and dying in the centre. We investigated how the fairy ring‐forming fungus Marasmius oreades interacts with its environment. We collected soil samples at four positions in nine fairy rings from three sites and analysed the physicochemical properties and microbiome. Sampling close to the fungal growth front allowed us to gain a fine‐scale perspective of the changes as M. oreades grew. We observed a consistently higher hydrophobicity and lower pH on the growth front and decreasing levels of total and organic carbon and total nitrogen from ahead to behind the growth front. The fungal richness and evenness were significantly lower on the growth front and the fungal community composition here was distinct, primarily due to the dominance of M. oreades. In contrast, we observed no differences in bacterial richness and evenness between positions. However, the bacterial community composition on and behind the growth front was different from that away and ahead of the growth front, suggesting that M. oreades causes a long‐term change in the bacterial community. Our results point to a significant role of M. oreades in shaping the heterogeneity and diversity of grassland soil ecosystems.

title: From Persistence to Prevention: A Holistic Review of Microplastics Sources, Impacts and Mitigation
content:
Microplastics move through soil, water, air, and plants, disrupting ecosystems and altering greenhouse gas dynamics. This review highlights their ecological and human health risks, oxidative stress, endocrine disruption, and toxicity while showcasing advances in detection and remediation, positioning microplastics as emerging climate‐influencing pollutants with direct implications for public health.

ABSTRACT
Microplastics (MPs) are present in terrestrial, aquatic, and atmospheric systems, causing environmental and several health issues. Their mobility and persistence link the two, allowing them to interface with ecosystems on several scales and are a tremendous target of ongoing research. MPs are formed as a by‐product of the biodegradation of plastics, as well as direct discharge from consumers and industry. Besides physical contamination, they also play roles as climate‐altering factors through the emission of greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, C2H4) during degradation and increased N2O emission by microbial‐climate interaction, controlling carbon cycling globally, thus affecting carbon sequestration by photosynthetic plants. The discovery of new techniques such as spectroscopy, thermal analysis, and microfluidics has increased surveillance in the various environmental media. On the other hand, protection approaches such as filtration, bio‐remediation, and adsorption by nanomaterials hold great promise. Human exposure to MPs can stem from inhalation, ingestion, and dermal uptake, and effects induced by exposure to MPs range from oxidative stress and inflammation to endocrine disruption and carcinogenic potential. The main aim of this review is to systematically compile all the current knowledge on microplastics origin, detection and removal strategies and their impact on human health and the environment.

title: Climate–trait interactions dominate vegetation light use efficiency distributions across China
content:
Climate–trait interactions dominate vegetation light use efficiency distributions across China
Yujie Wang, Mingzhu He, and Qian Zhang
Biogeosciences, 23, 8639–8654, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8639-2026, 2026
Light use efficiency (LUE) is a key parameter for estimating terrestrial carbon uptake, yet its spatiotemporal variations and drivers remain poorly understood, limiting the accuracy of LUE models. Through unraveling the critical role of climate-trait interactions to regulate LUE variations, our results provide direct suggestions to improve model performance and have potential implications for evaluating ecosystem functions and services, and helping regional-scale resource management.

title: Along‐Stream Changes and Seasonality in Denmark Strait Overflow Water Properties: Insights From Novel Oxygen Observations in the Irminger Sea
content:
Abstract
Denmark Strait Overflow Water (DSOW) is a key water mass transported by the lower limb of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation. DSOW facilitates the transmission of climate signals into the deep ocean, both directly from the Nordic Seas and indirectly from the Irminger Sea via entrainment. Here, we use new hydrographic observations and oxygen data from BGC‐Argo profiling floats and moored instruments along with a simple streamtube model to investigate along‐stream changes and seasonality in DSOW properties. The results suggest that the along‐stream changes in DSOW oxygen are consistent with mixing with entrained ambient waters. Novel year‐round moored oxygen measurements offshore of Cape Farewell, Greenland reveal seasonality in DSOW oxygen properties that is similar to the seasonality in DSOW salinity. We show that this observed seasonality likely reflects seasonality in the source waters upstream of the Denmark Strait and hypothesize that these anomalies can spread passively along the overflow pathway, as they have limited impact on density. This finding highlights the sensitivity of ventilation in the deep North Atlantic to changes in the water properties in the Nordic Seas, in contrast to previous studies.

title: Geochemical Partitioning Between Soft Tissues and Chitinous Tubes of Siboglinid Tubeworms as a Potential Indicator of Methane Flux
content:
Abstract
Fossil tubeworm tubes are routinely deployed to reconstruct ancient cold‐seep ecosystems, yet distinguishing biological signals from environmental overprints remains challenging. Here, we integrate carbon isotope (δ13C), trace‐element, and rare earth element (REE) data sets from soft tissues and serially sectioned chitinous tubes of Paraescarpia echinospica collected from two geologically distinct cold‐seep sites: the Ganquan Plateau (South China Sea) and the Wenhai seep (Okinawa Trough). Soft tissues from both sites exhibit nearly identical Post‐Archean Australian Shale (PAAS)‐normalized REE patterns, consistent with conserved thiotrophic symbiosis in this species. By contrast, the two specimens display substantial offsets in mean δ13C for both soft tissues (−24.8‰ at Ganquan Plateau and −34.7‰ at Wenhai) and chitinous tubes (−26.9‰ and −37.0‰, respectively). This isotopic divergence likely arises from variable mixing between seawater dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) and 13C‐depleted DIC sourced from methane, modulated by differences in local methane supply. The Wenhai tube preserves pronounced interfacial Fe–Mn–Co enrichment, stratified redox‐sensitive element accumulation, and REE fractionation changes, whereas the Ganquan Plateau tube records subdued geochemical variability. These intersite contrasts point to amplified redox cycling and porewater overprinting at Wenhai, consistent with elevated methane seepage intensity. This study establishes a modern reference framework for separating biological and environmental signals in tubeworm geochemistry and provides a testable baseline for assessing axial elemental zonation in chitinous tubes as a proxy for relative paleo‐seep activity.

title: High‐Resolution Ensemble Projections of Extreme Ocean Wave Events for the Chinese Marginal Seas Under Different Global Warming Levels
content:
Abstract
High‐resolution projections of extreme ocean waves are critical for understanding future coastal vulnerability, informing resilient infrastructure design, and mitigating the escalating risks posed by climate change to coastal communities and ecosystems. In this study, we investigated the high‐resolution projections of extreme ocean waves over the Bohai Sea, Yellow Sea and East China Sea (BYE) region under 1.5°C, 2°C, 3°C and 4°C global warming levels. The wave data were generated using the WAM wave model with a resolution of 0.1° driven by high‐resolution wind field data from six regional climate model simulations. A multivariate bias‐adjustment method based on the N‐dimensional probability density function transform is used to correct the raw simulated significant wave height and mean wave period. Results show that the mean intensity of extreme wave events in the BYE region will experience a significant increasing trend under future high warming levels, especially in the East China Sea, featuring high consistency among models. In contrast, the frequency of extreme wave events shows a decreasing trend with low agreement among models. Uncertainty of the extreme wave projections in the BYE is dominated by internal variability uncertainty (20%–90% of the total), with secondary contributions from model uncertainty; emission scenario uncertainty has the smallest influence.

title: A Pan‐Antarctic Observational Assessment of Eddy‐Flux Energy Partitioning
content:
Abstract
The Southern Ocean is a key component of the global climate system and ocean circulation. Processes along the Antarctic continental shelf and slope, including eddy‐driven heat fluxes and momentum exchanges, strongly influence sea‐ice formation and melt, dense water mass formation, interbasin connectivity, and the global meridional overturning circulation. This study explores records from 612 instruments deployed at 169 mooring sites, providing a consistent, circumpolar, observation‐based assessment of the spatial and temporal variability of eddy kinetic energy (EKE) and zonal and meridional eddy heat fluxes (ZHF, MHF) along the Antarctic margins. Based on vertically averaged estimates, eddy activity is consistently higher over the continental slope than over the continental shelf, with circum‐Antarctic sector‐mean EKE approximately 5 times larger and absolute ZHF and MHF typically amplified by an order of magnitude. Vertically averaged total ZHF is approximately 90% greater in magnitude than MHF along the shelf and 20% on the slope, indicating enhanced eddy efficiency in zonal heat transfer. Tidal variability dominates the EKE spectra along most of the Antarctic margin. Notably, the northwestern Ross Sea, near the Drygalski Trough, exhibits the highest eddy activity around Antarctica, with EKE and eddy heat fluxes approximately an order of magnitude greater than elsewhere. This circumpolar perspective reveals robust links between eddy activity, tidal variability and dense water formation that are not apparent in regional studies. Furthermore, the circumpolar eddy statistics presented here identify hotspots of enhanced eddy energy along the Antarctic margins and provide observational constraints to improve ocean and climate model predictions.

title: Evidence for Transmission Ratio Distortion at Major Histocompatibility Complex in a Sexually Monogamous Seabird
content:
ABSTRACT
Variations in the major histocompatibility complex (MHC), a cluster of genes with a key role in the adaptive immune response of vertebrates, have repeatedly been shown to be shaped by selection operating between individuals. In contrast, studies testing whether it can be shaped by selection operating within the pool of gametes produced by an individual are rare, although transmission ratio distortion (i.e., non‐random transmission of certain alleles) is observed for other genes in a wide range of taxa. In this study, we investigated transmission ratio distortion at MHC‐IIB genes in the black‐legged kittiwake, a sexually monogamous seabird. We tested whether MHC‐IIB diversity of the offspring and the probability for the offspring to carry the supertype ‘SUP6’ were higher than expected under random association of gametes. We tested whether these potential non‐random transmissions varied with sex and hatching‐order of the offspring because our previous studies have shown that the effects of MHC‐IIB diversity and ‘SUP6’ on fitness proxies can vary with these traits. We found that first‐hatched offspring had higher MHC‐IIB diversity than expected under random association of gametes. However, they did not inherit a combination of parental haplotypes with higher MHC‐IIB dissimilarity than expected or the more diverse maternal or paternal haplotype, suggesting that transmission ratio distortion for higher MHC‐IIB diversity might be due to differential embryo mortality. In addition, none of the chicks had higher probability to carry SUP6 than expected under random association of gametes. Our results suggest post‐copulatory selection for MHC‐IIB diversity in kittiwakes, and show that the hatching position of an offspring may influence its genetic traits.

title: Control of Sintering on the Maximum Size, Shape, and Orientation of Snow Dunes
content:
Abstract
Snow dunes are analyzed using a numerical model for snow transport that incorporates the effect of sintering. Under unidirectional winds and constant precipitation rates, snow dune fields reach steady state, exhibiting a transition from periodic barchanoid ridges to populations of barchans as cohesion increases. All of these dunes have a transverse orientation, with a maximum height that decreases as the square root of the mean sintering time. Below the minimum length scale for snow dune formation, in the limit of high sintering rate, small‐amplitude linear bedforms elongating in the transport direction emerge. These simulations reproduce the variety of shapes and orientations observed among snow dunes, suggesting that combination of fast sintering and limited snow supply is responsible for the ubiquity of longitudinal dunes in Antarctica. This study provides the basis for further research investigating how snow dune morphodynamics can constrain the time scale of snow consolidation processes.

title: From Flow to Fabric: Finite Strain and Fabric Development in the Earth's Inner Core Driven by Anisotropic Thermal Conductivity of Iron Crystals
content:
Abstract
Earth's inner core is seismically anisotropic with the fast axis aligned with the rotation vector. This property is attributed to crystallographic preferred orientation (CPO) of iron crystals. We previously showed that anisotropic thermal conductivity of iron crystals can generate large‐scale flow within the inner core through thermally driven buoyancy. Here, we quantify the finite strain induced by this flow and whether the deformation can explain observed seismic anisotropy. We model flow using the geodynamic code ASPECT and quantify the accumulated deformation using Lagrangian tracer particles. We relate finite strain to CPO development for iron aggregates with a viscoplastic self‐consistent formulation and find that the large‐scale flow can produce key features of the observed seismic anisotropy. However, thermal stratification in the inner core suppresses radial flow and significantly reduces strain accumulation. This suggests that CPO would form earlier in inner core evolution when stratification was weaker.

Mixing regimes of the world's lakes
content:
Abstract
Classifying lakes by mixing regime provides a framework for understanding their ecology, biogeochemistry, and impacts of global change. To assess and scale the climate warming impacts on lakes, it is imperative to know the current global distribution of lake mixing regimes. However, beyond a theorized schematic that was last updated by Lewis Jr. in 1983, we do not know how many lakes of each mixing regime there are in the world, nor how they are spatially distributed. Here, we present LakeMIX, a dataset of mixing regimes for ~ 1.4 million lakes in the world that are ≥ 0.1 km2. With these data, we conduct the first empirical assessment of global distributions and occurrences of lake mixing regimes and we compare our findings to Lewis' theoretical framework. Seven mixing regime types were distinguished with a deterministic, physically based model from satellite‐derived and re‐analysis data (2013–2021) of lake‐specific properties. We found that the world is dominated by small and shallow, cold polymictic lakes (58.9% of lakes), while deep, cold dimictic lakes comprise most (44.5%) of the global lake surface area. In mid‐ to low‐latitude regions, seasonally stratifying lakes are more abundant than shallow polymictic lakes (3.2% and 1.0% of all lakes, respectively). Cold amictic, cold monomictic, and warm dimictic lakes are rare (together, 0.3% of all lakes). LakeMIX fills a crucial spatial data gap in large‐scale limnological research, especially for the incorporation of small lakes and understudied geographies of remote regions. The data are openly available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.30698423.

title: A subtropical cyclopoid copepod can increase body size and maintain exoskeleton formation under ocean acidification and warming
content:
Abstract
Evidence is mounting that future marine ecosystems will be disrupted by ocean acidification and warming due to increasing concentrations of atmospheric CO2 and other greenhouse gases. One of the major concerns is the potential impact on zooplankton communities, which may influence the stability of food webs and energy flow in oceans. Since copepods are the most dominant group of zooplankton, we examined whether the subtropical cyclopoid copepod, Apocyclops royi, can optimize the performance of vital physiological processes, including food consumption, body growth, reproductive output, and exoskeleton formation, under ocean acidification (pH 7.8) and warming (ambient +4°C) across four generations. Compared to control conditions (pH 8.1, 22°C), we found that copepods consumed more food under ocean warming, possibly leading to the observed increase in fecundity. Body growth was also facilitated by ocean warming, which may be attributed to the increased chymotrypsin activity that can promote molting. While oxidative stress, represented by lipid peroxidation, was induced by ocean warming, copepods could counter this stress by boosting antioxidant capacity. Synthesis of astaxanthin in copepod exoskeletons was retarded by ocean acidification, but this adverse effect was mitigated by ocean warming. Overall, ocean warming exerted a stronger effect than ocean acidification on the health of copepods, while the transgenerational effect was not discernible. Our findings suggest that some copepod species may consume more food to obtain extra energy that supports various physiological processes under ocean acidification and warming so that their health, populations, and ecological contributions could be maintained in a future warmer, high‐CO2 world.

content:
An XBeach-informed machine-learning surrogate for rapid coastal flood prediction
Maria Emanuela Mihailov, Alina Spinu, Alexandru Cindescu, and Lucian Dutu
Ocean Sci., 22, 3863–3888, https://doi.org/10.5194/os-22-3863-2026, 2026
