We developed a fast computer tool to screen many storm scenarios along the Romanian Black Sea coast using local sea-level records, weather, wave and river data. The tool is very good at identifying where flooding is likely, but less precise for estimating the greatest water depths. It can help rank risky situations and guide where detailed simulations are needed.

title: Chinese hamster tissue and CHO cell transcriptomes reveal immortalization signatures and the factors driving lineage divergence
content: Chinese Hamster Ovary (CHO) cells dominate biotherapeutic manufacturing but still have a few limitations in post-translational modifications such as N-glycan branching, O-glycan core extension and inefficient protein folding/processing. It is yet unclear whether these CHO-specific traits reflect general Chinese hamster biology or arise specifically from cell line immortalization. We assembled a uniformly processed transcriptome compendium of 350 RNA-seq samples from 24 studies, integrating nine native Chinese hamster tissues with four CHO lineages (CHO-K1, CHO-S, CHO-DG44, CHO-DXB11). While CHO cells retain core proliferative and biosynthetic machinery when compared to Hamster tissues, it has undergone coordinated and selective loss of tissue-specific functions, and thus establishing these are immortalization-driven traits rather than general hamster-biology origin. Focused analysis of CHO cell lines further revealed that parental lineage and culture media as the dominant drivers of observed transcriptional heterogeneity where the cell identity is responsible for transcriptome variation in a higher proportion of genes. By integrating genome copy number or alternate promoter usage with gene expression data, we observed that while gene copy number variations contributions are almost negligible, alternate promoter usage governs the variation in about 20% of genes that showed cell line specific patterns while 60% had a buffering effect, indicating that additional, yet to be characterized regulatory layers drive CHO cell heterogeneity. Together, these findings establish a genomic and regulatory framework for understanding CHO lineage divergence, with direct implications for rational cell line selection and engineering in biotherapeutic manufacturing.

title: Cost-information trade-offs partially rationalize the feed-forward loop census
content: Gene transcription regulatory networks let cells encode an internal representation of their environment as patterns of protein expression. Among the thirteen connected directed subgraphs on three nodes, the feed-forward loop (FFL) is the one consistently over-represented in transcriptional networks relative to randomizations that preserve the node degrees, yet its eight structural variants occur very unequally: in Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae the C1 and I1 variants dominate and the other six are rare. We ask whether the trade-off between cost and information in these architectures can rationalize this asymmetry. Each variant is treated as a noisy channel from the environment to the output expression level, with a channel capacity obtained from the Lyapunov equation of the linearized chemical Langevin dynamics and a protein burden from the mean of the regulated proteins at steady state. The analytical capacity agrees with mutual information estimated from Gillespie simulations across families, gates, and Hill coefficients. We compare the eight variants on the Pareto frontier of the cost-information plane under four information measures and ten promoter logics. Two results follow. First, only C1, C3, I1, and I3 are ever Pareto winners within their family, while C2, C4, I2, and I4 never win, consistent with their rarity; C1 robustly dominates the coherent family, in agreement with the census. Second, no measure separates I1 from I3 by more than a few percentage points, and the measures disagree on which is ahead, so cost and information treat the two as nearly equivalent. In the census, by contrast, I1 outnumbers I3 by 21:1 in S. cerevisiae. Cost and information thus account for the exclusion of four variants and for the dominance of C1, but not for the dominance of I1, whose separation from I3 may require a measure of response timing, which our measures of the environmental level do not probe.

title: Maternal periconceptional nutrition is associated with the vaginal microbiome along pregnancy
content: The human vaginal microbiome has been repeatedly associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes, and therefore understanding lifestyle factors associated with it may provide insights into strategies for improving pregnancy and reproductive health. The periconceptional period is a critical time window in pregnancy, with nutrition seen as a key factor for pregnancy health. However, the associations between periconceptional nutrition and the vaginal microbiome along pregnancy remain underexplored. Using 280 vaginal microbiome samples from 101 women collected longitudinally throughout pregnancy, along with paired food frequency questionnaires targeting the periconceptional period, we characterized the associations between periconceptional diet, dietary supplementation, and the vaginal microbiome. We found that periconceptional dietary indices are not strongly associated with the vaginal microbiome during pregnancy. However, several dietary components are significantly associated with both Lactobacillus crispatus and Lactobacillus iners in the first trimester, and in opposite directions. Additionally, we identified several associations between consumption of periconceptional dietary supplements and the vaginal microbiome in the third trimester. Interestingly, an increase in taxa typically associated with vaginal dysbiosis, such as Sneathia and Megaphera, was associated with the intake of specific micronutrients. Among these micronutrients, copper and zinc were notable, as individuals reporting their supplementation had average intake levels that exceeded the recommended daily allowance. Overall, our findings reveal pregnancy-stage-specific associations of the human vaginal microbiome with periconceptional nutrition, and suggest the potential of specific nutrients to modulate the vaginal microbiome.

title: From Substrate to Short Chain Fatty Acids: An In Vitro Investigation of Bacterial Dynamics in the Porcine Colon using the Modified Hohenheim Gas Test
content: Background: Research on the development of pig colonic bacteria under in vitro conditions is limited. In this in vitro study, the modified Hohenheim Gas Test (modHGT) was used to improve the understanding of fermentation processes in the pig colon with respect to the underlying microbial community, in particular how different substrates modulate the microbial community structure during fermentation. Methods: Gas formation, short chain fatty acid (SCFA) production by HPLC, bacterial load by qPCR and bacterial community structure by 16S rDNA amplicon sequencing were assessed at 2, 4, 8 and 24 hours during the fermentation of wheat straw, inulin, sugar beet pulp and potato starch using pig feces as microbial inoculum. Results: The dominant phyla (Firmicutes, Bacteroidota, Proteobacteria) and genera observed were consistent with previous in vivo studies, but differences in abundance were found. Microbial activity varied significantly (p < 0.05) between substrates and time points, influencing gas formation and SCFA profiles (p < 0.05). Rapid shifts in bacterial communities within the first 2 hours highlight the strong substrate influence on fermentation dynamics. Conclusions: The modHGT is a valuable tool for advancing our understanding of the porcine gut microbiota. This method is accessible, requires minimal effort and is in line with animal welfare considerations. It has great potential to provide insights into functional aspects of the gut microbiota and host interactions in different (feeding) situations. Metabolic interdependencies, such as cross-feeding, influence microbial community structure and SCFA profiles. One approach to standardization could be the use of standardized microbiome reference communities, similar to human gut microbiota research. Future research needs to investigate the consequences of altering bacterial composition and its physiological functions and consequences.

title: NUP62 acts as T cell activation-dependent switch to regulate post nuclear import steps of HIV-1 replication in primary CD4 T cells
content: Resting CD4 T cells resist productive HIV-1 infection. T cell activation licenses replication, increases nuclear pore complex (NPC) density, and alters chromatin organization. Paradoxically, HIV-1 nuclear import is more efficient in resting than in activated CD4 T cells, despite lower NPC abundance. Using activation-neutral gene editing in primary human CD4 T cells, we show that T cell activation reshapes nucleoporin (NUP) contributions to infection. The FG-nucleoporin NUP62 switches from an inhibitor of HIV infection in resting cells to a dependency factor in activated cells. In resting cells, NUP62 depletion modestly increases nuclear import, shifts proviral integration away from transcriptionally active chromatin, and enhances viral transcript abundance and gene expression. In activated cells, NUP62 depletion leaves steps through integration unaffected but strongly reduces nascent viral transcripts and gene expression. T cell activation switches previously unrecognized post-nuclear-import functions of NUP62, uncoupling early and late steps of HIV-1 replication.

title: Colibactin-induced DNA damage activates cGAS-STING signaling that is amplified by mitochondrial DNA release
content: The microbiome-derived genotoxin colibactin induces oncogenic mutations that contribute to the development of colorectal cancer. Colibactin exposure also elicits inflammatory and senescence-associated responses. However, the cellular pathways that link colibactin-induced genotoxic stress to inflammation and senescence are poorly defined. Here, we show that colibactin causes cytoplasmic DNA accumulation and activates pro-inflammatory cGAS-STING signaling in human cells. Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of cGAS reduces colibactin-induced inflammatory gene expression and the accumulation of senescence-associated markers. We further show that these responses occur in two phases: an early response that is independent of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and a stronger late response that is amplified by mtDNA release. Inactivation of either cGAS or the mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization factor BAK suppresses cytoplasmic mtDNA accumulation and dampens late inflammatory signaling. Together, our data support a model in which colibactin-induced nuclear DNA damage initially activates cGAS-STING, which promotes BAK-dependent mtDNA release and thereby enhances inflammatory signaling. This work reveals a mechanism through which a clinically relevant microbial genotoxin reprograms host cell physiology and may contribute to the development or progression of colorectal cancer.

title: Retron-Eco9 ADP-ribosylates release factors to disrupt translation during phage infection
content: Retrons are a major form of anti-phage defense in bacteria, but how they provide defense remains incompletely understood. The most common retron effector is a predicted nucleoside 2'-deoxyribosyltransferase (NDT). Here, we demonstrated that the NDT of retron-Eco9 is, in fact, a protein histidine ADP-ribosyltransferase that associates with the bacterial ribosome through an interaction with the stalk proteins bL7/bL12. Through this interaction, the effector ADP-ribosylates translation release factors RF1 and RF2 adjacent to the conserved GGQ motifs that catalyze peptidyl-tRNA ester bond hydrolysis, resulting in increased stop codon readthrough and frameshifting. Using ribosome profiling, cryoEM, and in vitro reconstitution assays, we demonstrate that the modification of RF1 and RF2 severely disrupts translation in cells, leading to collided ribosomes at the 3' ends of transcripts, aberrant termination, and increased ribosome rescue. These disruptions to translation ultimately prevent phage replication and abort an infection. Although many defense systems block translation by degrading tRNA or mRNA, our results now demonstrate how post-translational modification of translation factors can also provide potent defense, while also revealing histidine ADP-ribosyltransferase activity as the biochemical basis of the largest class of retrons.

title: Modeling natural HIV-1 infection and immunopathogenesis in a lymphoid organ-chip
content: Secondary lymphoid organs are the principal sites of HIV-1 replication, immune dysfunction and reservoir persistence, yet physiologically relevant human models of this microenvironment remain limited. Here we show that a microfluidic lymphoid organ-chip supports productive HIV-1 replication without exogenous T cell activation or cytokine supplementation. All six HIV-1 strains tested, including three CXCR4-tropic (X4) and three CCR5-tropic (R5) viruses, replicated productively in the chip, whereas matched static three-dimensional cultures supported only three. Infection recapitulated key features of HIV-1 immunopathogenesis, including CD4 T cell depletion, a decreased CD4/CD8 ratio, loss of T follicular helper cells, and altered T cell turnover and activation. The chip also reproduced the greater pathogenicity of X4 over R5 HIV-1, concordant with observations in natural HIV-1 infection, and revealed previously unidentified divergent impacts of X4 and R5 strains on CD4 T cell proliferation and activation. Antiretroviral therapy rapidly suppressed HIV-1 replication, reduced reservoir size, and reversed infection-induced T cell phenotypic changes. The lymphoid organ-chip thus provides an immunocompetent, human relevant model in which HIV-1 infection and host immunity can be studied simultaneously.

title: Deciphering lung microbial EV pneumotypes in acute respiratory distress syndrome proteome wide
content: Background. Pneumotypes hold potential predictive value for pathogenesis, outcomes, and interventions. Lung microbiome releases extracellular vesicles (EVs). However, EV-derived pneumotypes in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) have not been studied yet. Objectives. We aimed to identify pneumotypes in ARDS patients by comprehensively profiling lung microbiome-released EV proteins in bronchioalveolar lavage fluid (BALF). Methods. We extracted EVs from 106 participants (57 cases and 49 healthy controls) enrolled in the ARDSNet and SPIROMICS clinical trials and subjected to nanoparticle liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) to create microbial metaproteomics. Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were identified by Wilcoxon rank-sum test, and spectral clustering of these DEPs was utilized to reveal patterns in microbial EV protein profiles. The association between pneumotypes and the disease was assessed. Pneumotype-associated DEPs were identified using logistic regression, and their functional annotation was performed based on the eggNOG 5 database. The taxonomy of lung microbes was determined at the species-level and ranked by biomass contributions. Results. Ninety DEPs were identified in ARDS lavage samples (53 upregulated and 37 downregulated) compared with healthy controls. There were five pneumotypes, namely, P1, P2, P3, P4, and P5, identified by clustering the differentially expressed microbial EV proteins. Few pneumotype-associated DEPs were shared among these pneumotypes and mainly correlated with ARDS etiology and organ functions. The significant difference in mortality was observed in P3 and P4 subtypes. In contrast, all patients in P1 and P5 subgroups survived. Patients in P2 and P3 groups experienced a significant reduction in both of central nervous system (CNS) failure-free days and the days without organ failure compared with other subgroups. Besides, patients in P3 and P4 exhibited a higher prevalence of baseline shock and hypertension, greater use of vasopressors or inotropes within the previous 24 hours, higher positive end-expiratory pressure during ventilation, and lower body temperature and hematocrit levels. Alpha and beta diversity analyses showed significant shifts in P2 patients. The taxonomy of the top-ranked microbes exhibited different pathogens in P2, P3, and P4. Conclusions. This study, for the first time, identified five EV expression patterns of lung microbiota in the BALF of ARDS patients. These intrinsically featured EV pneumotypes in the lung are associated with mortality, etiology, lung functions, medication administration, and disease severity in ARDS patients.

title: Beyond suppression: a stand-off effect of mitigation measure reduces seabird bycatch in pelagic longline fisheries
content: Bycatch in longline fisheries is one of the causes of population decline in albatrosses and other pelagic seabirds worldwide, and tori-lines and weighted branch lines are the mitigation measures most widely deployed to address this threat. Despite their widespread use, it remains unclear exactly how these devices reduce bycatch and whether combining them provides added protection beyond either device alone. Using experimental longline operations conducted in the western North Pacific with two albatross species commonly caught in the region, this study linked seabird attack behavior at the point of capture with the actual outcome of bycatch, revealing an overlooked mechanism. Deploying double tori-lines, rather than single, did more than reduce attacks near the vessel: it pushed birds away entirely, keeping them clear of baited hooks before capture could occur. Weighted branch lines, by contrast, reduced attacks but did not push birds away, and for one species even increased the likelihood that attacks occurred within reach of the vessel. This "stand-off effect" of a double tori-line, rather than attack suppression alone, was the strongest predictor of reduced bycatch, and its benefit did not simply add on top of the bycatch reduction by weighted branch lines. The two albatross species also responded differently to the same devices, reflecting differences in their foraging behavior. Conservation and fisheries managers designing bycatch mitigation programs should therefore evaluate candidate measures against the behavior of the seabird species actually exposed to local fishing grounds, rather than relying on standard specifications developed for different regions and species.

title: Buildings act as barriers to insects, decoupling the bacterial-dominated and insect-dominated phases of carcass decomposition
content: The dynamics of necrophagous insect communities and the decomposition of the cadavers they colonise can be modulated by ecological filtering limiting insect access. We examine how different degrees of confinement influence the decomposition of animal carcasses, their colonisation by necrophagous insects, and the link between these two processes. To this end, vertebrate carcasses were placed either outdoors or in sheds with open or closed windows in a replicated experiment. Over two weeks, decomposition and insect abundance were documented daily. The results indicate that increasing confinement altered insect-mediated decomposition processes, delaying the insect-dominated phase while leaving the bacterial-dominated phase unaffected. Thus, in indoor environments, a dissociation of the decomposition sequence normally observed outdoors was observed due to an increasing delay in the colonisation of most insects with increasing confinement. This indicates that buildings can act as ecological filters that structure the accessibility of carcasses to necrophagous insects. In addition, these findings suggest that cadaver decomposition in indoor environments follows a distinct trajectory, with direct consequences for postmortem interval estimations.

title: Biodiversity turnover in coastal marine eukaryotic plankton revealed by a 20-year metabarcoding time series
content: Long-term observations are essential to resolve how ecosystems respond to environmental variability, yet decadal-scale molecular time series of marine plankton communities remain rare. Here, we analysed a >20-year (2001-2023) high-frequency 18S rRNA gene (V9) metabarcoding time series of eukaryotic plankton from a coastal observatory in the Western English Channel. Community composition exhibited recurrent seasonal cycles driven primarily by seawater temperature and water column stratification. Superimposed on this seasonal baseline, we identified a pronounced but transient community shift between 2008 and 2011, characterised by reduced diversity, and distinct community structuring, indicating plankton ecosystem-wide biodiversity turnover. This period reflected marked community reorganisation, with potential declines in larger plankton taxa (including copepods and diatoms) and concurrent increases in picoeukaryotes and heterotrophic stramenopiles, consistent with a shift toward smaller-sized, microbial communities. While temperature explained much of the seasonal-scale variation, it did not account for the proposed biodiversity turnover. Instead, the shift was associated with negative phases of the North Atlantic Oscillation, implicating basin-scale climate forcing. Following 2011, communities returned to a state resembling earlier years, indicating a reversible, rather than persistent, change. These findings demonstrate that coastal plankton communities can undergo rapid, climate-driven but reversible biodiversity turnover that is not captured by seasonal dynamics alone and highlight the power of long-term metabarcoding time series to detect transient and recoverable ecologically significant community reorganisation.
